Title: Acting Governor BasSpeech to the Media
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: No: 2006 - 12 March 15, 2006 Dear Press Members, Pursuant to the Central Bank Law No. 1211, I was given the mandate of the Acting Governor by the Board, which met yesterday evening at the end of the business hours, to fill the vacancy in the Governors post due to the retirement of Mr. Sureyya Serdengecti. I would like to extend my gratitude to the Board of the Bank for their trust and kindness. I have been holding the Vice Governor position at the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey since October 2003. As you have been closely following, we have all together accomplished many achievements in recent years that will always be remembered as the turning points in our economic history. The first ones to come to mind are the removal of six zeros from our currency, the point we have reached with regard to transparency and accountability in monetary policy decision-making processes, and the transition to formal inflation targeting at the start of 2006. I could comfortably say that, as a result of these developments, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey has attained world standards in terms of independence, transparency and accountability, and become one of the most appreciated central banks of the world. Of course, the ultimate objective of these three principles is to achieve and maintain price stability. In 2006  the 75th anniversary of the establishment of our Bank, we can say with great pleasure that we have gone a long way on the road to price stability. Each and every member of the Bank has made significant contributions in this process. Dear Press Members, As you know, Mr. Sureyya Serdengecti, who played a critical role in the planning and management of disinflation process under the implicit inflation targeting regime implemented between 2002 and 2005, has retired as of yesterday evening. Among other members of the Executive Committee, Ms. Sedef Ayalp has retired as of 8 March 2006, and Prof. Fatih ozatay has submitted his petition for retirement to be effective as of 4 April 2006. Hence, Prof. ozatay will be able to participate in the Monetary Policy Committee meeting to be held on 23 March 2006. On behalf of myself and of the staff of the Central Bank, I would like to extend my most sincere gratitude, appreciation and respect to each of my colleagues. Distinguished members of the press, Being decision organs of the Bank, the Executive Committee needs the votes of at least three members to take a decision, and the Monetary Policy Committee needs the presence of at least five members to convene. While the appointment process is underway for the three very important positions vacated by retirement, it is necessary to ensure that the meetings are held and the decision-making mechanism operate without any interruptions. Therefore, Mr. Rifat Gunay, the Executive Director of Banking and Financial Institutions Department of the CBRT is appointed as the Acting Vice Governor as of 15 March 2006 for the Vice Governor position vacated by Ms. Sedef Ayalp by retirement, upon our recommendation and with the approval of State Minister Mr. Ali Babacan. Mr. Gunay will assume his duty as the Acting Vice Governor in the shortest time possible. You can have a copy of Mr. Gunays resume from the Communication Department. Dear Press Members, Our monetary policy will continue as detailed in The General Framework of Inflation Targeting Regime and Monetary and Exchange Rate Policy for 2006 announced in December 2005. Accordingly, we published our first Inflation Report, which contained the medium-term inflation expectations and a policy perspective, on 31 January 2006. Preparations are underway for the second Inflation Report that will be published on 28 April 2006. Meanwhile, we have been publishing another important communication instrument of the Bank, the Summary of the Monetary Policy Committee Decisions, every month since January 2006. The Monetary Policy Committee has started to make decisions by vote as of January 2006 as well. For the first time in Turkeys history, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey has set inflation targets for a three-year period jointly with the Government. These targets are: 5 percent for 2006; 4 percent for 2007 and 4 percent for 2008 and we have focused on achieving these targets. As you all know, we announced the uncertainty band as 2-percentage point around the target-consistent path for the year 2006. Hence, the accountability principle stated in the Article 42 of the Central Bank Law was applied concretely. The floating exchange rate regime is a sine qua non for inflation targeting. Therefore, our efforts for the widespread recognition of the risk awareness in the public and more frequent use of risk management principles and tools in both public and private sectors will continue under the floating exchange rate regime. In this framework, we have planned and started preparations of an international conference to be held in fall 2006 that will address the topics of dollarization and the resulting fear of float. I have the pleasure in expressing that the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey has taken many important steps in the past few years. The best examples of these steps include the re-denomination of Turkish Lira, the achievement of lowering inflation to single digits after a period of 30 years and the adoption of the inflation-targeting regime in order to reduce the inflation to the levels of price stability and to keep it there. Dear Press Members, I have a strong belief that every new step that we will make from now on will lead both the Central Bank and the Turkish Economy to a better footing compared to the previous position. Thank you for your participation.

Title: Speech of President Sreyya Serdengeti to the Parliamentary Plan and Budget Committee
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: CENTRAL BANK PRESENTATION OF THE PARLIAMENTARY PLAN AND BUDGET COMMITTEE KASIM 2001 Mr. Chairman, Distinguished Members of the Plan and Budget Commission, Today I will give you information about the monetary policy that our Central Bank has been implementing since the February 2001 crisis and the monetary policy that will be implemented in 2002 with the rest of 2001. For this purpose; First of all, I will briefly talk about the causes of the February crisis in our country and the monetary policy we implemented in March and April after the crisis. The third part of my speech will be the Transition to a Strong Economy Program and the monetary policy we implement in line with this program. Then we will dwell on the general state of the economy of our country; After talking about possible developments in the next period, I will end my speech by giving information about the inflation targeting regime that our Bank aims to implement in the last part of my speech. I. FEBRUARY CRISIS AND ITS CAUSES In terms of the Turkish economy, the year 2000 has significantly differed from previous years. For the first time, a stabilization program based on the exchange rate was introduced in December 1999. The medium-term objectives of the program are; reducing inflation to single digits at the end of a three-year period, reducing real interest rates to a reasonable level, ensuring more efficient use of the resources in the economy and increasing the growth potential of the economy. In the program, the main pillars of the program were the increase in the non-interest rate surplus with the tight fiscal policy, the acceleration of structural reforms and privatization, the income policy in line with the inflation target and the pre-determination of the exchange rate basket increase rate depending on the inflation target. Although the inflation targets foreseen in the program could not be reached in 2000, an important step was taken in the fight against inflation and inflation fell to the lowest level of the last 14 years. In addition, the public financing balance improved in 2000 and significant structural reforms were implemented. As a result of the decrease in exchange rate risk and the increase in the prediction opportunities of economic units, interest rates fell rapidly. This economic environment, on the one hand, encouraged capital inflows into the country and led banks to become more creditworthy, and on the other hand, stimulated domestic demand. Thus, the economy has entered the process of growth again. In addition to the decrease in interest rates, The specificity has also accelerated the renovation investments of private sector firms to increase productivity, and this phenomenon was another factor supporting the growth process in 2000. However, due to the revival in domestic demand and the rise in energy prices, especially crude oil, on the one hand, and the increase in the exchange rate on the other hand, the determination of the increase in the exchange rate according to the targeted inflation, while the fact that inflation realizations remain above the targeted inflation leads to the real appreciation of the Turkish lira; imports increased rapidly and the current account balance deteriorated. In addition, the depreciation of the euro against the US dollar in 2000 increased imports from European Union countries and led to the negative impact of exports to these countries. Thus, in 2000, the ratio of current account deficit to GDP increased to 4.8 percent. This is the first of the main reasons behind the failure of the program implemented in 2000 to achieve the desired results. The second root cause is the delays in privatization and structural reforms. In particular, the fact that the problems related to the banking system could not be solved before the start of the program constituted a significant obstacle. The situation that public banks are in need of short-term high borrowing has not been put an end to. Delays in structural reforms have led to increasing questioning of the sustainability of the programme in domestic and foreign markets since late August. This environment has increased uneasiness and adversely affected capital movements and interest rates. The limited scope of action of monetary board-like monetary policy in the face of the rise in interest rates has led to the deterioration of the financial situation of some banks that hold intensively government domestic debt securities in their portfolios, and at the end of this process, in the second half of November, insecurity in the financial markets has become extremely high. As a result, naturally, as in other countries that implement fixed or predictable exchange rate systems, a banking crisis has emerged, which has turned into a liquidity crisis. The third reason why the program does not give the desired results is that an "Additional Reserve Facility" to support foreign exchange reserves in the face of the negativities that may be seen in the program has not been available from the beginning of the program. The November crisis is also important in terms of showing the weak points of exchange rate-based stabilization programs. As seen in other similar stabilization programs, vulnerabilities in the banking system are subject to external shocks and negative expectations. The resulting developments eliminate the sustainability of the exchange rate regime. Studies examining the relationship between banking and currency crises show that within the framework of the fixed exchange rate regime, problems in the banking sector usually arise before the currency crisis and increase the severity of the crisis by creating a process that feeds each other. In other words, a central bank that implements a fixed or incremental rate of exchange rate policy is faced with two conflicting goals due to the need for liquidity resulting from weaknesses in the banking system. This central bank will either prefer to defend the exchange rate at the expense of the melting of its reserves and the uncontrolled rise of domestic interest rates in order to maintain the fixed increase rate exchange rate policy, which is one of the basic pillars of the current economic program, or it will prioritize the stabilization of the financial system and give up the defense of the exchange rate and leave liquidity to the system and declare the end of the applied program in a sense. Mr. Chairman, distinguished members, I would like to take this opportunity to emphasize one point in particular. What kind of exchange rate regime to implement is usually decided jointly by central banks and governments. The exchange rate policy to be implemented within the framework of this regime is the responsibility of the central banks. As a matter of fact, this understanding prevails both in the previous legal framework and in the new form of the Law on our Bank. That being the case, despite the increasing demand for foreign currency during the November crisis, it was unthinkable that the Central Bank would go for an extraordinary liquidity expansion that would lead to a further exacerbation of this demand and end the exchange rate regime applied. Such behavior would be tantamount to announcing the end of the applied exchange rate regime and therefore the program. The Central Bank acted with these constraints in mind during the November 2000 crisis. Considering that no contrary decision was made, efforts were made to maintain the current exchange rate regime and net foreign exchange sales of around USD 6 billion were made. As a result of these transactions, 3.9 quadrillion liras of liquidity was provided to the market between November 22 and November 30 through open market transactions in order to return the Turkish lira liquidity withdrawn from the market to the market. As a result of these developments, the restrictions placed by the program on the Central Bank's balance sheet have been exceeded and it has become necessary to revise these constraints. The "Additional Reserve Facility" provided by the IMF in December and the measures announced by the Government helped to overcome the November 2000 crisis. After the November crisis, two main problems emerged. First, the interest rates that rose with the crisis began to be much higher than the target of an increase in the exchange rate, despite the decline after the agreement reached with the IMF. In other words, there has been a significant mismatch between interest rates and the rate of exchange rate increase target. Second, the damage caused by the crisis to the financial structure of the banking system, especially the public banks, has increased the vulnerability of the system. When this incompatibility and increasing fragility, combined with the political tension that occurred before the Treasury auction in late February 2001, an atmosphere of panic was created in the markets that were in constant uneasiness, trust in the system was completely lost and on February 19, 2001, the Turkish lira faced a serious attack again. The demand for foreign exchange worth 7.6 billion a day on this date put significant pressure on the exchange rate. In order to remove this pressure, the Central Bank did not renew its repos, which were due the next day, and took back 6.1 billion of the currencies it had sold the day before as a result of purchase or cancellation transactions. However, the decreasing liquidity of the Turkish lira due to the sale of foreign currency as much as the difference has led to the aggravation of the problems of public banks, which are in need of excessive liquidity on a daily basis. Thus, the country's payments system is deadlocked, while on the other hand, the serious problem of confidence in the sustainability of the current exchange rate system has deepened. As a matter of fact, it was not possible to maintain the exchange rate regime and exchange rates were left to fluctuate on February 22. The point I wanted to underline here is that, as we have seen in other stabilization programs based on fixed or rate of increase, trying to defend the exchange rate under the conditions I have just mentioned would lead to the loss of all our reserves and would be a policy incompatible with the economic fundamentals at that moment. Regarding these discussions, I would like to dwell on two important points: First, it is impossible to restore lost confidence by replacing a fixed or growth rate fixed exchange rate regime that has collapsed with a crisis of confidence. If economic units no longer have confidence in the previous exchange rate regime, they have no reason to trust a similar exchange rate regime immediately afterward. Secondly, the increasing integration of international financial markets is a factor that complicates the implementation of the fixed exchange rate regime. It is no coincidence that in recent years many developing countries have abandoned the fixed exchange rate regime and switched to a floating exchange rate regime. In 1990, only the countries included in the definition of emerging markets were While 22 percent implemented a floating exchange rate regime, this rate reached 50 percent in 2001. Mr. President, distinguished members, I would now like to briefly touch upon the monetary policy pursued in the aftermath of the February 2001 crisis until the announcement of the Transition to a Strong Economy Program. II. MONETARY POLICY AFTER THE FEBRUARY CRISIS With the transition to the floating exchange rate regime, the problem of interest rate-exchange rate increase rate mismatch, which was the first of the two main problems that occurred after the November 2000 crisis, has disappeared. In this period, the Central Bank focused on solving the second fundamental problem. In other words, during the two months following the February 2001 crisis, the Central Bank prioritized the restoration of the payments system by meeting the market's liquidity needs. I would like to take this opportunity to highlight two key elements that eliminate the obstacles preventing the Central Bank from providing liquidity to the system. These two elements are completely overlooked by critics of the Central Bank's policies during the November crisis. First, with the introduction of a floating rate, there is no exchange rate level left to defend. In the first part of my speech, I went into the details of this point. Secondly, starting from December, some banks were included in the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (SDIF), thus beginning the process aimed at eliminating the "good bank-bad bank" distinction that had existed in the banking system before the November crisis. As of February 26, the Central Bank reduced the buying and selling quotations in the interbank money market; With its open market operations, it has mostly directed to providing resources to public banks and banks within the scope of SDIF through overnight quotation. Since mid-March, in addition to overnight funding through open market operations, futures funding has also been provided to the market. In this period, the Central Bank also went to the way of attracting excess liquidity in the market through the Repo and Reverse Repo Market at the ISE and the interbank money market at its own level when necessary, and also attracted excess liquidity through foreign exchange interventions that I will present in detail later. In addition, the Central Bank ensured that the financial system met its external obligations by providing the banking system with intensive foreign exchange deposits and providing foreign currency resources through foreign exchange interventions. At the end of March, in parallel with the delay in the announcement of the new stability program, the Central Bank started to implement multi-price auctions in the purchase and sale of foreign currency from the market in order to determine exchange rates in the market and to prevent excessive fluctuations. Mr. President, distinguished members, with your permission, in this part of my speech, I would like to talk about the Transition to a Strong Economy Program and the implementation of monetary policy within the framework of this program. III. STRONG ECONOMIC TRANSITION PROGRAM AND MONETARY POLICY The main objective of the new program is to ensure economic stability and to put our country in a sustainable growth process. Implementation of tight monetary and fiscal policies, implementation of structural reforms aimed at increasing economic efficiency and solving structural problems in the fields of banking and public finance, and strengthening social dialogue; are the cornerstones of the program. Structural reforms: Banking sector A number of measures have been taken regarding public banks. Rebuild these banks structuring processes were successfully completed, the governance structure in banks was improved, an independent joint board of directors consisting of experienced bank executives was formed to enable the decision-making process, fund management was made more effective, securities were given to these banks in exchange for duty losses, the necessary structure was established to prevent new duty losses and common interest was started to be applied to deposits. Undoubtedly, resolving the problems of the banks within the SDIF as soon as possible is important for the stability of the financial system and the reduction of the burden they impose on public finances. Therefore, within the SDIF, many measures have also been taken regarding banks. For these banks, a joint board of directors was established to cover banks other than Demirbank, securities were given to the SDIF by the Treasury and securities were given to these banks by the SDIF in order to meet their capital needs, and an action plan and timetable for the merger and sale procedures were put forward. The general approach of the program to the banks within the SDIF is to restructure these banks and ensure that they are sold, and if the sale fails to materialize, to liquidate these banks under the full guarantee declared for their deposits and other obligations. For the financing needs that will arise from the full guarantee given to the depositors and creditors of these banks, the guarantee has been further strengthened with the new regulation in the Banks Law, which allows the debt incurred in exchange for the Treasury papers given to the SDIF. The Transition to a Strong Economy Program also includes many regulations for private banks. The main purpose of these regulations is to ensure that banks have a healthy structure as soon as possible. For this purpose, banks were asked to strengthen their capital structures, legal infrastructure facilitating and encouraging bank mergers was provided, banks worked more efficiently by reducing their costs, and arrangements were made on restructuring of receivables and subsidiary and real estate sales. Structural reforms: Economic efficiency Many structural reforms have also been made to increase economic efficiency. Examples include the Turk Telekom Law, the professionalization of the board of directors of Turk Telekom, the adoption of the Sugar Law in the Turkish Grand National Assembly, the adoption of the Tobacco Law in the Turkish Grand National Assembly (vetoed by the President of the Republic, to be reintroduced to parliament), the constitutional amendment on International Arbitration, the Natural Gas Market Law, the Electricity Market Law and the Civil Aviation Law. Structural reforms: Fiscal policy and transparency Finally, I will give information about the structural reforms and the arrangements made in terms of fiscal policy and transparency. In order to strengthen fiscal policy and ensure its transparency, the completion of legal arrangements for the liquidation of 36 intra-budgetary and 6 extra-budgetary funds by 2002 in 2001, the adoption of new tax measures, the tax number system It is aimed to strengthen tax supervision by putting it into practice and to present the Public Debt Law to the Parliament. Another important objective is to ensure transparency and accountability in the process of resource allocation in the public sector, to prevent irrational interventions in a way that there will be no going back, to strengthen good governance and the fight against corruption, and to create the legal infrastructure of structural elements that will implement all these in an effective, flexible and transparent manner. Fiscal discipline The primary budget surplus target set by the program for the end of 2001 is a very ambitious target in terms of international criteria. From the point of view of the Central Bank, I would like to express with pleasure that it has become clear that this target will be achieved, even exceeded. Thanks to the structural reforms carried out, the possibility of implementing policies that disrupt the public sector balance and lack economic justifications has been reduced. However, I would like to underline one aspect of fiscal policy that we consider very important in this context: the quality of fiscal compliance. When we look at the experiences of other countries, we see that the fiscal adjustments that have a lasting and positive effect on expectations are especially the adjustments based on the decrease in current expenditures (wage, transfer and subsidy expenditures). On the other hand, it is observed that financial adjustment programs based on tax increases and decrease in investment expenditures are generally not permanent and do not have a positive effect on expectations. In the light of this experience, I would like to underline that in the realization of fiscal discipline, we should focus on measures to reduce current expenditures instead of focusing on tax increases and cuts in public investment expenditures. Monetary policy Within the framework of the Transition to a Strong Economy Program, the main objective of monetary policy is determined as controlling inflation and ensuring price stability by switching to inflation targeting when the necessary prerequisites are met. Since 22 February 2001, when the floating exchange rate regime was introduced, the exchange rate has ceased to function as a policy instrument that directs inflationary expectations to the targeted inflation rate. This situation caused the Central Bank situation to assume the role of a nominal anchor of the monetary base item. In monetary policy implementation, nominal anchors are used mainly for two reasons. These are the fact that economic units need easily understandable and observable sizes in their decision-making processes, and that the achievement of goals for the nominal anchor influences and coordinates expectations in the desired direction. The nominal anchors that can be used in monetary policy implementations are exchange rate, inflation and monetary magnitudes. The currency anchor was used in the 2000 program and was abandoned during the crisis for the reasons mentioned. In the inflation targeting regime, the targeted inflation rate emerges as the ideal nominal anchor for a central bank whose main objective is price stability. However, some of the prerequisites for the use of this anchor in our country have not yet been met. In light of these facts, the only nominal anchor we can use is to target at a certain level the rate of increase of the monetary base, which is a kind of anchor of monetary size. The monetary policy, the general framework of which was announced to the public on 15 May 2001, is based on this determination. The monetary base is the sum of the two items taken from the Central Bank's balance sheet, net internal assets and net external assets. In order not to lead to an inflationary monetary expansion, the implemented program imposes an upper limit on net internal assets and determines the base values that net international reserves, which constitute the basis of net external assets, can be taken for periodic changes. Mr. President, distinguished members, Within the framework of the new form of the law, the main purpose of the Central Bank is to ensure price stability. The main tool to be used towards this goal is short-term interest rates. In the implementation of monetary policy, developments at the level of the monetary base are compared with the targets set for the monetary base, in addition, the developments in the leading indicators of inflation, which I will mention later, are carefully examined and if an inflation-increasing development is foreseen as a result of this examination, necessary changes are made in short-term interest rates. In this context, the point I would like to underline is the fact that concerns about the sustainability of domestic debt make it difficult for the Central Bank to use short-term interest rates effectively. The changes made by the Central Bank in interest rates in the light of future inflationary developments may not show the expected effects due to the existence of concerns about the sustainability of domestic debt. This effectively fulfills the nominal anchor role of monetary policy in the economy. Because it fails to do so, it undermines the Central Bank's fight against inflation. In the light of this information, I would like to briefly give information about the changes made by the Central Bank in interest rates in July, August and September 2001. The Central Bank raised short-term interest rates in July, taking into account the developments observed in the Argentine economy that would adversely affect other emerging market economies and the danger of changing the inflation trend upwards through exchange rates due to the developments in the Turkish economy in the same period, which adversely affected expectations. Later, in a period when the intervention of the Central Bank has decreased to almost nothing, the foreign exchange market has come into equilibrium in line with its own internal dynamics, the current account surplus has increased, the developments that have stabilized the exchange rates at a certain level such as the signing of external credit agreements by the banks, the absence of internal demand pressure, the structural reforms carried out in our economy in domestic and foreign markets, the exchange rate regime, Argentina in terms of the monetary and fiscal policies being implemented In light of developments that would positively affect the inflationary trend, such as it becoming increasingly clear that it has significant differences compared to the economy, the Central Bank has lowered short-term interest rates three times, at the beginning, end of August and early September. Exchange rate policy As for exchange rate policy, at the beginning of May, the Central Bank announced that within the framework of the floating exchange rate regime, exchange rates would be formed according to the conditions of supply and demand in the market and would intervene in exchange rates only in extreme fluctuations. In addition, programmatic foreign exchange sales auctions were initiated to eliminate the effect of the use of internal financing for internal financing purposes from the additional external resources provided by the IMF to the Treasury within the framework of the program to increase the liquidity of the Turkish lira. One of the main reasons that led to the crises of November 2000-February 2001 was, as mentioned earlier, the disorders in the banking system. At the beginning of these disorders was a large amount of open positions carried by the system. This phenomenon put pressure on the exchange rate in the first months of the floating exchange rate regime. Mr. President, dear members, at this point, I would like to draw your attention to a very important issue regarding the exchange rate regime and dollarization. Many civil society organizations participated in the "Reputation for the Turkish Lira Campaign" three months ago to stop the dollarization process, which is a natural result of the fact that the economic foundations have been broken for many years, many programs aimed at eliminating this disorder have failed and the crises have shaken the trust in the policies implemented. The Campaign for the Recognition of the Turkish Lira, which has been widely echoed in the press and developed on the initiative of non-governmental organizations as it should be, is the most important reaction against dollarization in Turkey so far, although it has not been followed for now. Undoubtedly, it is not possible to get results only with the campaign without eliminating the root causes. However, if we look at why the reaction is in this period and in which environment, we can see important clues for the future. In fixed or predictable exchange rate regimes, as seen in many developing countries, foreign exchange controls are low and capital movements are free but stability cannot be achieved; then economic agents want to keep both their assets and liabilities in dollars. Because keeping their assets in dollars protects them against inflation, while borrowing foreign currency seems less costly than borrowing in domestic currency, since the exchange rate is predictable. Whenever risks are realized and countries switch to a floating exchange rate regime, after the initial devaluation, economic agents begin to be unable to manage their assets and liabilities, because the exchange rate is no longer predictable and there is a reaction to dollarization. Your long promise In short, it is not a coincidence that the back of dollarization cannot be broken in Argentina, where the Monetary Board regime is applied, but that there is a reaction against dollarization in countries that have switched to a floating exchange rate regime only after the transition to this regime. IV. GENERAL ECONOMIC SITUATION There are two main determinants of macroeconomic developments in 2001. First, the extremely high interest rates during the crises in November 2000 and February 2001 and the jump in the exchange rate after the February crisis deeply shook the banking system. In this environment, capital outflow abroad has begun. Banks have become unable to open new loans and have started to recall some of the loans they have opened before. Domestic demand has started to decrease in real terms due to both banks cutting consumer loans and increasing interest rates. Both phenomena have deeply affected the real sector. This earthquake in the real sector has led to the aggravation of the banks' non-performing credit problems and the further reduction of loans to the economy. The start of layoffs in the process has further reduced domestic demand. Thus, the economy began to contract, and the contraction was exacerbated because the process I have just outlined above was a self-sustaining process. Developments in industrial production underscore the extent of the contraction: Industrial production has shown a decreasing trend since February 2001 and contracted by 9.2 percent in September compared to the same period in 2000. In parallel, decreases in capacity utilization were observed. However, a significant improvement in the capacity utilization rate is observed from the summer months onwards. The economic contraction also affected the basic monetary magnitudes, with money in circulation decreasing by 6 percent in real terms in October compared to the same month of the previous year. On the other hand, the monetary size of M2Y Repo increased by 9.1 percent in real terms in October compared to the same month of the previous year due to the shift of economic units from Turkish lira investments to foreign currency investments and the depreciation of the TL. In order for the Transition to a Strong Economy Program to stop this negative trend, it would have to be able to turn the expectations into positive and thus the exchange rate would have stabilized and interest rates had to fall. However, in June and July 2001, especially the discussions within the framework of structural reforms and the developments in foreign markets, positive expectations prevented the implementation of the program at the level it deserved. As is known, although it is necessary to correct the economic foundations in order to achieve the desired results such as low inflation, rapid and sustainable growth, more equitable income distribution, it is not enough alone. Depending on whether economic expectations are positive or negative, the same economic fundamentals can produce very different economic results. Negative economic expectations not only caused movements in exchange rates to diverge from economic fundamentals in the summer months, but also raised interest rates as they increased perceived risks. This phenomenon has kept the debate on the sustainability of domestic borrowing on the agenda and narrowed the room for maneuver of monetary policy. Thus, the upward trend in the exchange rate did not stop and interest rates remained at high levels. This is the second determinant of macroeconomic developments. As a result of these developments, the economic contraction continued, and the inflation rate tended to exceed the initial estimates. The main reason for this jump in inflation is the high rate of increase in exchange rates. In parallel, the deterioration in inflationary expectations and public sector price adjustments were also factors that increased inflation. In contrast, wholesale prices, which were further affected by developments in public prices and exchange rates, rose by 81.4 percent in the same period. Secondly, the banking system's open position in foreign currency should be closed with the efforts of the Treasury and the Central Bank. Thirdly, by closing foreign exchange open positions, it is possible for the Central Bank's interventions in the foreign exchange market to decrease to a level that is almost non-existent, thus making it easier for economic units to get used to the floating exchange rate regime. Fourth, it is increasingly understood that the Argentine economy, which is experiencing adversities, and the Turkish economy are very different in terms of the economic policies implemented, especially the exchange rate regime. In this environment, banks are trying to renew their syndicated loans (from November 1 to 23). banks' external liabilities increased by a net 396.2 million). These positive developments have led to a fall in interest rates and a swing in the exchange rate around a certain level. Thus, the first signs of the longed-for stability in the financial markets have begun to form. However, the tragic events of September 11 led to high increases in interest rates and exchange rates within a few days, creating an upward trend in the exchange rate again. With the possibility of supporting the current program, which has a strong and consistent economic content, with a significant amount of new external resources, this negative trend has come to an end. Starting from mid-October, there was a downward trend in the exchange rate again, exchange rate volatility decreased again and there were significant decreases in interest rates. Mr. President, distinguished members, In the next part of my speech, after briefly touching on the expectations for the world and Turkish economy in 2002, I will talk about the basic conditions for the continuity of this positive trend. V. A LOOK AT THE FUTURE Export and tourism revenues and capital inflows, which are the basic pillars of our Transition to a Strong Economy Program, are likely to be affected by the negativities created by the September 11 attacks. Although the expected revival of the already recessionary world economy in 2002 may slow down somewhat, it is encouraging that the key economic indicators of many countries are more robust than in previous years and that central banks have responded to shocks in a coordinated manner. Nevertheless, the continuation of the contraction trend will reduce the external demand for our goods. It is estimated that the Turkish economy will start to grow again in 2002, especially due to the industrial and services sectors, and that GNP and GDP will grow by 4 percent. In this context, while the current account balance is expected to have a deficit of USD 1.9 billion in 2002, the primary budget surplus is estimated to be 5.7 percent and 6.5 percent of the GDP in 2001 and 2002, respectively, with the continuation of the tight fiscal policy. In order for our economy to enter a permanent growth process, it is of great importance that the positive developments in the financial markets continue. The prerequisite for maintaining the stability that has begun to form in the financial markets is to show the economic units that domestic borrowing is sustainable. Four basic conditions must be met for sustainability. First, a very significant non-interest budget surplus is planned in 2002. This must be accomplished. With the fulfillment of these four conditions, a decrease in interest rates and a stable course in the exchange rate will be observed. The stability that will be ensured by the fulfillment of the conditions I have mentioned so far means an environment in which residents will keep fewer and less foreign currency denominated financial assets in their portfolios. The fact that the foreign exchange deposit account has increased by only 5 percent to 40 billion dollars as of November 9, 2001 from the highest value it has reached last year shows that the depreciation of the TL has played an important role in the increase in the dollarization rate. In this context, it is thought that we will move towards a process in which the supply of foreign currency and the demand for the Turkish lira are gradually increasing. It is clear that the stability in the financial markets will be further strengthened in this process. Monetary policy undoubtedly has an important role in the creation of this process. In this context, in order to activate the nominal anchor task of the money base and strengthen the money program, the monetary base performance criterion, which was the benchmark target in the previous program, was translated. The monetary base, despite its generally accepted constraints, such as the difficulty of estimating and the fact that it is not completely under the control of the Central Bank, will be a highly effective and easily traceable size for the monetary program. Dear Chairman, Mr. Members, I find it useful to mention an economic fact that is very important and sometimes escapes attention. In every economy, the current inflation rate emerges as a result of what happened in the past. In other words, the cost and demand factors of the recent past and the expectations of the economic units determine the inflation rate in the current period with a certain delay. If the movements of these factors that determine the inflation rate in the current period continue in the future, there is no doubt that the inflation rate of the future will not be different from the current period and the past. On the contrary, if the probability that the past movements in the factors determining the inflation rate will not continue in the future and will be reversed is very strong, the probability that the inflation of the next period will gradually differ from the inflation of the current period will also be very strong. For this reason, central banks aiming at price stability evaluate the reasons behind the realizations in past and current inflation, examine the extent to which these reasons will be valid in the future and take their decisions according to the results of this examination. The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, in addition to the target set for the nominal anchor money base, shall also determine (i) the (ii) in international economic developments; (iii) inflationary expectations; (iv) total supply and demand; (v) at the exchange rate; (vi) the prices of goods and services under public control; (vii) Assessing the effects of developments in exports, imports and capital movements on the trend of general prices, it shall determine the monetary policy decisions to be taken in line with the main objective of achieving price stability and shall make the necessary changes in interest rates. One of the elements that will make the implementation of monetary policy even stronger in 2002 will be transparency. In addition, Monetary Policy and then Inflation Reports will be published periodically. In these reports, an analysis of the past and the current period will be made and some scenarios for the future will be created in the light of this analysis. Likewise, created under our new law, The Monetary Policy Committee will make statements that enlighten the public about monetary policy strategy and practices. Recent amendments to the Central Bank Act will also help efforts to ensure price stability. With this law, the Central Bank is prevented from making advances to the Treasury and public institutions and organizations, opening loans and purchasing the debt instruments issued by these institutions from the primary market. This principle, which is also in accordance with the Maastricht criteria, which are the economic criteria of the European Union, is also an extremely important independence principle in terms of preventing the printing of money without compensation. Mr. President, distinguished members, in the last part of my speech, I would like to dwell on the policy of "inflation targeting" that we intend to pass when the conditions arise. VI. MONEY TARGETING POLTKASININ CONCLUSIVE FRAMEWORK: INFLATION As the Central Bank, we announced to the public at the beginning of 2002 that the Inflation Targeting system would be introduced. However, in this process, both internal and external conjuncture prevented the formation of the necessary conditions for a successful inflation targeting. In the domestic conjuncture, the continued pressure of public finance on financial markets and the high level of inflation have revealed the need to postpone the transition to the inflation targeting system for a while. In the external conjuncture, especially after the terrorist attack on the United States, the uncertainty in the domestic and foreign financial markets was effective in this decision. Mr. President, dear members, the basic view adopted by central banks today is that a low and stable inflation rate is the basic condition for long-term economic growth, and that although the expansionary monetary policies implemented give positive results such as production increase and decreases in the unemployment rate in the short term, these gains gained in the short term cannot be maintained in the medium and long term. The short-term effects of expansionary monetary policy will not last long, and the economy will return to the rate of production and unemployment that existed before the implementation of expansionary monetary policy, with a higher inflation rate. In other words, a nominal There is no long-term relationship between money, which is variable, and production, which are real variables, and the unemployment rate. Although monetary authorities around the world apply different monetary policy strategies and use different tools, they have adopted the main objective of providing a low and stable inflation rate. The monetary policy strategy, which has increased in popularity in recent years and has yielded successful results, is the monetary policy targeting inflation. Under this practice, the monetary authority announces official inflation targets for future periods and declares that the achievement of these targets is the single most important goal for it. The Inflation Targeting Regime is a monetary policy framework in which the sole objective of the central bank is price stability and the inflation forecasts it creates within its own structure are determined as intermediate targets. Central banks that implement Inflation Targeting use all data that contains information about inflation except for variables such as monetary size and exchange rates when determining the policy instruments to achieve their publicly announced medium-term inflation target. It is no coincidence that inflation targeting has become widespread in many developed and developing countries. The application of inflation targeting reduces uncertainties on monetary policy and positively affects inflationary expectations to the extent that uncertainties decrease. In this context, an effective inflation targeting policy has an impact on social welfare through its channels that contribute to the development of long-term financial markets and reduce the frequency and severity of fluctuations in the conjuncture. When we look at the experiences of other countries, the inflation rates realized in the inflation targeting regime may vary from the targeted inflation rates. As it is known, the price index to be targeted by central banks may also be affected by variables outside the control of central banks. In countries where the inflation targeting regime is applied, central banks consider a number of factors that may explain deviations from the inflation target, starting from the fact that unexpected movements in these variables may prevent reaching the targeted inflation level. In this context, the CBRT aims to increase gradual increases in indirect taxes; increases in public prices that have an impact on inflation; fluctuations in oil and raw material prices in the world; fluctuations in agricultural production that may affect agricultural prices; unexpected natural disasters; as factors that may explain deviations from the inflation target. The Central Bank is in the process of completing many preparations for the transition to the Inflation Targeting regime in 2002 in the fields of legal, technical and public communication. When we look at the legal regulations, we see that one of the most important conditions of the Inflation Targeting regime, the condition that the main purpose of the Central Bank is price stability, is provided by the Central Bank Law that was changed in May. The law on the independence of the Central Bank, which is another prerequisite, is also a law on the independence of the instrument for the determination of policy instruments for the inflation target; both economic independence, which states that the Central Bank will not print money for free; as well as regulations on political independence, which set out the procedures for the appointment and dismissal of those who determine and implement monetary policy. Another feature of the Inflation Targeting regime is the increased transparency and accountability of the Central Bank. The changing law contains radical innovations in both areas. Technical preparations have also been made to transition to the inflation targeting regime. The Central Bank will make inflation forecasts based on a large data set using all variables related to inflation. In this context, in addition to the Economic Orientation Survey, which is used to obtain the WPI expectations of private manufacturing industry companies in the Central Bank's development of the information base, the collection of Inflation Expectation Survey data, which mainly aims to obtain the inflation, exchange rate and interest rate expectations of the financial sector twice a month, has also begun. In parallel, short- and medium-term forecast groups were established within the Central Bank to carry out inflation-related modeling studies. One of the most fundamental issues required by the Inflation Targeting regime is the Central Bank's increasing communication with the public. The Central Bank will inform the economic units about the decisions it takes, the objectives and results of monetary policy through periodic reports and other means of communication. This goal is also closely linked to the transparency and accountability of the Central Bank. The Inflation Targeting regime reduces uncertainties on monetary policy by means that the inflation target is a nominal anchor, flexibility against external shocks that will be brought about by independent monetary policy implementation, and a transparent money that increases communication with the public and tells the public what to do and for what purpose. It will provide many benefits to our country in terms of creating a policy framework. With the implementation of the inflation targeting regime in our country, positive developments such as the reduction of inflationary expectations, the decrease in the reflection of changes in the exchange rate on prices, and the facilitation of the sustainability of debt as a result of the decrease in interest rates will be observed. Inflation Targeting should be considered an important part of the overall economic program. In this context, the success of the Inflation Targeting application depends on its support with other economic policies. In short, the success of this regime depends first on some positive developments in the economy, for example, the stabilization of the exchange rate in the floating exchange rate regime and the reduction of its effect on inflation, the abandonment of the past inflation indexing system and the transition to future indexing, as well as the decrease in the dominance of the Treasury in the debt markets. In addition, ensuring fiscal discipline; financial deepening; The fact that the markets of goods and services are more flexible against relative price changes are also extremely important factors for the success of this regime.
