Title: Speech in Public Electronic Payment System Publicity Meeting
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Public Electronic Payment System (PEPS) Publicity Speech Erdem BAcI 13 April 2012, Ankara Honorable Deputy Prime Minister, Distinguished Minister, Esteemed Guests and Esteemed Members of the Press, Recent advancements in communication and information technologies have made it possible for money to move more fast and safely. The fact that money - the key object of the banking sector- - continues to function representatively in electronic environment has enabled the widespread and effective utilization of contemporary technological opportunities. This situation has given rise to the idea of electronic payment that ensures faster and risk-free transfer of money thanks to information technologies, and thus, the transition to electronic payment systems has gained momentum since the 90s. In this context, central banks have pioneered to establish national payment systems and their cross-border connections, after which a process of adjustment to global payment systems started. Developments and practices in payment systems as well as newly established standards have increased the roles and responsibilities of central banks with regard to ensuring stability in financial markets. Delayed payments, high intermediation costs and settlement risks are expected outcomes of an economy that lacks an effective payment system. In such a case, problems that emerge in a particular sector of an economy or financial system may rapidly spread to other sectors. As a result, systemic risks, which might interrupt the economic activity, may develop. The active role assumed by central banks in the design, operation and oversight of payment systems becomes more of an issue given the size of the global financial system. So following global trends in this field, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey cooperates with the Turkish financial system in order to improve and renew payment systems. . The Central Banks membership of the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS) of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) was finalized in 2009. In this platform, where key global principles and standards related to payment and settlement systems are set, Turkey is represented by the Central Bank, which is actively involved in studies conducted. 2 Moreover, as authorized by its Law, the Central Bank, considering the need for a regulation on general standards including all payment systems in Turkey, drew up a Draft Law on Payment Systems, which also complies with the European Union acquis, and the draft law has been shared with relevant institutions and agencies in order to hear their views. Once the draft law is addressed at the Grand National Assembly of Turkey as soon as possible after being revised in line with the views of the relevant institutions, an important step will have been taken in shaping the legal framework that conforms to EU acquis and international standards regarding payment systems. Distinguished Participants, On the back of recent developments in electronic payment systems, the public sectors effective cash management and understanding of high-caliber service provision, coupled with efforts to prevent the underground economy, have necessitated the processing of a large amount of public payments in the electronic environment. Developed country practices indicate that at the end of the 90s, the USA and the UK required public payments to be processed electronically. Accordingly, the US Treasury allowed social security payments and tax refunds, along with some other payments, to be made in the electronic environment in 1999. From 1972 to 2007, the Treasury Single Account system was functional in Turkey, whereby through the branches of Ziraat Bank, the accounting of domestic collections and payments of some accounting units of general budget was executed in a single account of the Treasury at the Ankara Branch of the Central Bank. As this system that was based on balancing the income and expenditures fell short of meeting needs in time, the Single Treasury Current Account system was adopted upon a protocol signed between the Central Bank, the Ministry of Finance and the Undersecretariat of Treasury on 31 July 2007. Thanks to the new system, the transfer of payments that are not in the daily cash program of the Treasury is prevented and collections can be transferred directly to the Treasury without being used for payments. 3 Today, we have completed a major phase of the Public Electronic Payment System (PEPS), the foundation of which was laid by the said protocol. It is owing to this system that the cash needs of general budget institutions can be transmitted, their needs can be met and their payment orders can be processed electronically. PEPS, which enables the processing of all these transactions automatically without the need for any external intervention, and can therefore be considered a global example, is an automation system that operates based on the end to end principle. In this system, every step of public payment transactions can be monitored by the Undersecretariat of Treasury and the Ministry of Finance simultaneously through the infrastructure prepared by the Central Bank using secure IT architecture. Within the system that became effective with 9 central accounting units in 2008, the payments of 19 central accounting units are successfully processed through the Central Bank. In figures, from the beginning of 2011 to the end of March 2012, the number of payment orders that were executed through PEPS was 399,775, amounting approximately to 179 billion Turkish liras. Distinguished Participants, Today, another important step is being taken for the countrywide expansion of the implementation of PEPS, the legal infrastructure of which was reshaped by the procedures and principles published on 18 June 2011, to cover payment transactions of provincial accounting units still successfully carried out by Ziraat Bank. With the utilization of PEPS by all accounting units throughout Turkey, all public payment transactions will be processed electronically and mistakes that may stem from manual operations will be minimized. Besides, in line with the e-government approach recently developed to increase efficiency in the public sector, PEPS is crucial for its positive contribution to environmental protection by preventing waste of paper and time. While delivering my concluding remarks, let me express my appreciation and gratitude to everyone who contributed to the development of the public electronic payment system in Turkey and made it a global model. Thank you for your attention. 4

Title: Speech of President Ba at the Conference on "Compulsory Provisions and Other Macro-Prudential Measures: Experiences of Developing Countries"
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Opening Speech of the Conference on "Compulsory Provisions and Other Macro-Prudential Measures: Experiences of Developing Countries" Erdem BACI 8 October 2012, Istanbul Dear Guests and Members of the Press, Welcome to the conference "Compulsory Reserves and Other Macro-Prudential Measures: Experiences of Developing Countries" organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. As you may recall, within the scope of financial stability, we hosted two more international conferences, one in November 2011 and the other in June 2012. In addition, in cooperation with the Banking Supervision and Regulation Board last month, "17. International Banking Supervisory Authorities" and last week we held the "Financial Systemic Risk" conferences with G-20 Presidency Mexico in Istanbul. All these events are of great importance in terms of providing the opportunity to listen to the opinions of respected economists from central banks and international organizations on policy frameworks that take into account financial stability, as well as providing platforms for the exchange of ideas between policymakers and academics. Dear Guests, Financial stability is known to be closely linked to growth and employment.1 The cost of preventing financial crises is much lower than the cost of these crises. Turkey's recent history is a good example of this. The financial crisis in Turkey in 2001 increased the public debt burden by 30 percentage points, and growth and employment were deeply affected. Since 2002, the focus has been on structural reforms to increase price stability, financial stability and productivity. The steps taken to reinforce financial stability enabled our country to recover rapidly after the deepening global economic crisis in 2008-2009 and to overcome the effects of the 2011-2012 European Debt Crisis with the least damage. In the recovery process after the global financial crisis, the Turkish economy faced a divergence in domestic and foreign demand, an increase in short-term capital inflows, a deterioration in the current account balance and rapid credit growth. 1 Reinhart, C. M. ve K. S. Rogoff. (2009). This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly. Princeton, NJ: Princeton Press; Taylor, A. (2012). The other main topic of the conference is the development of an operational framework that includes macro-prudential instruments in line with the aim of financial stability and the examination of country experiences and case studies in this context. In line with these two main themes, the first session will focus on how precautionary measures can support monetary policy in terms of softening demand fluctuations while maintaining financial stability and how mandatory reserves can be used as a credit policy instrument. In closing, I wish the conference to be beneficial and fruitful for all of us, and I would like to thank you for your participation and interest. 5

Title: OpeningSpeech of President Ba at the G20 Financial Systemic Risk Conference
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Opening Speech of the G-20 Conference titled "Financial Systemic Risk" Erdem BACI 27 September 2012, Istanbul 1 Dear Guests, Welcome to the "Financial Systemic Risk" conference organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey jointly with the G-20 Presidency Mexico. As you may recall, we hosted two more international conferences on the subject of financial stability, one in November 2011 and the other in June 2012. In addition, this month, in partnership with the Banking Supervision and Regulation Board, "17. International Conference of Banking Supervisors" conference in Istanbul. Again, next month, on October 8-9, we are hosting another international conference titled "Compulsory Provisions and Other Macro-Prudential Policies". Our aim with all these activities is to provide you with platforms where the exchange of ideas at both political and academic levels can reach a high level in this recent period when the issue of financial stability comes to the fore. We believe that this conference will provide you with the opportunity to listen to and exchange views with respected economists from central banks and international organizations. Dear Guests, Monitoring financial systemic risks is generally important for ensuring financial stability. Financial stability is known to have profound and long-lasting effects on growth and employment.1 The cost of preventing financial crises is much lower than the cost of those crises. Turkey's recent history is a good example of this. The financial crisis in Turkey in 2001 increased the public debt burden by 30 percentage points, and growth and employment were deeply affected. Since 2002, the focus has been on structural reforms to increase price stability, financial stability and productivity. In this way, the country's economic prosperity has increased rapidly, while at the same time the financial sector has gained a more resilient structure against external shocks. The steps taken to reinforce financial stability enabled our country to recover rapidly after the deepening global economic crisis in 2008-2009 and to overcome the effects of the 2011-2012 European Debt Crisis with the least damage. The most important leading indicator of financial crises is the excessive rapid increase in loans. Developing countries have learned about this relationship by experiencing it many times. Developed countries in 2008  1 Reinhart, Carmen M., and Kenneth S. Rogoff. (2009). This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly. Princeton, NJ: Princeton Press.; Taylor, A. (2012). The Great Leveraging, NBER Working Papers, No. 18290. 2 Thanks to the global crisis of 2009, he learned. The importance of systemic risk for financial stability and macro-prudential measures to mitigate it has led to a reconsideration of the framework between regulatory authorities and Central Banks. The introduction of the Dodd-Frank Act in the United States, the European Systemic Risk Board in Europe and similar new regulations in other countries aim to reduce systemic risk through macroprudential measures. Accordingly, the Financial Stability Committee was established in Turkey on 3 June 2011. In addition to the Central Bank, the committee includes the Undersecretariat of Treasury, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency, the Capital Markets Board, and the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund. The quantitative easing carried out by developed countries after the global financial crisis has led to extremely rapid credit expansion in our country as well as in other developing countries with sound economic foundations. The credit growth rate increased to over 35% by the end of 2010. It is aimed to reduce the loan growth rate to 25% by the end of 2011 and below 15% by the end of 2012. As a result of the macro-prudential measures taken, it is observed that these objectives have been achieved. As of today, the credit growth rate in Turkey has smoothly approached sustainable levels. As the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, we pursued a flexible monetary policy that will contribute to sustainable growth within the framework of measures aimed at price stability and financial stability in the post-crisis period. In order to limit the risks posed by capital flows, we have recently started to use tools such as a wide interest rate corridor and compulsory reserves in addition to the policy rate, and we have prevented excessive credit expansion with the contribution of other relevant institutions. I will briefly tell you about the positive results of this flexible monetary policy that we have implemented in tomorrow's panel in terms of both price stability and financial stability. Dear Participants, With your permission, I would like to continue my talk with the concept of systemic risk that gave the conference its name. As you know, over the last ten to fifteen years, financial systems around the world have become more and more complex and the interdependence between financial institutions has increased. Increasing correlations between asset prices in any part of the financial system 3 It has increased the likelihood that a nuisance looming in the region will expand and spread in a short time. This phenomenon is called contagiousness. The development of stabilizing measures against such systemic vulnerabilities has gained an important place in the research agenda of both policymakers and academia. In this context, our conference will be held in six sessions around four main themes. Accurate measurement of systemic risk, which is our primary goal, determines the scope of the first two sessions. A good understanding of the pros and cons of alternative risk indicators will increase the knowledge value of these indicators for policymakers; it will therefore allow for timely identification of vulnerabilities that could comprehensively affect the financial system. In this context, regulations that ensure that regulatory authorities have the necessary information at the earliest time will contribute to the timely and effective realization of financial oversight. These efforts, which require coordinated work and information sharing between different authorities, are among the issues that we expect to be addressed in the first two sessions. Another aim of our conference is to contribute to the understanding and development of macro-prudential measures implemented by different authorities. Today's third session will focus on the policies implemented within this framework; in particular, it aims to discuss the problems of designing capital and liquidity adequacy ratios. As highlighted at our recent conference on International Banking Supervisors, the general approaches proposed by the Basel Committee on these issues may differ from those in which the framework of countries' own financial systems will be taken into account. However, considering that the contagion effect may extend beyond the borders of the country in a crisis situation, it reveals the need for these differentiations to be discussed transparently within the framework of a globally consistent surveillance approach. In the third session, I hope that we will benefit from the views of valuable economists who have theoretical and practical knowledge on these issues. In the last three sessions of the conference, two interrelated themes will be emphasized. The first of these is the relationship of financial stability with monetary policy, and the second is the discussion of the country's experiences in this regard. Following the fourth session, where the relationship between measures for price stability and financial stability will be discussed, the fifth session will focus on the 4 It includes analyses of practical applications to be conveyed by the governors and vice-governors of the central banks of the countries. In the sixth and final session of the conference, there is a panel that aims to evaluate the 2008-2009 global crisis and the policies implemented after it from the perspective of developed countries. In addition to these six sessions, the conference will feature three highly valued invited speakers. Robert Engle on the first day of the conference; Markus K. Brunnermeier and Nobuhiro Kiyotaki will present on the second day. We hope that you will also benefit from these presentations by respected names of the academic world. In closing, I wish the conference to be beneficial and fruitful for all of us and thank you for your participation. 5

Title: Speech at the Conference on 'Inflation Targeting and Financial Stability'
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Conference on "Inflation Targeting and Financial Stability" Assoc. Prof. Dr. Erdem Bac President 25 November 2011 Istanbul Dear Guests, Welcome to our conference on "Inflation Targeting and Financial Stability". In this conference, you will have the opportunity to listen to valuable economists and respected academicians from central banks and international organizations. The main purpose of the conference is to evaluate the importance that central banks have recently given to financial stability and its reflections on monetary policies. The most important lesson we have learned from the country's experience is the fact that central banks' ignoring financial stability while formulating monetary policy leads to huge economic and social costs. As a matter of fact, this determination, which has found strong support in international platforms such as the G20, IMF and BIS, has raised many new questions about monetary policy implementation, as well as a new research agenda in terms of academic literature. The sessions at the conference are organized around two main interrelated themes. The first theme focuses on studies that will contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between the banking system and financial markets and the monetary transmission mechanism. The channels of transmission of macroprudential policy instruments such as reserve obligations, capital adequacy ratios, credit/value ratios, liquidity regulations and taxes stand out as the main elements of the first theme. The second main theme of the conference examines how to incorporate financial stability into monetary policy. We will have the opportunity to learn the practical applications on this issue more closely thanks to the country experiences that will be presented by the central bank governors and vice presidents of developing countries especially in the panel on the second day of the conference. 1 The dynamics that emerged after the global financial crisis brought with it increased responsibilities for financial stability for central banks. With the Law on the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, which was revised in our country in 2001, the Central Bank was tasked with taking measures to ensure stability in the financial system in addition to the main objective of price stability. Similarly, when we look at the examples of the world these days, we witness that financial stability is being added to the duties of central banks. Major examples of this are the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) established by the European Union, which is run by the European Central Bank, the Financial Policy Committee (FPC) established by the Bank of Great Britain, and the Office of Financial Stability Policy and Research established within the US Federal Reserve. In addition, in other countries that have implemented inflation targeting, such as Brazil, the Czech Republic, South Africa and Serbia, central banks have been tasked with contributing to financial stability. Dear Guests, After the global financial crisis we experienced in 2008-2009, the central banks of developed countries turned to "unconventional" monetary policy practices in order to control the crisis. We observe that many central banks in developed countries, especially in the USA, the UK and the European Union, have significantly increased their balance sheets by increasing liquidity by purchasing securities. Quantitative easing policies in developed countries have had important repercussions on developing countries. In Turkey, as in many developing countries, the volatility in short-term capital flows has been affected by macro financial 2 we have all witnessed how it can increase risks. For example, the extremely rapid credit expansion that has emerged since the last quarter of 2010 due to the effect of abundant and low-cost overseas financing can be considered as an example of these risks. In order to limit these risks in Turkey, we have started to use two more instruments in addition to the policy rate. These instruments are interest rate corridor and compulsory provisions. I will try to summarize in tomorrow's panel how we have used these new policy instruments over the past year, under what circumstances. However, in this short opening speech, I would like to state with pleasure that the measures we have taken to address the problem of excessive credit expansion have achieved their purpose. The annualized credit growth trend has decreased from levels above fifty percent at the end of last year to close to ten percent as of today. This is the most important development that will protect our country against external shocks in the current global conjuncture and should be continued in the coming period. The temporary risks to both inflation and the external balance will be possible thanks to the fact that the loans continue to grow at the reasonable levels they have reached. In order to achieve this goal, you can find the details of the implementation principles of the liquidity policy decided to be followed at the last Monetary Policy Committee meeting on our website in a moment. In closing, I would like to thank you for your participation and wish that the conference will be beneficial and productive for all of us. 3

Title: OpeningSpeech in Conference on Meeting on Global Financial Crisis: Lessons Learned and Experience Gained by ECO Member States
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic Of Turkey Meeting on Global Financial Crisis: Lessons Learned and Experience Gained by ECO Member States (Opening Remarks) Durmu Ylmaz Governor February 24, 2010 Tehran Distinguished Participants, It is a great pleasure and honor for me to be here among such a distinguished participants in Tehran. I would like to express my sincere thanks to the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) General Secretary for organizing this special event. The success of the economic policies of the member counties under the roof of the ECO depends on the formation of measures to increase trust and establishment of a close cooperation in economic and commercial areas. The closer cooperation and consultation among the ECO Member States, will contribute towards not only mitigating the gravity of the financial crisis on our states, but also accelerating economic and social progress, development and stability in the region. In this regard, our meeting is of great importance to develop a common approach to prepare necessary recommendations for regional cooperation to cope with the economic crisis and to take crucial steps to reduce the likelihood of future occurrences of such extremely costly events. Sharing the experiences of related countries that spread in a vast geography on economic and commercial is invaluable for all of us. Taking this opportunity, I would like to give you a brief picture of our policy implementations during the crisis. Dear Participants, The global crisis which erupted in developed markets and then spread across the world has continued to affect the global economic outlook. Data releases regarding the global financial system and economic activity displayed an ongoing recovery. However, budget deficits, especially in the developed economies, continue to rise, problems across credit markets linger, and employment remains in a precarious state. All suggesting that it would take a long time for the global economy to completely recover. Moreover, ongoing uncertainties regarding the exit strategies from unconventional fiscal and monetary stimulus continue to pose risks on the resilience of the recovery process. Turkey was not immune from the crisis like any other emerging country. Due to its high integration to global economy and financial markets, the headline growth of Turkey has deteriorated remarkably. But, I want to stress that neither price nor financial stability has been seriously jeopardized during this period. Turkey used to be one of the 1 emerging economies with historically high volatility and particular sensitivity to global risk perceptions throughout the 90s. However, this time the impact of the crisis has remained relatively limited due to our resilient financial system and prudent macro policies. Neither serious liquidity problems knocking on the door nor the domino-like fall of global finance giants was enough to agitate Turkish financial system. Turkey was the only country which did not have to intervene to its financial sector throughout this crisis across all the OECD countries. As is known, Turkey experienced a devastating crisis in 2001, which melted down one third of GDP and utterly crashed the banking system. Banking sector-restructuring plans along with the regulatory and supervisory reforms, at the cost of imposing a heavy burden on the public budget, were put into effect in the afterwards of 2001 crisis. These regulations have provided our banks with high level of capital adequacy, liquidity and deposit to loan ratios with mild leverage. In order to alleviate the short-term effects of the crisis on our real economy, a number of significant policy actions have been taken by Turkish Government and the Central Bank of Turkey. With the reversal of global developments fueling inflation, the Central Bank of Turkey took prompt action to cut interest rates and adopted a pioneer role among emerging markets. The policy rate cuts totaling 1025 basis points have alleviated the severity of the decline in economic activity. In this respect, we focused on containing potential adverse effects of global financial turmoil on the domestic economy without compromising our price stability objective. Additionally, borrowing and lending rate band has been gradually decreased in order to reduce fluctuations in the overnight interest rates. Also, liquidity need of the market in local currency has been provided in a timely fashion and at the required amount. We used our foreign exchange reserves primarily to support our banking system. We acted as a blind broker in the FX Market between the financial institutions and shouldered the counter party risk to facilitate the flow of FX liquidity in the system. Moreover, the maturity of the foreign exchange deposits borrowed by banks from the Central Bank in the FX Deposit Markets was extended and the lending rates were 2 slashed. Additional Turkish Lira (TL) and FX liquidity was provided to the banking system through reduction in the TL and FX required reserves ratios. Esteemed Participants, On the fiscal side, Turkish Government has introduced an investment incentive package, temporary tax cuts, a new credit guarantee scheme to lessen the gravity of the crisis, and launched a Medium Term Program (MTP) in September 2009, in order to reduce the adverse effects of the fiscal imbalances on expectations and to guide economic agents. The MTP aims to bring the public deficit and debt gradually down to reasonable levels by allowing the government to have a smaller share of resources, which is the key objective of the fiscal policy of between 2010 and 2012. The government is planning to introduce a fiscal rule by 2011 to ensure fiscal discipline, restrict the public debt-to-GDP ratio over the medium term and strengthen the institutional framework. According to the MTP, the legal framework for the fiscal rule would be completed until the end of the first quarter of 2010. These legal measures are intended to ensure a better management of expectations by enhancing the institutional framework of fiscal policy and its medium-to-long term predictability. Meanwhile, the fiscal rule aims to secure that the public sector budget deficit-to-GDP ratio is consistent with a sustainable public debt path over the medium-to-long term. To conclude my remarks, an outright depression in Turkish economy was prevented as a consequence of the measures taken by monetary and fiscal authorities. We expect that Turkey will be one of the countries that will emerge from the crisis relatively fast. I would like to extend my sincere gratitude to the ECO General Secretary for organizing this pleasant event by which we will have a chance to create a fruitful platform to exchange views, discuss ideas and share experiences. Thank you for your attention. 3

text: 81st ORDINARY GENERAL ASSEMBLY MEETING OPENING SPEECH ERDEM BAcI President 9 April 2013 Ankara Entrance 1. Dear Shareholders of our Bank, Distinguished Guests, Distinguished Members of the Press, 81st Anniversary of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey Welcome to the Ordinary General Assembly. 2. The ordinary General Assembly meetings of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey offer a good opportunity to evaluate the calendar year we have completed in terms of monetary policies. Today, I would like to summarize the important economic developments in the world and in Turkey in 2012 and the monetary policy measures taken. Global Financial Crisis and New Monetary Policy Needs Dear Guests, 3. The year 2012 we left behind was a year of very important developments in the world economy. The second round of the eurozone debt crisis took place in the first half of this year. During this period, the situation of major economies, especially Spain and Italy, led to the spread of concerns in Europe worldwide. The decisions taken by the European Central Bank in the second half of 2012 and the conditional unlimited liquidity support to the member states of the monetary union led to a degree of alleviation of concerns. In the US economy, which lagged behind expectations in the growth rate, the US Federal Reserve announced its third quantitative expansion package towards the end of 2012. Similarly, the Bank of Japan has increasingly continued its quantitative easing program. 4. In 2012, short-term interest rates in developed countries maintained historic lows below one percent, while long-term interest rates fell to unprecedented levels. When we ask what is the reason for this unprecedented level of quantitative easing, we are confronted with two answers. The first is the slowing economic growth rates, and the second is that there is no longer any room for movement in fiscal policy. 5. The extraordinary quantitative easing measures implemented by developed countries have also had a significant impact on developing countries. We can summarize these effects briefly under the heading of 'volatile capital flows'. Both the understanding that developing countries are more reliable and the interest rates in these countries 2 its higher levels have increased both the volume and volatility of short-term capital flows to these countries. We can call these two types of volatility financial instability in short. 10. In the years following the 2008 global crisis, developing countries sought to manage risks to financial stability by strengthening macroprudential policy frameworks while gradually lowering interest rates. This approach, pioneered by our country, is now becoming a global standard for developing countries. 11. We call this approach 'low interest, balanced growth'. Balanced growth means growth by taking into account the internal balance (i.e. price stability), the external balance (i.e. the balance of payments) and financial stability together. 12. I will continue my speech with the results we have obtained in the field of price stability. As you know, the main objective of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey is to ensure price stability. The Bank supports the Government's growth and employment policies, provided that it does not conflict with the aim of ensuring price stability. In December last year, we announced that we were maintaining the uncertainty range for 2013 at 2 percentage points around the 5 percent target. This range may be lower in some countries. We have two important volatility elements that determine this parameter. One is the volatility in the prices of unprocessed food and energy, and the other is the volatility in exchange rates and the rate of credit growth. If you look at the deviations from the inflation target in previous years, you will see that a significant part of them is due to excessive movements in the exchange rate. When there is a depreciation of more than 20 percent in 1 year, a deviation of 3 points can come to inflation due to a transitivity of 15 percent. This is quite a significant deviation. As the Central Bank reduces this volatility in the exchange rate, it will have taken a significant distance in terms of price stability. 15. I would like to underline here that thanks to this stabilization achieved in 2012, the risks related to the current account deficit have been significantly reduced and the initial conditions for a faster and more sustainable growth have been prepared for the period 2013-2015. 20. The next part of my speech summarizes the new policy approach we have developed and the new policy tools we have begun to use. Dear Guests, 21. The monetary policy pursued by our Central Bank in the past year is based on the new policy approach designed gradually since the end of 2010 in accordance with the conjuncture that emerged after the global crisis. In the aftermath of the global crisis, developed countries simultaneously implemented expansionary monetary policies and loose fiscal policies. These policies have led to an increase in liquidity on a global scale; This abundance of liquidity has had an effect on increasing risk appetite and capital movements in global financial markets. 22On the other hand, the recovery in global economic activity is still not at the desired level, although more than four years have passed since the onset of the crisis. The balance sheet correction process in both the United States and the Eurozone took longer than expected. The capacity of the fiscal policies implemented to support growth has been limited. This ongoing uncertainty has adversely affected the growth outlook and there has been a high rate of volatility in capital movements. Developing countries needed a flexible monetary policy approach that could react more quickly to shocks in the face of these developments, which may threaten macro-financial stability. 23. Increasing global liquidity as a result of overly expansionary monetary policies in developed countries is leading to the accumulation of risks in the financial systems of developing countries. 7 Causes. In other words, the increase in the volatility in capital flows on a global scale affects the economies that are the recipients of these flows through loans and fluctuations in the exchange rate. 24. First of all, when we examine the credit channel, we see that the balance sheets of the firm are positively affected by the exchange rate, which tends to appreciate with the increase in capital inflows. This positive effect may increase the risk appetite of the financial intermediary sector and cause a rapid increase in loans. An excessive increase in loans may cause systemic risks to become evident due to the increase in the risk of a decrease in credit quality and the fact that domestic demand grows faster than total income. Thus, excessive credit growth is suggested as a variable that precedes financial crises in economics literature. 25Similarly, an overvalued exchange rate can have a negative impact on macro-financial stability in an open economy by increasing systemic risk through many channels, especially the balance sheet channel, and disrupting the distribution of resources. In the light of these developments, it is important to reduce the volatility in capital flows in the new monetary policy designs of developing countries. In this context, the growth in loans and exchange rate developments should be closely monitored. The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and the New Monetary Policy Strategy Dear guests, 26. This economic conjuncture, where uncertainty is high, reveals that central banks should attach importance to financial stability as much as price stability. In this context, our Bank has established its new monetary policy design within a framework in which the inflation targeting strategy implemented since 2006 has been rearranged to include financial stability without compromising price stability. 8 Table1: Monetary Policy Framework OLD APPROACH NEW APPROACH OBJECTIVES Price Stability Price Stability Financial Stability INSTRUMENTS Policy Rate Structural Instruments Cyclical Instruments (Policy Rate, Liquidity Management, Interest Rate Corridor) 27. We have significantly improved our current policy framework in terms of objectives and means compared to the standard inflation targeting strategy implemented since 2006. In the new framework, price stability retains its main objective; in implementing monetary policy that is compatible with this end, we also take into account risks to financial stability more closely. This approach requires us to use more than one instrument in our monetary policy implementations, both structurally and cyclically. Accordingly, within the framework of monetary policy implementation in 2012, we actively used policy instruments such as interest rate corridor, effective liquidity management, reserve option mechanism. In this part of my talk, I would like to briefly tell you about two of these tools, the interest rate corridor and the reserve option mechanism. Interest Rate Corridor 28. One of the most important monetary policy tools that our Central Bank has used effectively in recent years to influence market interest rates and liquidity is the interest rate corridor. In the market, short-term liquidity can be provided to the banks in need by our bank during the day, and we can borrow from banks with a surplus fund in the overnight term. In this context, we can technically define the interest rate corridor as the area between the lending and borrowing interest of our Bank. Market 9 interest rates are formed within the interest rate corridor as a requirement of this operational structure. In the current structure, since we make our funding mainly through a weekly repo, we set the policy rate as the one-week repo funding rate. Both the policy interest rate and the interest rate corridor are reviewed and announced to the public at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting every month. 29. The interest rate corridor is used by many central banks that have traditionally implemented inflation targeting to prevent market rates from deviating significantly from the policy rate. In this context, the interest rate corridor, which is defined as a symmetrical and generally unchanging narrow band around the policy rate, assumes a passive role within the framework of liquidity management. In the new monetary policy approach pursued by our Bank, the interest rate corridor is used as an active tool. If deemed necessary, the interest rate corridor, the width of which can be adjusted by our bank, can be created in an asymmetrical way around the policy rate. With this structure, the interest rate corridor can be used as a monetary policy tool that can react quickly and flexibly to volatility in short-term capital movements and have an impact on credit growth. Reserve Option Mechanism 30. The reserve option mechanism, which is the second instrument I will mention, has recently been developed and started to be used by our Bank as a new monetary policy instrument aimed at reducing the negative effects of the increase in volatility in capital movements on macroeconomic and financial stability. With this design, we enable banks to voluntarily maintain additional foreign exchange and gold reserves by allowing them to keep a part of their Turkish lira required reserves in foreign currency and gold. We define a reserve option ratio to determine the extent to which this opportunity can be used. If the unit is the foreign currency or gold equivalent that can be established per Turkish lira mandatory provision, we determine it with the reserve option coefficient. 31. With the implementation of the reserve option mechanism, we expect that the ability of banks to adjust the foreign exchange reserves they hold at our Central Bank according to changes in external financing conditions will reduce the volatility caused by capital flows on exchange rates and loans. Also reserve option 10 mechanism, we anticipate that it will also contribute to the introduction of gold under the pillow to the economy. 32The reserve option mechanism is designed in such a way that banks internally adjust their reserve option utilization rates in response to external shocks. Therefore, this mechanism, which can be considered as a kind of automatic stabilizer, allows each bank to make the most appropriate choice in line with its own constraints. In these aspects, we can say that the reserve option mechanism is a more effective tool compared to other instruments used in foreign exchange liquidity management. However, we will also be able to use the reserve option mechanism as a cyclical tool to adapt to permanent changes in internal and external financing conditions when deemed necessary. The opportunities provided through the reserve option mechanism also positively affect our Bank's foreign exchange and gold reserves. Title: Speech at Instituto De Empresa Business School
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic Of Turkey IE Business School Speech Durmu Ylmaz Governor April 6, 2010 Madrid Distinguished Guests, First of all, let me express my pleasure to be here today to address such a distinguished audience in this prestigious school. I have prepared a short speech for this occasion, which will last about 20 minutes. Then, I will be happy to answer your questions. The main focus of my remarks covers the recent recovery in global economic activity and the main risks in this process. I will pay a special attention to fiscal policies and sustainability of fiscal measures. As a part of my speech, I also plan to discuss the recent noteworthy experience of the Turkish economy, a period when fiscal discipline generated expansionary impact on economic activity. Dear Guests, As you may all agree, we are witnessing green shoots around the globe, led by emerging market economies. The recovery process is supported by monetary and fiscal measures of unprecedented scale in advanced economies, as well as positive contribution from inventory adjustments and strong pick-up in demand in developing countries, especially in Asia. However, even though the recovery is under way, financial crisis has casted a long shadow on global economy. Where do the main risks lie? 1. First, households accumulated significant amount of debt during pre-crisis period, beyond their ability to repay out of current income. The ongoing uncertainty and lack of risk appetite may induce households to further reduce their debt through increased 1 precautionary savings, causing a substantial and prolonged slowdown in consumer spending. 2. Second, in comparison to typical business cycles, the pace of recovery in employment has been extraordinarily slow, which raises the question of whether the output and employment relationship has shifted. Indeed, unemployment rate have reacted much stronger to change in output during this crisis. Unemployment rates may stay elevated for a long time and turn out to be structural. This may hinder a strong rebound in private consumption. 3. Third, there has been no meaningful acceleration in bank credits. Given the dismal outlook for demand and unemployment, credit losses still pose a significant threat due to poor loan quality. Also, toxic assets in balance sheets have not cleaned up and underwritten yet, leaving many banks in need of new capital injections. 4. Last but not least, there comes the question of fiscal sustainability. The crisis has prompted large government interventions, both to restore confidence in the financial system and to contain the fallout of the crisis on the real economy. A sharp deterioration of investor confidence over fiscal sustainability is a looming danger threatening the future of global economy. 2 Ladies and Gentlemen, Let me further elaborate on my last point. During the second half of 2008, as concerns over global growth were heightening, decision makers realized that monetary policy might not be sufficient to avert a sharp contraction in output. Therefore, many countries launched fiscal stimulus packages of extraordinary magnitude. We can put these fiscal measures in two groups. First group of packages surfaced in the initial phase of the crisis to prevent meltdown of financial system. Hundreds of billions of US dollars were spent to support financial institutions that faced severe liquidity problems and to rescue the ones on the brink of bankruptcy. While bank recapitalization packages and government guarantees arguably prevented the collapse of the financial system, they were insufficient to lift the economic activity up in the short term. As the global crisis spread from financial sector to real economy, second group of packages came into forefront. The main goal of these packages was to compensate the severe contraction in demand caused by dwindling investment and consumption spending of the private sector. The amounts involved with these interventions have been extraordinarily large. As of June 2009, the ratio of fiscal packages to GDP has reached 38 percent in England, 24 percent in Japan and 13 percent in US and the Eurozone. The public guarantees extended to financial institutions and liquidity supports of Central Banks are not included in these figures. 3 These measures, together with contraction in economic activity raised budget deficits and public debt in both advanced and emerging economies. The economic contraction led to a reduction in tax revenues, while the decline in employment caused the payment of social security premiums to fall and unemployment benefits to rise. In recent months, the cost of protection against sovereign default has increased noticeably in several countries, mostly in Euro area. Concerns over high level of fiscal debt have been voiced in other parts of the world as well. It is clear that huge public sector imbalances have the potential to further deteriorate and constitute a major risk to the global financial system and sustainable economic growth. There are at least three ways in which, concerns over fiscal sustainability could thwart current and future economic growth. 1. First and foremost, in case the public deficits absorb an increasing proportion of national saving, sharp rise in long-term interest rates may lead to the crowding out of the private sector. 2. Second, financial markets may lose their faith on the sustainability of fiscal deficits and force a sudden adjustment by governments. This may lead to early exit from expansionary policies and the evaporation of public demand, which has been the engine of growth in most advanced economies. 3. Third, commercial banks could tighten lending standards if they were to suffer losses on their government bond holdings which in turn lead to a sudden, unexpected steepening of the yield curve. If market participants were to suspect about asset quality of the banks, the cost of funds would increase even without any change in other market 4 rates. Besides, any further deterioration of corporate and household financial balance sheets coming from collapse of economic growth prospects may also induce banks to restrict their lending. All in all, fiscal imbalances  either through higher interest rates or through a rise in expected loan losses  could very well result in a second dip in global economic activity. Distinguished Guests, Having laid the groundwork for the crucial role of confidence in public finances and sustainability of fiscal policies, in the second part of my speech, I will focus on the Turkish economy and discuss our experience. Turkey used to be one of the emerging economies with historically high volatility and particular sensitivity to global risk perceptions throughout the 90s. However, this time the impact of the crisis has remained relatively limited due to the resilience of our financial system and prudent macro policies. Of course, the growth rate has dropped sharply, but neither price nor financial stability has been seriously jeopardized during this period. In fact, Turkey was the only country among emerging market economies that end up with higher credit rating than pre-crisis level. How did the Turkish economy withstand the devastating impact of this global crisis? High and persistent inflation rates and towering public deficits were the main characteristics of the Turkish economy for almost 30 years until 2001. Throughout the 70s and early 80s, monetization of deficits was the primary choice of governments. In the second part of 1980s, domestic borrowings assumed the role of the favorite instrument in public finance. 5 Since the savings rate in Turkey was quite low, the size of financial markets was not sufficient to finance the needs of both the public and private sector. This led to very high interest rates and hindered the emergence of a typical banking system, serving the needs of households and firms. In early 90s, with the liberalization of capital flows, local banks relied heavily on short term external funding in foreign currency and financed the public deficit through government bonds. The appetite of public sector for new funding was relentless. The interest rates hovered around 20 to 30 percent, in real terms; the financial sector became extremely sensitive to swings in risk appetite due to short term FX positions; and inflation rate hovered around 70-80 percent. Soaring deficits and significant debt-to-GDP ratios imposed unreasonable costs on the economy. Due to fiscal dominance, the risk premium and fragility of Turkish economy happened to be a key concern, especially for the foreign investors. It is needless to point out that the fundamentals of the Turkish economy were not sustainable. Finally, we experienced a severe crisis in 2001. Overnight interest rate climbed to 6,200 percent, the local currency depreciated against the dollar by 36 percent within two days, economic activity contracted sharply, unemployment rate soared, many banks collapsed, a huge IMF rescue package was needed to rescue the economy and even larger rescue package by the government (equivalent of one third of our GDP) was put into action to rescue the financial system. 6 2001 crisis was a turning point for Turkish economy. Steps were taken to restructure the dynamics of the economy based on sustainable public finance, price stability, and high growth rates led by productivity and private sector. Furthermore, persistent distortions in the economy were removed and a sound financial system was restored. Hence three main factors of success were prudent fiscal and monetary policies, rapid structural reforms implemented without compromise, excuses or delays, and a comprehensive restructuring of once corrupted, inefficient and insolvent financial sector that aims at bringing the banking practices in line with the international standards. Disciplined fiscal policy has been the cornerstone of the program, allowing lower debt ratios, declining real interest rates and disinflation. Ambitious fiscal targets were set for primary surplus, as high as 5 percent of GDP. These targets have been almost totally achieved year after year. Between 2003 and 2007, the realization of primary surplus stood around 4.8 percent of GDP. Public debts positive response to sound fiscal policies was swift. Thanks to high primary surpluses, budget deficit to GDP ratio fell sharply from over 10 percent in 2002 to less than one percent in 2008. Subsequently, debt to GDP ratio dropped from 73 percent in 2002 to 39 percent in 2008. Besides; maturity, interest rate and currency composition of the debt stock also improved significantly. It is quite clear that having primary surplus of this magnitude was an enormous sacrifice for the society, but it worked. Fiscal consolidation, high primary surplus, and reduction in interest rates have encouraged private capital formation, building the foundation for sustainable growth. 7 Moreover, the risk premium came down with the decline in public borrowing as well. Hence a virtuous cycle formed; primary surplus causing a decline in public borrowing requirement, which diminishes roll over ratios resulting in significantly lower interest rates that cut back public spending and hence alleviates further fiscal consolidation. Of course there were also other pillars of the restructuring program that played a major role in normalization of the Turkish economy. Central Bank independence, implicit inflation targeting regime and floating exchange rates, more robust and comprehensive legal and institutional framework for better regulation and supervision of the financial system, restrictions on excessive risk taking by banks with the introduction of heavy personal liability of bank owners and top managers, strict limits on FX short positions and high standards for capital adequacy ratios were just a few highlights of the radical transformation that the Turkish economy has gone through since 2001. In summary, what many countries have experienced today had already been experienced in Turkey in the aftermath of the 2001 crisis at the cost of imposing a heavy burden on the public budget. Distinguished Guests, Fiscal discipline in public sector and consequent reduction in public debt during the pre-crisis period in Turkey have provided some room for fiscal stimulus unlike the previous crises. Turkey was able to implement stimulus package towards the real sector by cutting taxes and increasing public expenditures. Also, the tax cuts in certain items have stimulated demand instantly and pushed GDP up in second quarter of 2009. In accordance with the global trend, Turkeys public sector budget deficit 8 increased in 2009, pushing the debt-to-GDP ratio 6 percentage points higher to 45 percent, still well below the Maastricht criteria. This global crisis has proved the importance of reducing policy uncertainty and managing expectations. Announcement of credible medium term frameworks is critical in stabilizing the risk perceptions and reinforce the confidence on sustainability of fiscal policies. To that end, Turkish government announced a Medium Term Program (MTP) in September 2009. The MTP presents a comprehensive framework of policy actions to halt the rise in public debt-to-GDP ratio in 2010 and trim it down gradually in subsequent years. In addition, the government is also planning to introduce a fiscal rule to ensure fiscal discipline, limit the public debt-to-GDP ratio over the long term and strengthen the institutional framework. The legal structure of the fiscal rule is expected to be completed in mid-2010. These legal measures are intended to ensure a better management of expectations by enhancing the institutional framework of fiscal policy and its medium to long term predictability. Thanks to fiscal discipline and the resilience of the financial system, the Central Bank of Turkey was able to take prompt action to cut interest rates and adopted a pioneer role among emerging markets. The policy rate cuts totaling 1025 basis points have alleviated the severity of the decline in economic activity without compromising our price stability objective. 9 Distinguished Guests, To conclude my remarks; I believe the main challenge for policy makers in the near future would be unwinding the massive stimuli and support mechanisms that have been introduced to "prevent another Great Depression". The timing of the exit strategies should be evaluated thoroughly. One should always consider the risk that that, expansionary fiscal packages may undermine the sustainability of public finances going forward. Therefore, it is imperative to provide a credible medium term framework that explains how to control the sharp rise in public debt. This will help private consumption and investment recover and take over the role of fiscal stimulus. We should always keep in mind that fiscal discipline is not a goal by itself, but some sort of social contract between the people and the government to raise social welfare, ensure social harmony and build trust in government. The Turkish experience that I shared with you today may shed some light on continuing debates about the importance of implementing fiscal discipline in a timely manner to manage expectations and risk perceptions in times of crisis. Thank you for your attention. 10

Title: Speech on "Price Stability for Growth, Employment and Exports"
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey PRICE STABILITY FOR GROWTH, EMPLOYMENT AND EXPORTS Durmu Ylmaz, President 8 November 2007, Ankara PRICE STABILITY FOR GROWTH, EMPLOYMENT AND EXPORTS  Price stability refers to a low inflation rate to the extent that economic units do not need to take into account in their decisions on investment, consumption and saving. Stable prices are the cornerstone of a well-functioning market economy.  The consequences of the failure to ensure price stability, in other words, the attrition caused by inflation in the economic and social spheres, have been experienced very clearly in our country. The inability to distinguish relative price changes in decision-making processes, the inability to efficiently invest domestic resources and turn to non-productive areas, the establishment of the habit of indexing the past rather than looking to the future in the decision-making processes of individuals, the weakening of the competitiveness of the economy in foreign markets and the restriction of access to foreign capital markets, the decrease in long-term foreign capital inflow, the shortness of maturities in money and credit markets and financial the shallow structure of markets is the result of high and chronic inflation.  The growth rate we observed in the 1980s, which was achieved with high inflation, was not continuous, but was replaced by higher inflation rates, unstable and low-rate growth. What is necessary for our country is to make the gains we have achieved after 2001 permanent and to make growth sustainable. As in the whole world, the money and exchange rate received by the Central Bank in our country policy decisions affect the entire economy. Therefore, in these decisions, the Central Bank considers the economic situation as a whole throughout the country. Price stability is not at the expense of anything, especially growth. On the contrary, it is a prerequisite for sustainable growth. The greatest contribution that the Central Bank has made and will make to sustainable growth and employment growth is realized within the framework of the aim of ensuring and maintaining price stability.  It is also of great importance to follow a fiscal policy in line with monetary policy in ensuring price stability. The quality of fiscal adjustment is extremely important both in terms of combating inflation and in terms of the permanence of the high growth rate.  Bringing interest and exchange rate policies to the forefront causes structural reforms, which are prerequisites for sustainable and high growth, to be overshadowed. 4 WHERE ARE WE IN THE PRICE STABILITY TARGET? INFLATION DEVELOPMENTS IN TURKEY AND IN THE WORLD  While inflation in Turkey decreased compared to the end of 2006, it started to increase in other developing countries since the 2nd quarter of 2007. The upward trend is especially pronounced in Eastern European countries and China.  The increase in the prices of energy and commodities, especially food, can be considered as the increase in inflation in the world and the increasing domestic demand due to the high growth rate.  In Turkey, despite supply-induced shocks in food production, the general trend in inflation is downward, which is even more pronounced in non-food price movements. Title: Speech at the Competition Authority
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey COMPETITION & PRICE STABILITY Durmu Ylmaz President 10 February 2010, Ankara Dear Guests, First of all, I would like to thank the Competition Authority, which has made significant contributions to the formation of market economy conditions in our country with its work so far, for its invitations. One of the sine qua non conditions of price stability is that the pricing mechanism in the markets of goods and services operates according to the rules of full competition. In this context, I would like to emphasize that one of the most important stakeholders of the Central Bank in achieving inflation targets is the Competition Authority. Increasing the welfare level of our country depends on the increase in the share we receive from the added value created in the world. In the globalization environment we are in and in an open economy, it becomes imperative that we have a production structure that can produce the goods and services demanded by the world markets at the lowest price and with the highest quality. The cornerstone of this economic structure is the distribution and use of the country's resources among the sectors in the most effective and efficient way. In free market economies, the use of resources in the production of which goods and services, and in what quantity, is determined by the price mechanism that Adam Smith describes as the "invisible hand" and which is essentially an accumulation of knowledge and information. Prices act as a signal that enables communication between consumers and producers, transforming the preferences of millions of consumers and producers into a digital set of information in a virtual auction. The fact that these signals deliver the right information, at the right time and completely to the decision makers makes it necessary to ensure a fully competitive environment in the markets. There are a number of prerequisites for the establishment of an effective competitive environment in an economy. Ensuring macroeconomic stability, liberalizing foreign trade, facilitating the entry and exit of firms into sectors including foreign-owned firms, reducing taxes and similar public obligations, establishing an effective regulation-supervision structure, preventing informality, preventing transparency and monopolistic behaviors by developing a regulatory and supervisory institutional structure, ensuring transparency in the procurement of public goods and services, and an effective justice The establishment of the system is at the top of the list of regulations required for the establishment of the competitive environment. 1 Significant progress has been made in these areas in the recent past. Reducing the inflation rate to single-digit levels, stabilizing financial markets, reducing the debt burden of the public are just a few of the advances made in the field of macroeconomic stability. The liberalization process in foreign trade was completed with the regulations put into place to ensure compliance with the World Trade Organization legislation and the Customs Union that entered into force in 1996. Effective and independent regulation and supervision mechanisms have been established and put into operation both in the financial sector and in markets such as energy. On the other hand, as a result of the structural arrangements carried out in the micro field, significant progress has been made in issues such as the period of establishing a new company, the registration of property, the execution of contracts and the payment of taxes. The results of the Doing Business Report conducted by the World Bank confirm the progress made in these areas. However, there are steps that need to be taken in front of us. For example, one of the issues that shows the importance of competition policy for the Central Bank is the informal economy. As it is known, when employment is taken as a basis, the informality rate in our country is close to 50 percent. Informality prevents companies from reaching the most appropriate production scale and consequently producing at the lowest level of unit costs. Companies that cannot reach the lowest unit cost scale price their products at a relatively high level. One of the factors that cause informality is the financial burdens of being in the register. Companies do not want to expand their scale in order to stay out of the register, are reluctant to use bank loans, and delay the renewal of their technological structures due to lack of financing. On the other hand, companies that try to continue their activities within the register lose their competitive power and have difficulty in increasing their scale in the face of competitors who benefit from a number of advantages brought by being out of the register. Companies that are exposed to such unfair competition at home cannot find resources for the branding and research and development expenditures they need to make in order to compete with their competitors abroad and our exports are limited to relatively low value-added products. Another issue that we need to focus on is the pricing behaviors in the food sector, in free market conditions and in a fully competitive environment. 2 is to ensure that it happens. As you know, food products have a very high share of 28 percent in the Consumer Price Index. The recent developments in food prices constitute an important source of uncertainty on both the inflation outlook and inflation forecasts. The analyses carried out within the Central Bank show that the size of the fluctuations in unprocessed food price inflation is high and that factors other than seasonality are at the forefront of this volatility. Considering that the supply-side shocks in the food sector are not unique to our country and are mostly experienced on a global scale, I think it is necessary to carefully examine why food prices in our country exhibit a higher volatility compared to other European countries. Intermediary costs in the food sector and the inadequacy of the competitive environment play an important role in explaining the volatility and unhealthy price formations in the food market. Especially in products such as fruits and vegetables, the length of the distribution chains from the producer to the final consumer can exacerbate the reflections of the shocks on the economy on inflation by affecting the pricing behavior at each stage. This situation points to the importance of structural adjustments on the way to price stability. In this context, it is of great importance to complete the preparations for the law on the regulation of vegetable and fruit trade, which has been going on for a long time, and to achieve the targeted objectives in practice. In this way, the volatility in food prices will be reduced and competitive price formation in the sector will be ensured. Although cheap labor force and competitive exchange rates that will provide cost advantages to our companies are important in increasing our exports, they do not seem to be sufficient for our companies to take place as important actors in international markets in today's conditions. In addition to the difficulty of competing with China and India on the cost of labor, it is inevitable that the Turkish Lira will appreciate to some extent with the increasing confidence in our economy and the improvement in the macroeconomic field. In this context, it is necessary to increase the number of qualified manpower in our country, to have a corporate structure open to innovations and to have a structure that demands and produces technology in our industry. To this end, the decisive implementation of well-designed microeconomic reforms is of paramount importance. 3 Undoubtedly, competition policy constitutes one of the most fundamental parts of these reforms. One pillar of a well-designed competition policy is to encourage the entry of new firms equipped with the latest technology and corporate structure into the markets. The other pillar is to make it easier for companies that have become cumbersome and have difficulty in adapting to change to leave the market. With the emerging competitive environment, companies will begin to allocate more resources to activities focused on increasing productivity and enriching the product pattern. It is clear that today the ability to access information, to produce knowledge and to use knowledge has gained great importance. In such an environment, companies that closely follow the changes in consumer preference, have a flexible organizational structure, are institutionalized, prone to cooperation with other companies and research units, and create resource allocation plans with a long-term perspective and targeting increasing production capacity will continue to exist in the global competitive environment. Dear Listeners, To summarize, although important steps have been taken to establish an effective competitive environment in the Turkish economy recently, there are many reforms and regulations that need to be made. In the post-crisis period, it is of great importance that the momentum achieved by our country in the macroeconomic field is supported by structural reforms at the micro level. In this context, it is important to develop policies aimed at improving the competitive environment by going beyond general practices and taking into account the elements in sub-distinctions and the interactions between these elements. Undoubtedly, part of these policies is information sharing and cooperation between public institutions. Among these institutions, naturally, there are also the Competition Authority and the Central Bank. Strengthening the relations between the relevant institutions, including these two institutions, is of great importance for price stability for the Central Bank and for achieving a higher level of prosperity for our country. In closing, I would like to reiterate my belief that the Competition Authority will contribute increasingly to the prosperity of our country in the coming years. I greet you all with respect and thank those who contributed to the organization of this organization. 4
