Title: Speech at the Press Conference of the TL Symbol Contest
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: "TL Icon Contest" Press Conference Assoc. Prof. Dr. Erdem Bac President 1 March 2012 Ankara Mr. Prime Minister, Distinguished Guests and Distinguished Members of Our Press; Welcome to the meeting organized by our Bank where we will introduce the symbol of the Turkish lira. On behalf of myself and my institution, I greet you all with respect. As a result of the disciplined fiscal, monetary and financial sector policies implemented in our country since 2002, the period of chronic high inflation that lasted for more than thirty years ended in 2004 and price stability came to the forefront. As a result of the macroeconomic stability achieved in our country, as the first stage of the monetary reform in 2005, six zeros were removed from our currency and the "New Turkish Lira" banknotes and coins were put into circulation. As the second stage of the monetary reform, the phrase "New" was removed from our currency and the original and traditional name of our money, "Turkish Lira", was returned. The Turkish lira and the New Turkish lira banknotes and coins remained in circulation throughout 2009, after which the New Turkish lira banknotes and coins were removed from circulation without any problems as of January 1, 2010. Dear Guests, Our Bank's Law mandates our Bank to "take the necessary measures to protect the internal and external value of the Turkish lira together with the Government." In accordance with this task, a symbol was needed in order to strengthen the reputation of the Turkish lira and to increase its awareness in the world, and the "TL Symbol Competition" was organized to determine a symbol that could represent the Turkish lira in an understandable, original, aesthetic, easy to write by hand and memorable way. The idea of the "TL Symbol Competition" was first included in our Bank's 2011-2015 Strategic Plan as "to determine a symbol for the promotion of the Turkish lira in our country and in the world". After the conditions were determined, the opening of the competition was announced to the public on September 8, 2011. Our citizens showed great interest in the competition and a total of 8,362 applications were made to our Bank within the competition calendar. As a result of the work of the evaluation jury, which was convened many times during the competition process, the seven finalist designs were presented to the management of our Bank. Reflected in these seven finalized designs are seen. 1 As a result of a rigorous evaluation process, the management of our Bank determined the work that was deemed worthy of the first prize and the three works that were deemed worthy of the incentive award among these seven designs. You are seeing these designs reflected right now. The top design awarded the first prize belongs to Mr. Tulay Lale. The three designs in the lower row that were deemed worthy of the incentive award belong to Mr. Hamdi Akgozlu, Mr. ozlem ozkal and Mr. Huseyin Artuk, respectively, starting from the left. The award-winning design owners will be invited to the General Assembly of our Bank to be held in April and their certificates will be presented to them. Dear Guests, On the reflection, you see the symbols of the major currencies in the world. Now you can see the symbol determined for our Turkish lira on the reflection. When the competition was announced, with the relevant provision of the TL Icon Competition Specification, we were entitled to make changes on the design that was awarded the first prize. In this context, in line with the recommendations of the Bank's management, the first selected design has been placed on a geometrically aesthetic basis with the work of our Bank's graphic designers. In addition to the work on the widespread and secure implementation of the icon in different operating systems on personal computers and smart mobile devices, 2 The fact that it required time caused the date of this meeting, where we introduced our Turkish lira symbol, to be moved forward by a week. In line with the principles adopted by the management of our Bank, while determining the symbol of our currency, two distinctive features of the Turkish lira and the Turkish economy were brought to the forefront. These are: "trust" and "value rising in stability".  The similarity of the symbol to the anchor is the means of storing the value of the Turkish lira it emphasizes that it has "become a safe haven".  The fact that the parallel lines are inclined upwards means that the Turkish lira and Turkey symbolizes the "steadily rising value" of the economy. Dear Guests, Now I would like to briefly tell you about the technical features of our icon. From the lowest point of the icon there is a 90-degree circle arc to the right. Also the parallel lines of the letter "t" have an upward slope of 20 degrees. The parallel line on top is bounded by the outer wall of the circle. Most of the shapes that look pleasing to the eye in nature are in harmony with the "golden ratio". From the way the apple kernels are located to the spiral shape of the seashell; from the human body to the star on the Turkish flag; many aesthetic images are known to be compatible with the golden ratio. Many artists and architects in history have created their works that are pleasing to the eye by using golden ratios. The ratio of the part of our Turkish lira symbol below the parallel lines of the letter "t" and the part above it, in the same way, the ratio of the parts of the lines on the right and left sides of the lines in question to each other gives the "golden ratio". The shape of the symbol is geometrically based on an aesthetic basis, it is aimed to draw easily by everyone and to spread its use by adopting it by our citizens. To this end, an intense campaign will be carried out throughout the year to promote our icon. 3 Dear Guests, We are aware of the need for multifaceted efforts in various fields in order for our Turkish lira symbol to take its place in the natural flow of daily life. First of all, starting from the world of informatics, we will take steps towards the use of the symbol in practical business life. In this context, we will ensure that our symbol can be included in the character code tables that are used as a standard worldwide. Companies that produce computers, printers, mobile devices, cash registers and similar hardware that are still used by our citizens, institutions and organizations, and companies that produce operating systems, office software and other basic software that work with these hardware, will be able to write and process our Turkish lira symbol with a shortcut by updating their products. As the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, we took the first step towards the recognition of the symbol, its rapid inclusion in practical life and its popularization, and we updated it by taking a sample font and adding our symbol. The CD that will be presented to you at the exit contains this font and a program that will automatically install the icon on your computer. When the icon is clicked, this program runs and your computer is capable of processing our icon. From other currency symbols in commonly used computer systems; - Using the "AltGr" and "E" keys for the symbol of the Euro, - Using the "AltGr" and "4" keys for the symbol of the US dollar As it is, similar to the generally accepted application, the "AltGr" and "T" keys are used for the symbol of our Turkish lira in the program we offer you. Inside our icon 4 hosting sample font and program; It is developed to run on all computers running Windows, different Linux distributions including Pardus and Mac operating systems, and is strengthened with security elements and is signed. Our citizens, relevant persons and organizations can easily access all these sections and benefit from this service safely. Dear Guests, As a result of the reputation gained for our money, the use of the Turkish Lira in international markets has been increasing in recent years. According to the results of the survey conducted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on the use of different currencies in global markets, the use of the Turkish lira in 2010 increased more than 3 times compared to 2007. Now, the Turkish lira is traded for 24 hours not only in our country, but also in a wide geography extending from Europe to America, from America to Asia. On 1 November 2011, we signed a bilateral Currency Swap Agreement with Pakistan at a ceremony held in Istanbul. On February 21, 2012, we signed an agreement of the same nature with the People's Republic of China in Ankara. The main purpose of these agreements is to enable trade in the local currencies of the two countries. As a result of these agreements, in addition to the development of bilateral trade between Turkey and these countries, the use of the Turkish lira at the international level is expected to increase. However, I would like to emphasize that the contributions of the Banks Association of Turkey, Turk Eximbank and the Turkish Exporters Assembly will be of great importance in order to ensure that the agreements do not remain on paper. 5 While concluding my speech, I wish that the "trust" and "value rising in stability" represented by the Turkish lira symbol will be permanent and that the Turkish lira's feature of being a world currency will be strengthened, I wish that our symbol will be beneficial to our country and nation, and I offer my respects. 6

Title: Speech in Panel on Global and Regional Outlook and the Effects of the Global Financial Crisis
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic Of Turkey PANEL ONE Global and Regional Outlook and the Effects of the Global Financial Crisis Durmu Ylmaz Governor April 09, 2010 Istanbul Dear Governors, Distinguished Participants, In my introductory remarks, I would like to first discuss the performance of the Turkish economy during the recent global financial crisis. Then I will share my views on potential decoupling of countries in the post-crisis period and discuss its determinants. The global turmoil, which emerged in the second half of 2007, adversely affected economic activity around the world; and Turkey was no exception. Our economy, which grew for 27 quarters in a row, fell into recession in 2009. The higher share of investment goods and durables in our exports, firms dependence on external financing, and elevated level of production capacity were the factors that exacerbated the severity of the contraction. The growth rate dropped sharply, from its average of 6.8 percent between 2002 and 2007 to minus 4.7 percent last year. Unemployment rate increased by almost 4 percentage points. Exports declined by 23 percent. However, I should emphasize that neither price nor financial stability has been seriously jeopardized during this period. Turkish economy has rebounded sharply from the recession in the second half of 2009 and it is likely to return its pre-crisis level some time this year. This was a significant achievement in itself, because Turkey used to be one of the emerging economies with historically high volatility and particular sensitivity to global risk perceptions. However, this time the impact of the crisis has remained relatively subdued. A sound financial system, strong macro fundamentals and assertive monetary and fiscal policy stance were the main factors that prevented a prolonged recession and a financial turmoil in Turkey. Neither serious liquidity problems of global scale nor the bankruptcy of international financial institutions was enough to trigger a meltdown in our financial system. Unlike most of its peers, Turkish banking system has not required any rescue packages or other forms of government support. In fact, Turkey was one of the few emerging market economies that ended up with higher credit rating than its pre-crisis level. How did the Turkish economy withstand the devastating impact of this global crisis? 1 I believe it is fair to say that we had already gone through in 2001, what the world has been experiencing today. Some of you may remember we had a very severe crisis in February 2001. Overnight interest rate climbed to 6,200 percent, the local currency lost almost half of its value within two days, the economy contracted sharply, as much as 6 percent, many banks collapsed and a huge IMF rescue package was needed to rescue the economy and even a larger bail-out package was put into action by the government to clean up the financial system. After the 2001 crisis, we have implemented a very comprehensive reform agenda. Three main pillars of the reform program were fiscal consolidation, central bank independence and rapid structural reforms, especially in the financial sector, which were implemented without any compromise, excuses or delays. Fiscal discipline was the cornerstone of the program, allowing rapid decline in debt ratios, facilitating a swift disinflation period and a permanent drop in interest rates. Ambitious fiscal targets were set for primary surplus, as high as 5 percent of GDP. These ambitious targets have been achieved almost to the point year after year. Between 2003 and 2007, the realization of primary surplus was as high as 4.8 percent of GDP. Secondly, the monetary policy framework was changed quite radically. The Central Bank of Turkey started implementing inflation targeting and it was granted independence with the official mandate of price stability. The monetization of budget deficits through short-term advances from the Central Bank to the Treasury was abolished. These developments, coupled with a successful floatation of the national currency, internalized the risks to markets, reducing moral hazard problem in the private sector. The Turkish banking system was overhauled and restructured almost completely, from top to bottom. Regulations on financial system put Turkish banks under strict discipline in terms of capital adequacy, liquidity, FX position and leverage ratios. The government injected fresh capital into the banking system, equivalent to one third of our GDP, to rehabilitate several private banks and to clean up the balance sheets of public 2 banks. Without any doubt, using public funds of this magnitude was an enormous sacrifice for the society. Therefore, once the banking system was cleaned, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency has kept a close eye on the banking system to make sure that Never again, the taxpayer has to pay the price of reckless, irresponsible and sometimes outright fraudulent practices of the banking sector. Strict limits on FX-denominated consumer loans eliminated the vulnerability of households to exchange rate shocks. As you all know, the currency mismatch was particularly problematic for many Eastern European countries preventing the scope for accommodative monetary for many emerging market economies. The Central Bank of Turkey followed a prudent monetary policy during the precrisis period, limiting a rapid expansion in bank credits and excessive rise in households indebtedness. Hence, when the global crisis started in mid-2007, Turkey had already accumulated modest, but vital capacity to put into action counter-cyclical monetary policies and fiscal stimulus. Distinguished Guests, Having discussed our experiences during the global turmoil, now let me turn to the present and share with you my views on economic outlook. As you may all agree, we are witnessing green shoots around the globe, led by emerging market economies. The question is What will be the speed of the recovery and how the performance of economies will differ in the aftermath of the crisis? I believe there are at least three factors that will lead to the decoupling of countries during the post-crisis period. First and foremost, there is fiscal sustainability. The crisis has prompted large government interventions, both to restore confidence in the financial system and to contain the fallout of the crisis on economic activity. A looming danger threatening the future of global economy is a sudden deterioration of investor confidence over fiscal sustainability and a sharp rise in long term interest rates. Therefore, it is imperative to put forward a credible medium term framework to stabilize risk perceptions and to reinforce the confidence on fiscal policies. 3 To that end, the Turkish government announced a Medium Term Program (MTP) in September 2009. The Medium Term Program presents a comprehensive framework of policy actions to halt the rise in public debt ratio in 2010 and reduce it gradually in subsequent years. In addition, the government is also planning to introduce a fiscal rule to ensure fiscal discipline during economic booms, facilitate countercyclical policies during economic slowdowns, and strengthen overall public governance in policy making. The legal structure of the fiscal rule would be completed in mid-2010. Both the Medium Term Program and the fiscal rule would contribute to better management of expectations by enhancing the institutional framework of fiscal policy and its long term predictability. Having a healthy banking sector would be the second important factor that will lead to decoupling of economies. Looking at developed countries, we see no signs of meaningful acceleration in bank credits. Toxic assets in balance sheets have not cleaned up and underwritten yet, and many banks are likely to need new capital injections. Restoring the effectiveness of the credit mechanism is crucial in supporting the aggregate demand. As far as the banking system in Turkey is concerned, we are pleased to observe that it is regarded as one of the healthiest, robust, and profitable banking system among the emerging market economies. Therefore, our banking system is well positioned to support private sector for a sustainable economic growth in the foreseeable future. The last critical ingredient of a rapid recovery in economic activity is a strong and sustainable rise in private demand. This requires a meaningful improvement in employment prospects and low indebtedness of households. In comparison to typical business cycles, employment has been extraordinarily slow to recover. Continuing high unemployment rates due to rigidity in labor markets has the potential to depress private demand. Unfortunately, Turkey is at the top of OECD countries in red tape and strictness of employment protection. Labor market reforms should clearly be at the top of our priority list to raise our potential growth rate. Households debt level is the second crucial determinant of private demand. Households in many countries accumulated significant amount of debt during pre-crisis period, which is beyond their ability to repay out of current income. For a meaningful correction in economic imbalances, savings rate has to stay elevated for many countries 4 for years to come. In comparison, household indebtedness is quite low in Turkey. Therefore, a strong recovery in private consumption is not only probable but also sustainable in our economy. Let me conclude my remarks by a quote that caught my eye recently: Nobody can go back and start a new beginning, but anyone can start today and make a new ending. It is the responsibility of policy makers to ensure that regardless of our starting point, we reach a better equilibrium. The key determinants of a better equilibrium are fiscal sustainability, a healthy banking system, a productive labor market and low household indebtedness. Now, I would like to give the floor to Mr. Mark Allen. Thank you. 5

Title: Speech at South East European Cooperation Process Meeting
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic Of Turkey Global and Regional Outlook and the Effects of the Global Financial Crisis (Closing Remarks) Durmu Ylmaz Governor April 10, 2010 Istanbul Dear Governors, Participants, and Guests I would like to extend my sincere thanks to our keynote speaker, Mark Allen and esteemed Governors for their informative presentations and valuable discussions. This conference contributed significantly to our understanding of the effects of global crisis on our region. As Mark Allen explained quite clearly yesterday, systemic risks to global financial markets have eased substantially since the first quarter of 2009 and global economy has been recovering from the recession steadily, albeit very slowly and gradually. It appears that Europe, especially Western Europe is lagging behind the US and Japan. This is of course bad news for its trade partners. The major trade destination of many countries in our region is Western Europe. You may all remember the famous saying: If the US sneezes the world catches cold. In our case it is the prospects of the core Europe that matter. According to consensus forecasts, the US economy will return to pre-crisis level by the end of this year. For the Euro zone, a similar recovery is expected to take a longer time, prolonged well into the next year. My colleagues also made a very important observation on regarding the fragility of the recovery. Threats to financial systems have not completely disappeared. Significant rise in sovereign debt and heightening risk perceptions due to doubts on the sustainability of budget deficits are of major concerns. The crisis has caused a massive damage in public budgets. Due to large government interventions, both to restore confidence in the financial system and to contain the fallout of the crisis on the real economy, budget deficits have reached levels not seen since the World War II. The ratio of public debt to GDP is likely to reach triple digits in the US, as well as in several major economies in the Euro zone. It is quite understandable from a Keynesian point of view to compensate the severe contraction in private demand through higher government investment and consumption. However, we should be mindful of the fact the capacity of developing countries is rather limited in pursuing expansionary fiscal policies. Developed countries should also be very 1 cautious. Following a countercyclical fiscal stance and accommodative monetary policies for too long prolongs the desired correction in global imbalances. Listening to the presentations of governors, it is quite clear that during the last decade, South Eastern European economies had benefited considerably from the era of abundant liquidity and the Great Moderation. Many countries in the region achieved high economic growth driven by booming domestic demand, foreign capital flows in ample quantity and rapid credit expansion. But, that was not the whole story. The financial crisis has also revealed that most emerging economies, which were previously seen as a danger zone, were not as risky as once believed. I attribute this resilience to longlasting memories of the developing world on past crisis. Let me quote a short passage from Animal Spirits, the recent book of Akerloff and Schiller: Peoples memories of essential facts are indexed in the brain around stories. Facts that are remembered are attached to stories. Other facts may enter shortterm memory. But such memories tend not to be influential, and they are eventually erased. Unlike mature economies, authorities in developing countries accustomed to have frequent crisis and consequently, bad memories of previous crises were fresh in their minds. Thus, during the pre-crisis period, many developing countries strengthened their fiscal positions, reduced public debt, accumulated FX reserves and kept a close eye on financial systems. Mr. Radovan Jelasic, the Governor of National Bank of Serbia made a very good point, when he said Counter-cyclicality is highly praised today although it was heavily criticized during the boom years. As I was listening to the Governor, I recalled William Martin, America's longest-serving central banker, who defined the job of a central bank as taking away the punch bowl just as the party gets going." Central bank governors are not supposed to be popular and praised by the market. Nobel award winner Paul Krugman once said During the last decade some people 2 thought central bank governors should do nothing as the party got crazy, and be ready to be the designated driver afterwards to take the market home safely. This crisis has demonstrated that this was the wrong approach. Sometimes the aftermath of boom years may leave such a legacy that, to clean up the subsequent mess you may need unprecedented scale of public money and social sacrifice. All in all, this crisis has proved that policy makers in general, policy makers of developing countries in particular should always consider leaning against the wind, rather than surfing on the waves of investors risk appetite. During expansionary phase of the cycle, central banks should reign on excessive credit growth and formation of bubbles in asset prices. Fiscal authorities should reduce public debt to accumulate enough fiscal space for the lean years. This is particularly true for developing countries. Unlike major economies, we are quite sensitive to capital flows. Dependence on external savings makes our region extremely vulnerable to shifts in risk perceptions and fluctuations in global capital flow. Developing countries also suffer from the so-called original sin. In times of crisis they are more likely to face difficulty in borrowing in their local currency. Therefore, like prudent farmers, we should store away extra grains in times of prosperity to mitigate the suffering in hard times. Dear Participants, This program, which takes place at a time of an unprecedented global financial crisis has provided us with an opportunity to reflect on the challenges confronting us and to consider the issues emerged in the context of the global financial crisis. I hope you have benefitted from our discussion as much as I do. Thank you for your participation. 3

Title: Opening Speech at the Third International Economic Conference of the Turkish Economic Association on "Debt Dynamics, Financial Instability and the Great Recession"
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: "Third International Economic Conference of the Turkish Economic Association: Debt Dynamics, Financial Instability and the Great Recession" Opening Speech Erdem BACI 1 November 2012, Izmir Dear Guests and Members of the Press, Welcome to the Third International Economic Conference on "Debt Dynamics, Financial Instability and the Great Recession", organized by the Turkish Economic Association and supported by the International Economic Association. Such conferences are of great importance in terms of providing the opportunity to listen to the ideas of respected economists from central banks and international organizations, as well as providing platforms for the exchange of ideas between policymakers and academics. Dear Guests, Financial stability is known to be closely linked to growth and employment.1 The cost of preventing financial crises is much lower than the cost of these crises. Turkey's recent history is a good example of this. The financial crisis in Turkey in 2001 increased the public debt burden by 30 percentage points, and growth and employment were deeply affected. Since 2002, the focus has been on structural reforms to increase price stability, financial stability and productivity. In this way, the country's economic prosperity has increased rapidly, while at the same time the financial sector has gained a more resilient structure against external shocks. The steps taken to reinforce financial stability enabled our country to recover rapidly after the deepening global economic crisis in 2008-2009 and to overcome the effects of the 2011-2012 European Debt Crisis with the least damage. The Lehman Crisis has had global impacts. All economies were caught unprepared for this crisis and all of them were affected to some extent. When we look at the European Debt Crisis, we see that its effects are much more selective. Countries that adhere to fiscal discipline and observe financial stability have been relatively less affected by this process. When we look at the problem countries, it is observed that they have moved away from fiscal discipline in particular and thus the ratio of public debt stocks to GDP has reached very high levels. In the academic literature, it has been found that growth slows down in countries where this rate exceeds 90%.2 The Eurozone is an important example of this so-called financial dominance. For the last two years, the monetary transmission mechanism in the Eurozone has been as it should be. 1 Reinhart, C. M. ve K. S. Rogoff. (2009). d2This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly.d3 Princeton, NJ: Princeton Press; Taylor, A. (2012). d2The Great Leveraging,d3 NBER Working Papers, No. 18290. 2 Cecchetti, S.; M S Mohanty ve F. Zampolli (2011) ). d2The Real Effects of Debt.d3 BIS Working Papers, No. 352. 2 does not work. The European Central Bank's policy rate and the short-term treasury bond yields of countries with debt problems are incompatible. In Turkey, the monetary transmission mechanism is working quite well as the ratio of public debt stock to GDP is at 39% as of the end of 2011. Dear Guests, After the global financial crisis, previously untested monetary policies began to be implemented in developed and developing countries. The central banks of developed countries that have reduced short-term interest rates to zero are providing additional quantitative easing through liquidity policies, including credit policies. The central banks of developing countries also actively use the liquidity tools at their disposal, especially in reserve requirements.3 A central bank that can manage foreign exchange liquidity and local currency-denominated liquidity independently can more easily eliminate the negative side effects caused by short-term capital flows. The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey now has this opportunity thanks to its newly developed policy instruments. Accordingly, the sterilization of short-term capital flows within the scope of credit expansion and exchange rates in Turkey can be carried out effectively. Dear Participants, The conference includes a total of 12 invited and more than 50 selected sessions on almost every branch of economics. Some of the session topics are: Schools of Economic Thought and Depression, Turkish Economy and Exports, Crisis and Debt Dynamics. In addition, our researchers and economist friends from our Bank contribute to the conference with 19 studies. I sincerely believe that all these presentations and discussions will be very useful for the participants. In closing, I wish the conference to be beneficial and fruitful for all of us, and I would like to thank you for your participation and interest. 3 Goodhart, C. (2009). d2Liquidity Management,d3 Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Symposium at Jackson Hole, August 2009. 3
