Title: Speech at Euromoney Central and Eastern European Forum
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey In Search of an Appropriate Policy Mix for Emerging Economies: Monetary Policy in Turkey in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis Durmu Ylmaz Governor January 18, 2011 Vienna Dear Guests, During the global financial crisis, almost all countries focused on containing potential adverse effects of the crisis on domestic economy; Turkey was not an exception. Following the intensification of the crisis, the Central Bank of Turkey (CBT) delivered sizeable and front-loaded cuts in policy rates, reaching 1025 basis points from November 2008 to November 2009. During this period the CBT not only cut policy rates rapidly, but also pursued a counter-cyclical liquidity policy to support the functioning of money and credit markets, thereby strengthen the impact of the rate reductions on economic activity. These efforts were successful in bringing back Turkey on a strong recovery track. The healthy household balance sheets and solid banking system allowed a rapid rebound in domestic demand. Starting from mid-2009, the Turkish economy has been facing a domestic demand driven rapid recovery. Meanwhile, strengthening capital inflows has further exacerbated the divergence between the domestic and external demand, creating new policy challenges. Rapidly widening current account deficit coupled with short term capital inflows and exchange rate appreciation called for a different approach to monetary policy. In order to cope with this new situation, we have slightly modified our existing framework of inflation targeting by explicitly highlighting the increasing role of financial stability in our objective function. Accordingly, first we have announced the details of our exit strategy from crisis measures in April 2010. As a first step, we have normalized the liquidity support facilities and brought back the TRY reserve requirement ratios to pre-crisis levels of 6 percent. Second, we started to highlight the macro financial risks and contingent policy responses. For example, we have stated through our policy documents that, if divergence in growth rates between domestic and external demand continues in the forthcoming period, and if this pattern of growth coexists with rapid credit expansion and deterioration in the current account balance, it would be necessary to utilize other policy instruments such as reserve requirement ratios and liquidity management facilities more effectively. 1 The primary objective of the CBT is to achieve and maintain price stability. However, the recent crisis has taught us that this single objective may not be enough for attaining macroeconomic and financial stability. In this respect, we reminded the public that financial stability is one of the fundamental duties of the CBT as stipulated in our Law, and we approach financial stability from a macroeconomic perspective. From an emerging market point of view, the concept of macroprudential measures may not be the same as it is perceived in advanced economies. It is important to note that each country has its own characteristics and every country has to design the policy framework according to its own needs. From the Turkish perspective, financial stability risks under the current conditions are most evident as the rapidly increasing current account deficit fueled by short-term capital inflows. The divergence between domestic and foreign demand growth coupled with a rapid credit expansion is increasing the current account deficit, thereby raising financial stability concerns. Moreover, the recent developments and related policy decisions in the European and US economies have been exacerbating these risks, necessitating a different domestic policy mix than we have implemented in the past. What do we mean by policy mix? When the external and internal equilibrium requires different interest rates, monetary policy has to use more than one instrument. In our case we utilized two more instruments to limit the macro-financial risks associated with short term capital inflows coupled with appreciating currency and rising current account deficit. Let me explain these extra tools in turn. In order to curb the domestic demand and widening current account deficit, our first aim was to control the rapid credit expansion. Therefore, we have made it clear that one of the goals of our current policy mix should be reducing the pace of credit growth. To this end, we stated that reserve requirement ratios should be used as an active monetary policy tool. Moreover, to use the required reserve ratios as one of the policy tools to mitigate the macroeconomic and financial risks more actively in the future, the remuneration of Turkish lira required reserves is also terminated. 2 We have been very open with the public regarding these measures. We stated that the measures implemented by the CBT are necessary but not alone sufficient to safeguard financial stability. We underscored the crucial role of coordination across all institutions. To this end, I should mention that, as a support to our policies, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BRSA) has taken a set of measures to (such as restricting loan to value ratios for certain segments of bank credits, increasing the minimum payments on credit cards) in order to contain the credit supply. BRSA eliminated the ban designed to safeguard investor demand for government debt, and permitted Turkish Banks to sell TRY denominated securities starting from October 2010. Finally, the government also supported our efforts by saving most of the extra revenues acquired by the faster-than-expected pickup in economic activity. In addition, government raised Resource Usage Support Fund (KKDF) deductions on consumer loans to roll back measures taken during the global crisis. Another issue we considered while formulating current policy mix is lengthening the maturity of capital inflows. This is important for improving the quality of the capital account and avoiding exchange rate misalignments. We decided to adopt a policy mix to deal with this situation. We lowered the policy rate and widened the corridor between overnight borrowing and lending rates so as to allow fluctuations in the short-term interest rates, when needed. This policy so far has been quite effective. We observed a significant drop in the short term speculative inflows. In addition, we differentiated Turkish lira required reserve ratios according to the maturity structure of deposits in order to lengthen the maturity structure of liabilities and reduce the maturity mismatch. Of course, one crucial communication issue not to be neglected during this process is convincing the public that these measures do not mean giving up on our primary mandate, which is price stability. Accordingly, we used a cautious tone for the inflation outlook. We have explicitly stated that, given the rapid pace of domestic demand and rising commodity prices, general price setting behavior should be closely monitored. In this respect we have forcefully signaled that the net impact of 3 the macroprudential policy package implementedand to be implementedboth by the CBT and other institutions should be on the tightening side. We anticipate the hikes in required reserve ratios to curb the credit growth through the cost and liquidity channels. Needless to say, there is a lot of uncertainty regarding the timing and the extent of the impact of our measures. In order to overcome the possible communication problems associated with this uncertainty, we have announced that we will monitor the effects of our decisions from both price stability and financial stability perspectives, and do not hesitate to implement additional measures if necessary. Although it looks quite complicated at first sight, the framework we adopt in spirit is not significantly different from the conventional inflation targeting framework. The only difference is that, previously our policy instrument was the one week repo rate, but now our instrument is a policy mixwhich consists of a combination of short term interest rates, reserve requirement ratios and interest rate corridor. We seek to use these instruments in the right combination in order to cope with both inflation and macro-financial risks. The monetary policy stance in this framework is not only determined by the path of policy rates, but as a mixture of all the policy instruments, as I just mentioned. Just like the conventional inflation targeting framework, the policy is forward looking and contingent on economic outlook. The course of the policy mix in the forthcoming period will depend on the factors affecting price stability and financial stability. In sum, we are going through a period in which central banks policies have to be creative in dealing with the new normal. However, it is also important to consider country specific features in designing these strategies. In our part, we believe that a lower policy rate and a wider interest rate corridor combined with higher required reserve ratios may serve as an effective policy mix in dealing with rapidly increasing macro imbalances driven by short term capital inflows. Thank you. 4

Title: Speech within the Scope of the "Financial Stability Report"
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey "FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT" PUBLIC PRESENTATION Sureyya SERDENGEcT President August 2005, Ankara "FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT" PUBLIC PRESENTATION Dear Members of the Press, At the point we have reached in the normalization process of the Turkish economy, in parallel with the experiences gained, the issue of financial stability is becoming increasingly important in terms of the course of our economy in the future. Within the framework of the importance we attach to this issue, we organized a very comprehensive international conference titled "Financial Stability and Basel II Practices" in May this year. Given the interest shown in this meeting, the nature of the speakers and panelists, and most importantly, the content of the speeches and presentations; It is understood how important the issue of financial stability is not only for us, but for the whole world. Today, we have organized this meeting in order to make public the public presentation of the first issue of the Financial Stability Report, which we have been working on for a long time at our Central Bank. The general framework of the speech I will make within the scope of the introduction of the Financial Stability Report, which will be distributed to you after the meeting and will be put on our website as of today, will be what financial stability means, why it is important, its relationship with price stability and monetary policy, and the place of the Financial Stability Report in this process. In addition, in the last part of my speech, I will give more detailed information about the content of the Report in question. Dear Listeners, Financial stability is defined in the narrowest sense as the formation and movement of stocks, exchange rates, interest rates or housing certificate-like prices in financial markets at a level that does not cause illusions in the investment and consumption decisions of economic units 1 When a broader and systemic definition is made, financial stability; It is expressed as the continuation of the effective allocation of savings undertaken by the financial system for the healthy functioning of the economy in an uninterrupted and trouble-free manner. Depending on this definition, the distance of the financial system from the point of not being able to perform the function of resource allocation is called the measure of financial vulnerability. 1 Issing, O. (2003). Monetary and Financial stability- is there a trade-off? Speech at the Conference on "Monetary Stability, Financial Stability and the Business Cycle" . Basel. In this context, financial stability is a different concept than macroeconomic stability. It is extremely difficult to make a clear definition, to set measurable targets, to determine how long the policies implemented will affect the economy. Achieving financial stability also requires much greater cooperation and cohesion of institutions in the economy than other policy practices. After this brief definition, I would like to underline that in order to understand the meaning of financial stability and its importance for the functioning of the economy as of today, it is necessary to understand the process of change that the global economy has undergone since the 1980s. One of the features of this process, and perhaps the most important, is the increasing spread and deepening of liberalization in financial markets. When we look at the development of the global economy over the last thirty-five years, with the end of the Bretton-Woods system; We see that economic policies were first implemented in developed countries in the 1970s and in developing countries since the late 1980s with the aim of completely liberalizing capital accounts and financial systems. As a result of the increasing liberalization of the capital accounts and financial systems of the countries, the capital transitions between countries have increased in both speed and size. With the contribution of the great developments in information and communication technologies in recent years, the limits in front of capital flows have been largely removed as of today. Undoubtedly, this rapid and large-scale movement of capital has played an important role in the development of inter-country trade in goods and services and in the more efficient use of the resources of production on a global scale. However; The effects of financial liberalization differed from country to country within the framework of the specific characteristics of the countries, the timing of liberalization, the macroeconomic conditions at the beginning of liberalization and the economic policies implemented. The fact that capital can move so quickly and intensively between countries, coupled with economic vulnerabilities, has caused financial crises from time to time and even a crisis that started in one country to spread to other countries. 2 In academic studies, it has been determined that there have been 117 financial crises in both developing and developed countries since the 1970s2 Banking crises in Latin American countries in the 1980s, difficulties in savings and loan institutions in the USA, Scandinavian, Latin American and South Asian countries in the 1990s and finally financial crises in our country in 2000 and 2001 are the main examples of these many crises. After all, financial crises have had a wide range of violent effects on economies; the national incomes of countries experiencing crises have shrunk; welfare losses have been experienced. For example, while the cost of the crisis in Finland in the 1990s was about S percent of the national income, this rate reached up to 24.5 percent of the national income in the crisis in Korea3 And after each crisis, it was better understood how important financial stability is for the healthy functioning of the economy. In fact, although financial crises are instructive experiences about the importance of ensuring financial stability, it is clear enough without crises that the existence of a healthy functioning financial system is an essential prerequisite for a strong economy. Both the academic literature and the country's experience show that a stable financial environment and a healthy banking system are key elements of the economy, as well as ensuring price stability in order to achieve sustainable high growth and sustainable employment growth. Considering that the economy consists of many segments, it is seen that the effects of financial markets and indicators on the spending and investment decisions of economic units, and therefore on other segments, are very important in inter-segment interaction. The financial sector is of vital importance in the economy as it ensures that the supply of capital matches the demand for capital. After all, for the effective use of resources in the economy, the financial system must effectively perform its intermediary function. Only in this way will companies be able to find the resources they need to produce more at less cost. In many empirical studies, it has been concluded that the level of financial development explains a significant part of the differences between the growth rates of countries in the long term. 2 Caprio G. and Klingebiel , D. (2003). Episodes of Systemic and Borderline Financial Crises. World Bank Database. 3 BankofEngland. 3 Countries with more developed and efficient financial systems are able to grow faster. In some studies, it has been concluded that an economy that has an average ratio of private sector loans to national income for 35 years has been 18 percent can grow one point more per year than an economy where the same ratio is 12 percent4. Moreover, a more developed financial system does not only indicate higher growth rates: A healthy financial sector supports more resources for research and development by more efficient flow of funds in the economy; helps firms diversify their risks and helps companies achieve a more effective level of corporate governance. way. Ultimately, all this means more profitable and less risky investment projects and a higher level of capital accumulation. It is also necessary to know how a deterioration in the economy would affect the banking system in order to understand the dynamics of the operation of the entire economy5 Therefore, both the importance of a stable financial system in economies and the role of the institutions that perform this function place the issue of ensuring financial stability in a very important framework within the scope of macroeconomic policies and monetary policy. That is why ensuring and maintaining financial stability are among the priorities of macroeconomic policies. Dear Listeners, The importance of financial stability within the framework of macroeconomic policies raises the debate between both academics and policy practitioners from time to time whether the policy priorities of central banks are price stability or financial stability. As is known, within the framework of modern central banking, central banks bear the responsibility of providing a stable economic environment in which the economy will operate effectively in the long term. The necessary conditions for the formation of a stable macroeconomic environment or sustainable growth environment are the provision of both price stability and financial stability. 4 Hemandez L. and Schmidt-Hebbel K. (2001) "Banking, Financial Integration, and htemational Crises: An Overview". Central Bank ofChile Working Papers. No: 100. 5 Schuerman T. (2004). "Why Were Banks Better off in the 2001 Recession?" Current Issues in Economics and Finance. FEDNY. Vol. 10. No: 1. 4 Thus, there are extremely strong reasons for financial stability to be included in the policy functions of central banks. When we look at the relationship between the two, first of all, inflation, especially chronic inflation, is one of the main causes of financial instability due to the uncertainty environment it causes. High inflation, in the simplest terms, prevents relative prices, including financial prices, from acting as signals, such as interest rates in the economy. Thus, both the money and credit markets are adversely affected by inflation and the confusion it creates. In other words, it is almost impossible to achieve strong financial stability without price stability in the long term. Moreover, price stability ensured by reliable monetary policies is an advantage for the economy when there is uncertainty in the financial system and financial imbalances are encountered. On the other hand, the benefit to the economy of the existence of a strong and effectively functioning financial system is extremely important for ensuring price stability. But a well-functioning financial system can ensure that central bank decisions affect the real economy in the desired way and at the desired time. Imbalances in the financial system prevent the healthy functioning of the financial transmission channel of monetary policy. In other words, an effective financial system is necessary for effective monetary policy. A strong financial sector increases the effectiveness of monetary policy while providing the flexibility necessary for the economy to more easily overcome external shocks. At this point, I would like to underline one more point on the subject. As is known, when price stability is defined as the primary objective of central banks, the duration of the monetary policies implemented to achieve this goal to affect the economy is generally medium term, as the Central Bank has often stated in its recent monthly inflation announcements. The likelihood that financial stability will get in the way of all other policy objectives is high in cases where financial instability is experienced, in other words, in the short term. In such a case, the view that the measures to be taken by central banks to ensure financial stability will jeopardize price stability, which is the main objective, is automatically invalid due to the fact that the policies to be implemented by central banks to achieve both goals and the duration of influence of the regulations to be made are different. Moreover, effective use of communication paths allows policymakers to manage waits and thus achieve both goals in the short term without sacrificing reliability in cases of financial imbalances. 5 As a result, in the medium and long term, these two policy objectives do not contradict each other, but complement each other. Depending on this situation, financial stability is already being set as a supporting objective by an increasing number of central banks, as in our country. Dear Guests, At this point, I would like to emphasize once again: It is a fact that both the economic literature and the developments in the world economy put before us that price stability is an indispensable prerequisite for financial stability. However, the experience of the country shows that price stability alone is not enough to ensure financial stability. Even in an environment where price stability is achieved, it is seen that economies can experience financial turbulence. In line with the purpose for which the Financial Stability Report was published, Eichengreen's analogy in a study of financial crises will help to create the right approach to policies aimed at achieving financial stability. Think. Eichengreen likens financial crises to heart attacks6 Just as heart attacks are less damaging to the body when they are small and can cause the end of a person's life when they are large, financial crises leave less damage to the economy when they are small, and stop the functioning of the entire economy when they are large. Moreover, similar to the fact that a person recovers from the effects of a heart attack more easily when he is generally healthy, when the functioning of the economy outside the financial system is strong and healthy, he is less affected by the financial crisis and starts the recovery process quickly. If the macroeconomic fundamentals are weak, a financial crisis to the same extent can, on the contrary, cause very serious damage to the economy. In terms of determining the direction of the policies to be implemented, both from the analogy of Eichengreen, which I have just mentioned, and from the experiences of both us and other countries, it is seen that two elements come to the fore within the scope of ensuring and protecting financial stability. The first is the macroeconomic of an economy. 6 Eichengreen, B. (2002). "Financial Crises and What To Do About Them". Oxford University Press. 6 The stronger its foundations, the more resilient the country's financial system is to shocks and the less costly financial stability is achieved. The second is that discipline is essential in the financial system in order to avoid financial turmoil and shocks. As a natural consequence of this second element, in the 1990s, risk management developed as a separate field within banking in the world, new tools and methods for risk management were developed, which played an important role in the growth of the financial sector and the development of instruments. As a result, an effective supervisory and regulatory mechanism has become a vital part of the discipline I mentioned in the financial markets. In addition, as an element of discipline in the financial sector, it is of great importance to analyze in a transparent manner sufficient information about the general course of the economy, the financial sector and especially the inter-segment relationship. In this context, in order to ensure financial stability, central banks and other authorized institutions and organizations have to take appropriate measures and implement coordinated policies by making the necessary analyzes. Dear Guests, At this point, before referring to the policies aimed at ensuring financial stability, I would like to open a parenthesis and briefly mention the international cooperation efforts put forward for the purpose of financial stability or the creation of a strong financial system on a global scale. The most important development achieved to date as a result of long-standing international efforts to create a healthy global financial system is the general acceptance that modern risk management techniques are part of the usual financial intermediary activities. In this context, Basel II is a very important step. The Basel regulations were mainly aimed at introducing international and institutionalized standards into the global financial system and were significantly successful. Basel II, which is the stage of this process reached today, draws attention with its emphasis on the risk management aspect of the financial intermediation system. In parallel, first of all, risk management in the modern sense requires that both financial market players and other units be aware of the various risk foci that may create fragility in their balance sheets under market conditions. Aims. 7 Analysis and arrangements made within this framework; It is extremely important to ensure that many indicators and calculations related to capital risk, credit risk, non-return risk, exchange rate risk, interest rate risk, maturity risk, liquidity risk and operational risks are taken into consideration and to increase the effectiveness of markets while reducing their vulnerability. The number of countries participating in the "Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP)" carried out within the IMF and the World Bank within the scope of global cooperation has been increasing in recent years. As of today, there are 118 countries that have completed or announced that they will participate in this program7. Dear Guests; In fact, economic policies aimed at stabilization are not only crisis avoidance or crisis management policies, but are comprehensive enough to include the creation of the best financial environment necessary for the normal functioning of the economy in the long run. is open. In this context, in this part of my speech, I would like to explain the role of monetary policy and central banks in this process, rather than the role of each economic policy in ensuring financial stability. Within the scope of financial turbulence prevention policies, the most important and perhaps the only step to be taken by a central bank is to prepare the necessary ground for a healthy macroeconomic environment by ensuring a low and stable inflation environment, in other words, price stability. However, in addition to ensuring price stability, the responsibilities of central banks and the tools they use to ensure financial stability vary from country to country, within the framework of the specific conditions of the countries. In this context, the task of some central banks may be limited to monitoring the financial system or ensuring that payment systems function smoothly, while others also act as supervisors. When we look at the world in general, it is possible to say that central banks have three basic functions in ensuring financial stability. The first of these concerns the payment systems of the country. The smooth operation of countries' own payment systems is essential in this context. 7 IMF (February 2005). "Financial Sector Assessment Program-Background Paper, Supplement I", SM/05/67. Are. 8 The creation of the necessary structure for the healthy functioning of the clearing and custody transactions of the financial markets is mostly given to the responsibility of the central banks. The second of the main functions of central banks in terms of financial stability is that they take the necessary measures for the uninterrupted functioning of the markets in the event of a financial crisis, or more generally, an extraordinary development. Perhaps the most well-known application of this function is to provide liquidity to the markets as the final borrowing authority during financial turmoil. Liquidity, of course, is only given in exchange for guarantees that can be easily cashed out. In each country, which of the easily cashable securities depends on which are the commonly used debt instruments in that country and the depth of the markets in which these instruments are traded. The third of these functions of central banks is to collect data from financial markets and monitor these markets. In addition, central banks today increasingly share their views on the financial system with the public. Today, many central banks regularly work on financial stability and publish financial stability reports with analyses of financial vulnerability. Dear Guests, In this last part of my speech, I will talk about the practices of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey in recent years within the framework of the financial stability functions I mentioned in the previous section and the "Financial Stability Report" that we are introducing today. As we all know, the Turkish economy experienced a two-stage economic-financial crisis in November 2000 and February 2001, the banking crises at its core. The Turkish economy has been seriously affected by this crisis; In 2001, national income shrank by 9.5 percent. The policies pursued after the 2001 crisis are very important steps both in terms of crisis management and crisis prevention. With these policies, priority was given to the prevention of financial turmoil with the help of the transition to a floating exchange rate regime after the crisis. In the first phase of the operations carried out within the framework of these policies, approximately 21.7 billion New Turkish Liras were transferred to the financial system at today's exchange rates, at the rate of 16 billion US dollars, or in other words, 12.1 percent of GNP. In this context, while our Bank helps to provide resources to the financial system within the framework of restructuring, on the other hand, 9 it has successfully used its monetary policy tools to ensure that the liquidity expansion created by this resource does not create an inflationary pressure. Again, in line with these operations, necessary arrangements have been made to provide flexibility to the liquidity management of the banks in the system; In order to reduce the vulnerability of the system, restructuring practices of public and fund banks were carried out. All these crisis-era measures ensured that the banking sector emerged from the crisis without further damage and provided the necessary environment for the formation of a strong financial sector. has prepared. In this context, after the measures taken in the short term, important steps were taken forward. The BRSA's effectiveness in the supervision and supervision of the financial sector has been increased and a structural transformation process that is still ongoing today has been initiated. In this process, the Law on Financial Institutions, which is becoming law in accordance with the European Union and Basel II norms, is one of the important steps taken in this direction. In this sense, it is thought that the new Financial Institutions Law will make positive contributions to the risk measurement and assessment of financial markets and will allow market discipline to be strengthened. Considering that the Basel II principles, which allow banks to measure their exposure more precisely and encourage effective risk management, will be implemented in the European Union in 2007, the preparation process for Basel II should be understood as part of the process of adaptation to European Union norms. The announcement of the draft "Roadmap for the Transition to Basel II" by the BRSA on 30 May 2005 is of great importance in terms of increasing the awareness of all units that will contribute to this process on Basel II and directing the process in the healthiest way and is evaluated positively by our Bank. In addition to the banking sector, which has made an important step in terms of risk perception and management, it is of great importance for the successful operation of the system that companies have adequate risk assessments and use risk hedging tools effectively. A factor that will contribute to this process is that the firm's balance sheets will become transparent after the transition to Basel II. Today, with the increase in their reliability, companies find financing opportunities outside the banking sector and increase the amount of funds they use from abroad. This increase in the exchange rate risk of the companies 10 While increasing their sensitivity to this risk, it is important to create awareness and develop financial instruments for protection purposes in order to manage this risk. Dear Guests; Instead of explaining all the reforms and regulations that have been made and will be made with your permission here today, I will continue to speak within the framework of the policies of central banks and our Bank in this context. Firstly, with the amendment made to the Law on Our Bank in April 2001, financial stability was determined as the supporting objective of our Bank. In the fourth article of the Law, our Bank's responsibilities to ensure financial stability are defined within the framework of the functions of the central banks I have just mentioned. According to this article; The bank monitor financial markets; To regulate the volume and circulation of the Turkish currency, to establish payment and securities transfer and settlement systems, to make all necessary arrangements related to these systems; is authorized to determine the methods and principles related to the compulsory reserves and general disponibility obligations of financial institutions. The relevant Article also states that in the face of a sudden development, our Bank will take the necessary measures to ensure the stability of the financial system and make arrangements regarding the money and foreign exchange markets. In case of need, Turkish currency or foreign currency can give liquidity to the markets within the predetermined limits, and in the application of the late liquidity window, in exchange for unlimited and easily cashable guarantees, which are still DIPS in Turkey. Both the events of September 11 and the measures taken during the Iraq War in 2003 proved this. In addition, the Central Bank made the necessary statements immediately during these periods and used its communication policy effectively in crisis management. As a result, our Bank is able to take the necessary measures without delay in the face of developments that threaten financial stability. At this point, I would like to emphasize a point regarding the monetary policy being implemented and the provision of financial stability within this framework. As I have often pointed out in many of my speeches, in economies where capital movements are free, central banks cannot control both the exchange rate and interest rates at the same time, and this is due to the financial situation. 11 It is an important determinant in the liquidity policies implemented by central banks in times of turbulence. I want to be more specific. As is known, in fixed or predictable exchange rate regimes, central banks have to defend a certain level of exchange rate. Under these exchange rate regimes, it is normal for interest rates to be determined in the market if capital movements are also free. Under such conditions, in the event of a financial turmoil in which the transition from national currency to foreign currency, whatever the reason, is experienced, central banks cannot give the market liquidity at every time it is requested and in every amount demanded in order not to jeopardize the exchange rate regime and therefore the system as a whole by creating additional demand pressure on exchange rates. In this case, interest rates are allowed to fluctuate. This practice is included in the literature under the name of passive monetary policy. On the contrary, in active monetary policy, while capital movements are free, exchange rates fluctuate and short-term interest rates are managed by central banks. Under this strategy, where exchange rates are no longer a policy tool, it is possible to implement a more effective liquidity policy with controlled short-term interest rates and to transfer resources to the markets according to demand. In our country, as it is known, the exchange rate regime changed with the 2001 crisis, and the transition from a fixed or predictable exchange rate regime to a floating exchange rate regime was made. Now, the authorities do not have any target regarding the exchange rate. In this context, the applied monetary policy has also been differentiated and an active monetary policy strategy has been adopted, in which short-term interest rates are used as the main policy tool. In a financial turmoil under the implementation of active monetary policy, it is natural that the Central Bank is able to act much more flexibly in its liquidity policy than the passive monetary policy it has applied in the past. Since it does not have to defend any exchange rate level, it is able to provide liquidity to the markets under certain conditions when necessary and to implement an effective liquidity policy by controlling short-term interest rates. This situation plays a very important role in preventing financial instability due to liquidity crunch. Think. 12 Dear Guests, As I mentioned earlier, an important principle to be considered in the steps to be taken towards ensuring financial stability and the creation of a strong banking sector is to ensure transparency and information sharing at the highest level. At this point, I would like to emphasize that the mutual cooperation and information sharing with the BRSA and other relevant authorities has always shed light on our work on financial stability. The fact that information flow is strong and can be shared equally by all market participants is very important for financial markets to function effectively. Financial stability reports are also published by an increasing number of central banks as a requirement of this principle. Financial stability reports were first published in the 1990s by the central banks of the United Kingdom and the Nordic. As of today, the number of central banks issuing financial stability reports has increased to 32. From a geographical point of view, it is seen that 21 of these central banks are located in Europe. In addition, the central banks of 23 of the 30 OECD member countries, including Turkey, publish financial stability reports. On the other hand, when all countries that publish financial stability reports are examined in terms of institutional structuring methods for the supervision and supervision of the banking sector, it is seen that central banks in 1O countries are also responsible for banking supervision and supervision, while in 22 countries the supervision and supervision authorities are separate independent institutions. In parallel, all countries that have published financial stability reports have either announced or completed the "Financial Sector Assessment Program" that I mentioned earlier, and only Mexico and Luxembourg are applying stress tests without participating in this program8. At this point, I would like to happily state that Turkey is a country that conducts stress tests on the financial sector and publishes the Financial Stability Report before starting the program. Financial stability reports in country practices differ from reports that explain monetary policy and give more weight to future scenarios in terms of drawing attention to risks such as exchange rate, interest and non-payment in the financial sector and identifying vulnerabilities in the financial system. 8 IMF and World Bank (February 2005). "Analytical Tools of the FSAP". 13 With the financial stability reports they publish, central banks reveal a comprehensive picture of the financial system, determine the status of the institutions in the system, provide information and opinions about the difficulties that the system may face in the future by identifying the main risk foci and ultimately measure the adequacy of the system to cope with a possible crisis. When the practices are examined, it is seen that central banks draw attention to the risks in the whole system in a macro framework and analytical manner instead of analyzing the institutions that make up the financial system one by one. It is observed that this approach is followed jointly in the reports of almost all central banks that do not have the responsibility to supervise and regulate the financial sector. In this context, an analysis within the macro framework is quite different from the micro-based analysis, which envisages the evaluation and auditing of each institution in the system one by one. This broad perspective is crucial to measuring the financial system's response to shocks that could affect the economy as a whole, and then assessing the impact of that response back on the economy. These analyses carried out by central banks are complementary to the audit of financial institutions. Dear Listeners, In the Financial Stability Report, the first of which we have published today as the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, as I have just mentioned, it is aimed to give a macro perspective on the entire financial system. In this context, I will mention a few points regarding the topics and contents of our Bank's Financial Stability Report: In the section of the Report titled "Macroeconomic Elements of Financial Stability", the public sector, households, firms, the outside world and the banking sectors were analyzed as a whole. In this section, on the developments in each segment and the interaction of the sectors with each other, evaluations have been made. In the evaluations made, it was examined which channels were used more effectively in inter-sector interaction in the Turkish economy and some determinations specific to our country were examined. Made. 14 In this first Report, in addition to many analyses that I think you will find interesting, there is also a very remarkable analysis of the money substitution or dollarization process that took place in our country in the past. In the past, currency substitution, which developed in the process of chronic inflation and macroeconomic instability and constituted a significant obstacle to the effective functioning of the financial system, was reversed with the floating exchange rate regime that has been implemented since 2001 and the successful stabilization program that has been in place. saptamadr. In the section of the Report titled "Banking Sector and Other Financial Institutions", the financial system, especially the banking sector, is examined in detail. In the analysis made in this section, since 92 percent of the financial sector in our country consists of the banking sector, special emphasis is given to this segment. In this section, especially the recent developments in the banking sector are underlined; In addition to all these developments, the institutions other than banking in the sector are also analyzed. Are. The topic in this section, where the risks in the banking sector are evaluated, constitutes a privileged part of the Financial Stability Report compared to similar reports of other countries. In the relevant section, the risks of the banking sector are analyzed under the main headings of credit risk, market risk and liquidity risk and the risks in the economy are pointed out within the framework of the modern risk management indicators I mentioned earlier. Under the possible scenarios related to these risks, the developments that may occur in the financial sector constitute an important part of the analysis. It is extremely important that both the financial sector and other economic units read this section carefully and take into account the existing risks and make economic decisions. In this context, the Futures and Options Exchange, which started operations in Izmir in February, is a big step in terms of managing market risks more effectively. In the opinions and evaluations on the state of the financial system and the stage we have achieved in financial stability, the main point in the report is that the increase in confidence in the economic policies being implemented, the positive course of macroeconomic developments, the resolute continuation of the policies being implemented, the implementation of legal regulations related to the financial sector and the supervision and supervision authority BRSA's 15 It was emphasized that their effective work is positive signs that stability in financial markets will continue to strengthen. In this context, it is necessary to underline that it is of great importance for the actors in the economy to adapt their risk perceptions according to dynamic conditions and to maintain the financial structures of financial institutions in a healthy line. Dear Members of the Press, As the Central Bank, I would like to express that the implementation of monetary policy is a very complex task, given all the uncertainties arising from the nature of the economy. In order to put forward a clearer monetary policy in the midst of all these uncertainties and risks, it is very important for us that economic units understand the why and how of our policies as well as our views on the economy as a whole or the financial sector as a function. I think that the Financial Stability Report, which will be published twice a year, will make important contributions in this context. Increasing transparency and effective communication will always be part of our policies. Thank you. 16

Bu durumun likidite skklna bal finansal istikrarszln nlenmesinde olduka nemli bir rol oynadn dnyorum. 12 Deerli Konuklar, Daha nce de belirttiim zere, finansal istikrar salama ve gl bir bankaclk kesiminin oluturulmas ynnde atlmas gereken admlarda dikkat edilmesi gereken nemli bir ilke, effafln ve bilgi paylamnn en yksek dzeyde salanmasdr. Finansal istikrar raporlar da, giderek artan sayda merkez bankas tarafndan, ayn zamanda bu ilkenin gerei olarak yaymlanmaktadr. "Analytical Tools ofthe FSAP ". 13 Merkez bankalar yaymladklar finansal istikrar raporlar ile, finansal sistemin kapsaml bir resmini ortaya koymakta, sistemdeki kurumlarn durumlarn belirlemekte, balca risk odaklarn saptayarak sistemin ileride karlaabilecei zorluklar hakknda bilgi ve gr salamakta ve nihayetinde sistemin olas bir krizle baa kma yeterliliini lmektedirler. Bu erevede, ekonomide yer alan aktrlerin risk alglamalarn dinamik koullara gre uyarlamalarnn ve finansal kurumlarn mali bnyelerinin salkl bir izgide srdrlmesinin byk nem tadnn altn izmek gerekmektedir. Deerli Basn Mensuplar, Merkez Bankas olarak, para politikasnn uygulanmasnn ekonominin doasndan kaynaklanan btn belirsizlikler dikkate alndnda olduka karmak bir grev olduunu ifade etmek istiyorum. Title: Speech at Istanbul Chamber of Industry
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: 27 September 2006 Istanbul Chamber of Industry, Istanbul Dear Industrialists and Businessmen, Today, I am very pleased to meet with you in Istanbul and to have the opportunity to share my knowledge and opinions about the outlook of our economy. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Istanbul Chamber of Industry for this meeting. In my speech today, I would like to first talk about the independence of the Central Bank and effective communication policy, which are of vital importance in terms of monetary policy implementation, and then to mention the latest developments in the economy in the context of inflation, monetary policy decisions, floating exchange rate regime, recent developments in financial markets, growth, employment and current account deficit. Dear Listeners, With the amendment made to our Bank's law in 2001, the determination of the main purpose of our Bank as ensuring and maintaining price stability and the free determination of the monetary policy instruments to be used by our Bank was a turning point in terms of monetary policy practices in Turkey. The instrument independence we have gained with this amendment to our law has allowed us to formulate our policies for the last 5 years in a medium-term perspective, away from politics and daily vicious debates, and directly towards the realization of our goals. This change has made a great contribution to reaching the lowest inflation figures in the last 30 years of our country's history. This distance taken in the fight against inflation and the gains achieved reveal the importance of an independent Central Bank both in the legal framework and in practice. That is why all segments of society should pay special attention to the issue of the independence of the Central Bank; They should not forget that the discussions that may take place on this issue may damage the credibility of economic policies and targets, which will have a high cost to Turkey. In this context, no one should doubt that; The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey will continue to use its instrument independence without any hesitation and taking into account all kinds of risks in order to ensure price stability, which is its ultimate goal, and to make the necessary warnings in this regard. 1 Dear Guests, In order to convince a society that has lived with high and chronic inflation for 30 years that we aim to ensure price stability and that we will fight inflation decisively in this context, it is of great importance for the Central Bank to be able to fully express itself and to explain the policies it implements and the reasons for the decisions it has taken to the public correctly. This requires an effective communication policy. Our Bank implements its communication policy on the basis of trust, transparency, consistency and determination. Within the framework of this policy, while explaining the Bank's policies and developments in the economy, on the other hand, important economic concepts were brought to the country's agenda and it was aimed to increase the awareness of the society to these concepts in the normalization process of the economy. Thanks to this effective communication policy we have been implementing, confidence in the policies we have implemented since 2001 and the targets we have set has increased over time, and inflation expectations have converged with our targets. Dear Guests, As I mentioned before, a significant distance has been covered in the fight against inflation since 2002; inflation has fallen to single digits from 70 percent levels at the beginning of 2002. However, price stability in Turkey has not yet been achieved; In this context, our determined struggle against inflation continues. It should be remembered that this is a long and difficult process. In this context, I would like to briefly touch on the recent inflation developments and the monetary policy response. As you all know, there was an upward trend in inflation in the first 7 months of 2006; As of July, inflation rose to 11.69 percent. This upward trend in inflation was influenced by supply-side factors and external conditions in this period. Unprocessed food prices have risen rapidly since the last months of 2005 due to adverse weather conditions and increased by 21.8 percent year-on-year as of July 2006. 2 Another factor that adversely affects inflation is the increase in crude oil and energy prices since the first quarter of 2006 as a result of the upward trend in crude oil prices in foreign markets and the rise in exchange rates in the May-June period. The contribution of these increases in energy prices to monthly inflation in July was 0.3 points. Due to the fluctuations in international markets and the depreciation of the Turkish currency, the increases in gold prices in the first seven months of the year, which reached an annual rate of 72.6 percent as of July 2006, also adversely affected the inflation figures. In addition, the depreciation of the Turkish currency as a result of the volatility in the financial markets in May and June caused high increases in the prices of goods priced in foreign currency and imported goods; As a result, the effect of increasing consumer inflation in the May-June period reached 1.5 points. By August, inflation had fallen by 0.44 percent month-on-month, consistent with our projections; it was 5.3 percent in the first eight months and 10.26 percent year-on-year. In this decrease in inflation; Decreases of 1.21 percent per month in food and non-alcoholic beverages group prices and 6.92 percent per month in clothing and footwear group prices and the elimination of the base effect in alcoholic beverages and tobacco group prices played an important role. The special comprehensive CPI indicators, which increased in the May-July period due to the effect of increases in the exchange rate, declined overall, consistent with our forecast that the effect of developments in the exchange rate on inflation will decrease in August. This improvement in inflation developments in August is an important development in terms of reaching single-digit inflation figures by the end of the year. Dear Listeners, In countries like ours with a history of high and chronic inflation, economic units tend to exaggerate the negative effects of shocks in general. Therefore, inflation is due to seasonal reasons 3 Even temporary increases can sometimes lead to a deterioration in medium- and long-term inflation expectations and pricing behavior. The recent rise in inflation in our country has led to a deterioration in medium and long-term inflation expectations with the effect of fluctuations in financial markets due to internal and external developments. Against this background, 12-month inflation expectations increased from 5.47 percent in April to 8.07 percent in July; 24-month inflation expectations slightly moved away from targets, rising to 6.07 percent in July from 4.67 percent in April. In order to stop this deterioration in both inflation and expectations and to achieve medium-term targets, our Bank effectively used short-term interest rates, which are its main policy instrument, in line with the medium-term perspective; In this context, the Monetary Policy Committee increased policy rates by 425 basis points to 17.5 percent by going to a strong monetary tightening. I would like to state here that Turkey is not the only country that reacts to the negative effects of the turbulence in international markets on financial markets and inflation; many other countries have also raised their short-term interest rates during such periods, sometimes even higher than ours. Following the strong monetary tightening of the Monetary Policy Committee, extreme volatility in financial markets began to decrease and medium- and long-term inflation expectations began to improve. Thus, by September, 12-month inflation expectations decreased to 7.54 percent and 24-month inflation expectations to 5.99 percent. Dear Listeners, When we look at the course of inflation in the future, we anticipate that the negative impact of exchange rates, which increased in the May-June period, on inflation will gradually decrease, as in August. In addition, the consumption trend of the turbulence in the financial markets in the May-June period 4 It is anticipated that its slowing effect on it may be temporary and therefore cause only a limited decline in aggregate demand growth in the second half of the year. It should not be forgotten that the effect of the interest rate decisions we take on economic activity and inflation is revealed with a certain delay. In this context, we expect that the impact of our interest rate decisions on aggregate demand will begin to emerge towards the end of 2006 and will be strongly felt in the first half of 2007. Dear Guests, Thanks to the measures taken by our Bank since June and the recent improvement in global liquidity conditions, we expect that the secondary effects of the movements in exchange rates and commodity prices on inflation will be limited, the pressure that may occur on inflation in 2007 will decrease and the process of decline in inflation will continue. At this point, I would like to make one point. After the monetary tightening and the measures we have taken for the stability of the financial markets, there has naturally been a decrease in the amount of liquidity in the markets. The impact of this change in the amount of liquidity on economic activity is also closely monitored by us. Accordingly, due to the relative improvement in the medium-term inflation outlook and inflation expectations and the more favorable international liquidity conditions, the Monetary Policy Committee decided not to change the short-term interest rates in August and September. However, the Board will continue to maintain its cautious attitude as the risks in front of the disinflation process continue and the medium-term inflation expectations are not yet at levels compatible with the targets; In the event of developments that will adversely affect inflation in the medium term, it will not refrain from additional monetary tightening. Dear Guests, As I mentioned earlier, there are a number of risks in the medium term of inflation falling in line with our projections. 5 Although there has been a recent decline in oil prices, it is not yet clear whether this decline is permanent. There is always a risk that oil prices will increase, especially due to political developments. Another important risk factor is the rapid changes in global risk perceptions and international liquidity conditions that may arise from the monetary policies of developed countries. If such a situation occurs, our Bank will not react to temporary increases in inflation in line with the medium-term perspective, but will closely monitor the medium-term course of inflation. The deterioration of pricing behaviors, more precisely, going back to past habits and referencing variables other than the inflation target in pricing behaviors is another important risk factor in front of the disinflation process. Our Bank will not abandon its cautious stance until medium-term inflation expectations converge to the targets in order to prevent such a risk. Another element of risk that we carefully monitor is price rigidities in the services sector. In order to break these rigidities, it is of great importance to apply practices that increase supply and competition in this sector. Political risks are also carefully monitored by our Bank. I would like to take this opportunity to draw your attention to two issues of great importance in the disinflation process. First of all, the resolute continuation of the tight fiscal policy and the uninterrupted continuation of structural reforms are necessary in order to combat inflation and achieve medium-term inflation targets. In this context, it is of great importance in the fight against inflation that public revenues and pricing policies are established in accordance with inflation targets and that there is no need for non-program public price adjustments by complying with budget spending limits. Secondly, expectations in our country can change rapidly and shift to extremes due to past negative experiences. For this reason, all kinds of practices, initiatives and discourses that will lead to deterioration in risk perceptions and expectations should be avoided as much as possible, disinflation process and macroeconomic 6 it is of great importance for the continuation of stability. In this sense, relations with the IMF and the European Union are two important anchors, especially in terms of medium- and long-term prospects. Dear Guests, It should be ensured that our Bank evaluates all kinds of risks in the scenarios it creates in order to predict inflation and creates its predictions accordingly. In this context, I think that provided that the cautious stance of monetary policy, fiscal discipline and structural reforms continue, the inflation targets of 4 percent for 2007 and 2008 can be achieved. As the Central Bank, we implement all our policies to achieve these goals. Dear Guests, After talking about inflation developments in this way, I would like to briefly touch on the basic elements of the floating exchange rate regime and exchange rate policy that we are implementing. As you know, under the floating exchange rate regime, it is essential that the exchange rates are determined by the conditions of supply and demand in the market. In this context, while determining the short-term value of the Turkish currency with short-term expectations, developments related to foreign exchange supply and demand and the behavior of market players; its medium and long-term value is determined by economic fundamentals, structural reforms and expectations for the medium and long term. Thus, under this exchange rate regime, the Central Bank does not have any commitment, express or implied, regarding the level of the exchange rate, the exchange rate is not a policy instrument. The determination of exchange rates under market conditions does not mean that the Central Bank will not trade in foreign exchange markets at all. The Central Bank trades in the foreign exchange markets mainly for two purposes. The first of these is the daily foreign exchange purchase auctions that we make with transparent and rule-based methods in periods when the supply of foreign currency in the market is high in order to accumulate reserves. Our foreign exchange reserves have increased by 180 percent in the last four years and reached 56.8 billion as of September 15, 2006. Our second type of trading in the foreign exchange markets is to determine the causes of volatility and 7 are direct interventions that we make taking into account their potential consequences. These interventions may be in the form of the Central Bank entering the foreign exchange market and buying or selling foreign currency, or they may be through announcements and verbal warnings. However, these interventions, unlike the tenders we make for the purpose of accumulating reserves, are not mechanical applications. Each situation is evaluated specifically under its own circumstances and the decision to intervene is taken accordingly. With these two types of transactions in the foreign exchange market, our Bank has realized a net foreign exchange purchase of approximately USD 43.7 billion since 2002. Dear Guests, The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey carefully monitors developments in the foreign exchange market due to its direct impact on inflation and financial stability. In this context, I would like to briefly evaluate the turbulence in the financial markets in the May-June period. Due to the interest rate policies of the central banks of developed countries, the change in international liquidity conditions to the detriment of developing countries since the first quarter of 2006 has adversely affected Turkey as well as all other developing countries. However, the increase in domestic risk perceptions on inflation, current account deficit and political issues in this period led to the effect seen in Turkey being stronger compared to other countries. Due to these effects, there was some capital outflow abroad over a period of two months. What is noteworthy here is that most of these outflows are met by the foreign exchange sales of the residents. Dear Guests, In a country with a thirty-year inflationary history, it is very difficult to permanently eliminate the fragility of expectations with structural gains based on only five years of history. For this reason, in this recent period of financial turmoil in all developing countries, short-term market movements resulting from foreign outflows in Turkey have been perceived more negatively than necessary, even though there is no permanent deterioration in macroeconomic fundamentals. 8 Similarly, in the recent period, we see that the discourses "The second wave is coming" and "The markets will fluctuate again" are frequently on the agenda. For this reason, I find it useful to repeat a point that we have emphasized many times before. Under the floating exchange rate regime, such volatility is experienced depending on both external factors and developments originating from our country and may be experienced in the future. In this context, since 2001, when we started to implement the floating exchange rate regime, Turkey has experienced such fluctuations eight times in total. However, as the current economic program and structural reforms are resolutely continued and macroeconomic fundamentals are strengthened, on the one hand, the main trend in which the Turkish currency appreciates has been returned, and on the other hand, the negative impact of such fluctuations on our economy has been less. It should not be forgotten that under the floating exchange rate regime, movements in exchange rates are not an uncertainty, but a risk factor and it is possible to protect against this risk. In this context, it is of great importance for all economic units to protect themselves against interest or exchange rate risk on their balance sheets within the framework of modern risk management principles in order to reduce the negative effects of such turbulences on the economy. Izmir Futures and Options Exchange offers an important opportunity in this regard. Dear Listeners, As the main trend, the appreciation process of the Turkish currency is also the process of gaining the reputation of the Turkish currency. The most important indicator of this is the reverse dollarization that has been taking place since 2002. In this context, the ratio of foreign currency denominated deposits to total deposits decreased from 56.6 percent in 2001 to 36.7 percent in August 2006; The share of investment instruments in Turkish currency in the total has increased. As long as the floating exchange rate regime functions properly, inflation is kept under control with reliable macroeconomic policies, and structural reforms are continued, reverse dollarization and thus the process of reputation and appreciation of the Turkish currency are expected to continue. The Central Bank closely monitors the financial markets and takes the necessary measures within the framework of financial stability, which is its supporting objective. Today, as in the past, our Bank is committed to the medium-term course of market movements and inflation. 9 If it determines that it will have a negative impact, it will not refrain from sharing this opinion with the public and giving the necessary policy reaction. Dear Guests, After talking about inflation and developments in the financial markets in this way, I would like to briefly touch on the growth and employment issues that you are all following closely. The Turkish economy has been growing at high rates for 18 consecutive quarters. In line with this trend, the economy grew by 8.5 percent in real terms in the second quarter of 2006; thus, since 2001, total real growth has reached 39.6 percent and average annual growth has reached 7.9 percent. The striking point here is that these high growth figures, unlike in the past, are not from public sources, but rather from the consumption and investment expenditures of the private sector. In the period from 2001 to the second quarter of 2006, the investment expenditures of the private sector increased by 126.9 percent in real terms, while the investment expenditures of the public sector increased by 15.9 percent. On the consumption side, we see that the expenditures of the private sector increased by 35.9 percent and public expenditures increased by 11.7 percent in the same period. This also shows that the investment-driven base of growth is expanding. In this context, the public sector is no longer interested in growth, but with the expenditures it makes; It contributes by assuming a strong supervisory and regulatory role within the framework of good governance principles and focusing its policies on increasing competitiveness. In this way, the decrease in the need for public borrowing from financial markets also allows the private sector to find cheaper and longer-term resources. In parallel with the process of structural change in the economy, the high increases in productivity also significantly support the high growth process. In addition, these increases in productivity improve the quality of growth and make a significant contribution to its sustainability. 10 In addition, as a result of the increasing opening of our economy to the outside world, exports, which have increased by 151.5 percent cumulatively since July 2006 since 2001, have also made a very important contribution to the high growth figures. It should not be forgotten that in order to sustain export increases in the long term, efforts to increase productivity and specialization in technology and capital-intensive sectors that create high added value are important rather than the advantage provided by exchange rate changes. In this context, when we look at the sectors that are growing the fastest and increasing their exports the most, we see that these are the sectors that have increased their productivity the most. As a result of more companies turning to exports and opening up to international markets due to opening to the outside, domestic and foreign competition has increased in our country. In order to be permanent in this highly competitive environment, it is essential to create medium and long-term strategies instead of short-term approaches. For this, the public and private sectors need to act together and in cooperation. In this context, while the public sector is trying to create an environment in which the private sector can compete with its competitors in international markets under market conditions, the private sector should continue to take measures to increase its efficiency, create strong and transparent balance sheets, turn to capital markets, pay attention to risk management principles, and strive to allocate resources to research and development activities. Dear Listeners, When we look at the outlook for growth up to and after the end of the year, we anticipate that the uncertain environment that emerged due to the fluctuations in the financial markets in the second quarter of the year may adversely affect domestic demand from the third quarter onwards, albeit limitedly, and thus the growth rate may slow down slightly in the second half of 2006 and the first half of 2007. Dear Guests, Structural reforms are extremely important in maintaining high growth rates. These reforms should be strengthened with micro measures and a strategic vision should be observed according to changing needs and new structures. This is the Ninth Development Plan 11 It constitutes an important ground in the field and therefore should be implemented without losing time. Dear Listeners, In parallel with the high growth performance in our country, the number of employed people is gradually increasing. Accordingly, 857 thousand new jobs have been created in non-agricultural sectors in the last year. In addition, depending on the structural change process in the economy, the sectoral distribution of employment is changing, and there is a rapid transition from the agricultural sector to other sectors. The share of the agricultural sector in total employment decreased from 38 percent in 2001 to 29.2 as of June 2006. High growth has also led to an improvement in unemployment rates; The unemployed population and the unemployment rate reached their lowest levels since the third quarter of 2001. In June, the unemployment rate fell 0.3 percentage points to 8.8 percent compared to the same period last year; the non-agricultural unemployment rate decreased by 1 point to 11.5 percent. Similarly, there is a relative improvement in urban unemployment rates. The unemployment rate among the young population, especially in the urban sector, decreased by 2.1 points from 22.5 percent to 20.4 percent. Despite all these positive developments, the desired improvement in unemployment rates has not yet been achieved. The reason for this is that unemployment is a structural problem in our country. Due to the structural change in the labor market, the fact that employees in the agricultural sector leave this sector and join the labor force in cities prevents unemployment rates from falling faster. In addition, the fact that the population growth rate in our country is still at high levels causes the working population to increase rapidly; Despite the increase in the number of people employed as a result, unemployment rates remain high. In addition, the high employment taxes in our country adversely affect employment figures on the one hand and encourage informal employment on the other. The high level of informal employment increases its volatility by preventing employment increases from being permanent. 12 Dear Listeners, It is only possible to solve the unemployment problem in our country permanently and to achieve a sustainable employment increase with long-term and supply-side policies. In this context, our country should follow active policies that will create employment; In this context, in order to provide adequate financing to the real sector, the relationship between the real sector and the financial sector should be strengthened, the investment environment should be improved, the stability in the macroeconomic environment should be ensured permanently and the employment creation capacity of growth should be increased. In addition, training policies should be implemented to increase the skilled labor force in accordance with labor demand, employment taxes and other burdens on employment should be gradually reduced in order to register informal employment, and regional markets for unskilled labor should be created for the unskilled labor force that will emerge with the shrinkage of the agricultural sector. In this context, the framework drawn by the Ninth Development Plan in accordance with the European Union Employment Strategy is a road map in terms of what needs to be done. Dear Listeners, The high growth process we have been experiencing since 2001 has brought about increases in the current account deficit. In this context, as of July 2006, our current account deficit reached 29.6 billion dollars on an annual basis; The ratio of national income to national income was 7.5 percent as of the second quarter of 2006. At this point, I would like to make a point; We, as the Central Bank, have never said in our discourse that the current account deficit is not a problem. We only said that it is necessary to look at whether the current account deficit is sustainable rather than its size, and within this framework, its causes and how it is financed. In this context, increasing financial integration and openness rates in Turkey allow higher current account deficit ratios to be maintained to the extent of consolidation in macroeconomic fundamentals. 13 In addition, the reasons behind the current account deficit are different from those in the past. Today, the current account deficit in our country is mainly due not to increases in consumption, but also to investment increases that increase production capacity. Crude oil prices, which have been on an upward trend in international markets in recent years, are another factor underlying the upward trend in the current account deficit. When oil prices are fixed on the basis of the year 2000, the ratio of current account deficit to national income is 1.4 points lower in the second quarter of 2006. Dear Guests, The quality of financing is also of great importance in maintaining the current account deficit and not perceiving it as a risk. In this context, the improvement of macroeconomic conditions and the structural change process in our country have improved the financing quality of the current account deficit on the one hand and increased the resilience of the economy against possible shocks on the other. Today, the structure of capital movements towards Turkey is changing in favor of long-term capital and foreign direct investments. As of July 2006, long-term capital alone accounts for 77 percent of the current account deficit. In addition, foreign direct investment reached record highs with an annual cumulative level of 16.6 billion in July. Even during the fluctuations in the financial markets that began in May, there was no interruption in the inflows of foreign direct investment. This is an indication of the progress made in macroeconomic stability and confidence in the future. We expect this financing structure, which is dominated by long-term capital and foreign direct investments, to continue in the coming years within the framework of the structural change process in our country's economy and the perspective of full membership of the European Union. Dear Listeners, When analyzing the current account deficit ratios, it should not be forgotten that Turkey's economic structure is different from the past. Now the amount of open positions in the banking sector is much less, the financial sector is much stronger. Tight monetary and fiscal policies are being implemented decisively. Our foreign exchange reserves are high 14 levels, and the floating exchange rate regime successfully performs its shock-absorbing function. Despite these positive changes in the structure of the economy, the current account deficit and its financing, it is normal for the perception of fragility towards the current account deficit to increase and come to the agenda more in an environment where there are turbulences in international markets and uncertainty perceptions are increasing. At this point, I would like to conclude that; The potential of the current account deficit to create risks for the economy is known and closely monitored in coordination with other units responsible for the economy. Dear Guests, Today, I am delighted to meet with you and to be able to share my views on the economic issues on the agenda. Thank you. 15

Ayrca verimlilikteki bu artlar, bymenin niteliini iyiletirmekte ve srdrlebilirliine nemli katkda bulunmaktadr. 10 Bunun yan sra, ekonomimizin giderek daha fazla da almas sonucunda 2001 ylndan beri 2006 yl Temmuz ay itibaryla birikimli olarak yzde 151,5 orannda artan ihracatn da yksek byme rakamlarna son derece nemli katks olmutur.
