Dolaysyla, bugnk bilgilerle oluturulan para politikas duruu ile ilgili varsaym kamuoyu tarafndan gelecee ynelik bir taahht olarak alglanmamaldr. Enflasyon hedeflemesi rejiminde para politikas duruunun gncellenmesinin bir istisna deil bir norm olduunun altn nemle izmekte byk yarar grmekteyim (ekil 2). ekil 1: Tahmin Modeli ve Enflasyon Hedeflemesi Veriler Para Politikasnn Duruu Enflasyon Tahmin Modeli Enflasyon Tahmini Enflasyon Hedeflemesi Rejimi 7 st belirsizlikband 6 5 Nokta Hedef 3 Alt belirsizlikband 2 1 Kontrol ufku: 1,5-2yl Orta vadeli bak as ekil 2: Para Politikas Duruunun Gncellenmesi Veriler (Orta vadeli enflasyon grnmn etkileyen her trl veri) Enflasyon Tahmin Modeli + Enflasyon Hedeflemesi Rejimi Para Politikas Duruu Bu erevede, orta vadeli ngrlerimizden bahsederken ifade etmi olduum para politikas varsaym politika faizlerinin nmzdeki aylarda kesintisiz olarak indirilmeye devam edilecei eklinde bir taahht olarak alglanmamaldr. Aklanan verilere bal olarak politika faizlerinin nmzdeki aydan itibaren bir sre sabit tutulmas mmkn olabilecei gibi, artlarn izin vermesi durumunda az nce ifade etmi olduumdan daha hzl veya daha uzun sreli bir indirim sreci de gndeme gelebilecektir. Konunun daha iyi anlalmas asndan Kurulun 14 Eyll karar nemli bir rnek tekil etmektedir: Hatrlanaca gibi, Temmuz Enflasyon 14 Raporundaki orta vadeli tahminler yln son eyreinin bandan itibaren ksa vadeli faizlerde ll bir indirim yapld varsaym altnda oluturulmutu. Bu varsaymn bir taahht olmad ayn Raporda ... olas faiz indirimleri d talebe, kamu harcamalarna ve orta vadeli enflasyon grnmn etkileyen dier deikenlere dair veri ve bilgi akna bal olarak, daha erken gndeme gelebilecei gibi daha ileriye de ertelenebilecektir ifadesiyle aka belirtilmiti. Nitekim Kurul, hizmet sektr enflasyonundaki iyilemenin beklenenden olumlu olmas ve ABD kredi piyasasndaki sorunlarn i ve d talebe ilikin beklentileri aa ynl ekmesiyle, son eyrei beklemeden Eyll aynda ll bir faiz indirimine gitmitir. Deerli Basn Mensuplar, Konumamn bu son blmnde, nmzdeki dnemde enflasyon ve para politikasnn grnmnn her iki ynde gncellenmesine neden olabilecek temel risk unsurlarn zetlemek istiyorum: Uluslararas likidite koullarndaki ve kredi piyasalarndaki gelimeler yakndan izlenmektedir. Bugn itibaryla dnya ekonomisinde sert bir yavalama olmayaca gr n plana kmakta ve gelimekte olan lkelere olan sermaye akmnda belirgin bir azal gzlenmemektedir. Bununla birlikte finansal piyasalarda risklerin fiyatlanmasnda halen glk yaanmas temkinli olunmasn gerektirmektedir. nmzdeki dnemde riskten ka eiliminin derinlemesi ve bu durumun gelimekte olan piyasalara olan yatrm itahn azaltmas durumunda, Merkez Bankas, etkin likidite ynetimiyle ve gerektiinde dier politika aralarn kullanarak olas dalgalanmalarn orta vadeli enflasyon grnm zerindeki etkilerini snrl tutmay amalayacaktr. Kredi piyasalarnda yaanan son dalgalanma bir nceki Enflasyon Raporunda toplam talep koullarna ilikin ifade edilen yukar ynl riskleri ksmen azaltmtr. Bununla birlikte, toplam talep gelimelerine ilikin her iki ynde de riskler bulunmaktadr. Yukar ynl riskler esas olarak uzun vadeli faizlerde son dnemde gzlenen aa ynl hareketin kredi talebini ne lde uyaraca konusundaki belirsizliklerden kaynaklanmaktadr. Dier yandan, dnya ekonomisinde beklenenden hzl bir yavalama olmas durumunda, gerek d talep gerekse finansman koullarndaki muhtemel daralma nedeniyle i talep beklenenden daha zayf seyredebilecektir. Aa ve yukar ynl bu riskler nedeniyle Merkez Bankas nmzdeki dnemde finansman koullar ve kredi gelimelerini yakndan takip etmeye devam edecektir. Yurt d finansman koullarnn beklenenden daha olumlu seyretmesi ve i talepte bir ivmelenme olmas durumunda, politika faizlerinde daha temkinli bir duru sergilenebilecei gibi munzam karlklar ve benzeri dier politika aralarna da bavurulabilecektir. Toplam talep zerindeki aa ynl risklerin ortaya 15 kmas durumunda ise politika duruu da enflasyona ilikin aa ynl riskleri giderecek ekilde gncellenebilecektir. Orta vadeli enflasyon ve para politikas grnm oluturulurken 2008 yl btesindeki harcama hedeflerine bal kalnaca varsaylmtr. Bu varsaymdan sapmalar enflasyon ve para politikas grnmn etkileyebilecektir. 2008 ylnda gelirler politikasnn enflasyon hedefi ile byk lde uyumlu yrtlecek olmas, beklentilerin ve i talebin ynetimi asndan olumlu bir gelimedir. Ancak faiz d bte dengesindeki sapmann ksmen giderilmesine ynelik abalarn daha ok dolayl vergi artna ynelmesi, enflasyonun tahmin edilebilirlii asndan risk oluturmaktadr. Gda fiyatlarndaki artlar enflasyon grnmne ilikin nemli bir risk unsuru olarak deerlendirilmektedir. Orta vadeli tahminlerimiz gda fiyatlarndaki artn kademeli bir ekilde yavalayarak hedef enflasyon dzeylerine yaklaacan varsaymaktadr. Ancak, 2007 ylnda tahl rnlerindeki retim kayplarnn srmesi ve gda fiyat artnn kresel bir eilime dnmesi yukar ynl riskleri artrmtr. Dier yandan gda fiyatlarnda oluan yksek baz aa ynl bir dzeltme olasln ykseltmitir. TFE iinde gda fiyatlarnn arlnn yksek olmas ve gda fiyatlarndaki oynakln srmesi, enflasyon tahminlerine ilikin her iki ynde de risk oluturmaktadr. Merkez Bankas, ikincil etkiler snrl kald srece gda fiyatlarndaki gelimelere tepki vermeyecektir. Enerji fiyatlarndaki gelimelerin orta vadeli enflasyon grnm zerindeki etkisine ilikin belirsizlikler bulunmaktadr. Yakn gelecekte elektrik fiyatlarnda yksek oranl bir fiyat ayarlamas gerekleebilecektir. TFE iinde bir dier enerji kalemi olan su fiyatlar ise yine yln son eyreinde il baznda farkllasa da yksek artlar gstermektedir. Bunun yannda uluslararas petrol fiyatlarndaki art da devam etmektedir. Enflasyon beklentileri ve fiyatlama davranlar olumsuz etkilenmedii srece, enerji fiyatlarndaki gelimelerin orta vadeli enflasyon zerindeki etkileri snrl kalacaktr. Ancak, enerji fiyatlarnn iktisadi faaliyetlerlerde nemli bir girdi tekil etmesi nedeniyle enerji fiyatlarna ilikin risklerin Merkez Bankasn faiz indirimlerinde greli olarak daha ihtiyatl olmaya sevk ettiini de belirtmeliyim. Dier yandan, elektrikte maliyet temelli otomatik fiyatlamaya geilmesi halinde hem arz gvenlii hem de fiyat istikrar zerindeki riskler azaltlm olacaktr. Deerli Basn Mensuplar, Saygdeer Konuklar, Enflasyonla mcadelede son yllarda nemli mesafeler alnmtr. Ancak, gelinen noktay fiyat istikrar olarak tanmlamak henz mmkn deildir. Merkez Bankas para politikas aralarn, fiyat istikrarn salamak ve dolaysyla toplumun uzun vadedeki refahnn artmasna katkda bulunmak amacyla kullanmaya devam edecektir. Bu dorultuda, dier ekonomik birimlerin de ksa vadeli karlar uruna 16 uzun vadeli kalc kazanmlardan dn vermemeleri makroekonomik istikrara ulamann maliyetini azaltacaktr. Szlerime son vermeden nce, fiyat istikrarna giden yolda, para politikasnn yannda maliye politikalarnn ve yapsal reformlarn desteinin byk nem tadn bir kez daha hatrlatmakta fayda grmekteyim. Bu erevede Avrupa Birliine uyum ve yaknsama srecinin devam etmesi ile ekonomik programa ilikin yapsal reformlarn hayata geirilmesi konusundaki abalarn devamll nemini korumaktadr. zellikle mali disiplinin kalitesini artracak olan yapsal reformlar konusundaki gelimeler, gerek makroekonomik istikrar gerekse fiyat istikrar asndan yakndan izlediimizi belirterek konumama son veriyor ve hepinize teekkrlerimi sunuyorum. 17

Title: Speech in Finance Club
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey The Global Financial Crisis and the Central Bank Durmu Ylmaz Governor 18 May 2009 Istanbul Distinguished guests, It is a great pleasure for me to address the pioneers of the world of finance at this conference held by the Finance Managers Trust of Turkey, one of the prominent non-governmental organizations in the field of Turkish finance that conducts studies to enhance the financial markets in Turkey. In the first part of my speech, I would like to share my views about the global financial crisis. The turmoil in the US subprime mortgage market, which erupted in the second half of 2007, started to spillover to the overall credit markets challenging both financial and economic stability. I believe that there are mainly two reasons underlying the widespread and devastating effects of this crisis. The first of these is the globalization phenomenon that has gained pace since early 1980s reaching its peak in the 2000s. Globalization led the world economies and financial systems to become highly integrated. A natural consequence of this integration is the increasing commonality among the business cycles of individual economies. The second factor is that this is a financial crisis and that erupted in many developed economies simultaneously. Empirical studies indicate that financial crises are more severe and long-lasting compared to other types of crises and that emerging from such crises is a slow and gradual process. Derivative products, which comprise a large portion on the balance sheets of financial institutions, and which are too complex to be priced, exacerbate the loss. Therefore, I believe that it would be more realistic to adopt a cautious approach in the face of the claims that the global crisis will come to an end in the short-run. A certain degree of optimism has predominated the financial markets in recent weeks. The stress tests applied to banks in the USA turned out to yield better-thanexpected results. This development, along with recent data on economic activity and first quarter balance sheets of companies in the USA, stimulated perceptions that the global crisis may have already hit the bottom and that the economic recovery process may start earlier than predicted. 1 However, we should remember that this crisis produced tremendous losses on the balance sheets of financial institutions as well as with the assets of households. The total losses incurred by financial institutions have reached USD 2 trillion and is still on the rise. The total loss in the assets of households is estimated to reach USD 11.5 trillion in the USA alone in 2008. Assuming that the wealth effect on consumption expenditures is 0.04, a simple calculation leads us to predict a USD 500 billion fall in consumption expenditures in the USA solely due to the wealth effect. The loss of confidence and deterioration in risk perceptions on the back of the ongoing crisis has led to a reduction in both the lending tendency of banks and investment expenditures of the corporate sector. Asset write-downs coupled with the negative expectations of households pertaining to the future has effected an increase in the precautionary saving tendency. Moreover, in line with the severe contraction in demand, massive slumps have been witnessed in production and employment not seen since the World War II. Considering the size of the loss incurred by financial institutions and households, it is not very probable to eliminate the financial squeeze, to restore confidence and/or to revive global demand in the short-run. The recent optimism witnessed in global markets is mainly attributable to economic data not being as bad as expected rather than showing signs of recovery. This should be perceived as an indicator of the extent of the loss that the crisis produced on expectations. Distinguished guests, As I have just mentioned, because of the globalization process and the crisis originating from the financial system, the current global crisis is expected to be deeper and last longer than previous ones. Meanwhile, this crisis also has a distinctive favorable characteristic, which is the implementation of global fiscal and monetary measures of the size, speed and coordination that were never witnessed before. This raises ambiguity pertaining to the responses from financial markets and economies in the upcoming period to these measures. In spite of the recent slight improvement in expectations, it still remains uncertain as to when recovery in the global economy will start. The gradually accelerating downtrend of global industrial production indices since the second half of 2008 decelerated in March 2009. However, the indices are still in decline, albeit at a slower pace. Monthly growth rate forecasts for developed countries continue to be 2 revised downwards each month. Likewise, despite some recovery recently, indicators such as the volume of future orders, real sector confidence indices, house sales and credit conditions of banks indicate that economic contraction still persists. To sum up, as the Central Bank of Turkey, we maintain our opinion that the credit crunch in international credit markets still persists, that there is yet to be a significant recovery in the global economy and that global economic recovery to be slow and gradual. Distinguished guests, After a short assessment of the global developments, I would like to devote the second part of my speech to the recent developments in the Turkish economy and the monetary policy that we have implemented. The global turmoil, which emerged in the second half of 2007, adversely affected financing facilities and foreign demand, and led to a significant slowdown in economic activity in developing countries, and Turkey was no exception. Parallel to the contraction in aggregate demand coupled with the sharp drop in commodity prices, inflation plummeted markedly. Easing of concerns over inflation enabled us to focus on containing potential adverse effects of global financial turmoil on the domestic economy without compromising our price stability objective. Slowdown in domestic demand conditions, low level of exchange rate pass-through, tight financing prospects, declining import prices, the relative resilience of the Turkish financial system and improving inflation expectations not only necessitated but also facilitated a controlled but quite rapid rate cut cycle.With the reversal of global developments fueling inflation in the last quarter of 2008, the Central Bank took prompt action to cut interest rates and adopted a pioneer role among emerging marketsThe analysis conducted by the CBT indicates that policy rate cuts of a total of 750 basis points have alleviated the severity of excessive volatility in economic activity. The developments observed since November 2008 in domestic financial markets and especially the recent inflation data have confirmed the accuracy of the CBTs projections and the policy rate-cut decisions thereto, thus have increased confidence in monetary policy. 3 Besides policy rate-cut decisions, a series of measures have been taken to ensure the mobilization of the financial system and efficient functioning of credit markets. The liquidity need of the market was met via auctions in due time and overnight interest rates were meticulously kept close to Central Bank borrowing interest rates. During times of increasing global uncertainties, the CBT took measures to maintain foreign exchange liquidity in order to avoid any liquidity squeeze and to ensure smooth operation of foreign exchange markets. The CBT has also taken measures to mitigate the adverse effects of global financial turmoil on the corporate sector and has introduced some new arrangements regarding export rediscount credits. These arrangements led to a sharp increase in the volume of export rediscount credits extended via Turkish Eximbank. While the total credit utilization in 2008 was USD 1.7 million, credit utilization in the first four months of 2009 rose to USD 550 million. As a consequence of the measures taken and the limited recovery in risk perceptions, the level of market interest rates is below the pre-global crisis level in real terms. The realization of neutral interest rates at lower levels during economic recessions, which is an expected development in well-functioning economies, has never been experienced in Turkey before. This development should be perceived as an indicator of the normalization of the Turkish economy. The considerable decline in policy rates and interest rates of government securities is not commensurately reflected on credit interest rates and this causes the additional tightness in financial conditions to persist, though at a lesser extent. We believe that the run-up in default risk of credit users, maturity mismatch between deposits and credits, and limitations on the financing facilities of banks are some of several factors curbing banks tendency to extend credits. As I have mentioned before, the necessary measures to avoid a possible TL liquidity squeeze were taken in due time. However, it should be borne in mind that even if the liquidity facilities provided by the CBT alleviated the liquidity squeeze in the market; with respect to maturity, they cannot be a substitute to the financing facilities that the banks used to utilize. The Bank Loans Tendency Survey conducted by the CBT indicate that the investment-driven credit demand has significantly decreased recently; a large portion of the credit demand stems from the intention of companies to restructure their 4 corporate credits and that the risk perceptions of banks play an important role in banks tightening their credit conditions. Distinguished participants, In the first part of my speech, I explained our expectations for the global economy and stated that it would take time for growth rates to turn positive. In the last part of my speech, I would like to share with you our expectations for the Turkish economy. Subsequent to the recent rate cuts and fiscal measures, we anticipate that domestic demand in Turkey might gain relative stability in the second quarter of 2009 and growth will post positive figures from the last quarter onwards. In other words, the recovery in the Turkish economy might start earlier than that of the global economy. Our expectation is underpinned by two main factors. The first of these is the sound and stable structure of our financial system. Unlike its emerging market peers, the Turkish banking system has not required a stimulus plan up to now. The volatility in the financial markets in Turkey  one of the emerging economies with historically high volatility and particular sensitivity to global risk perceptions  has remained relatively limited since October 2008. The restructuring plans along with regulatory and supervisory reforms, which were put into effect in the aftermath of the 2001 financial crisis at the cost of imposing a heavy burden on the public budget, enhanced the Turkish banking systems resilience to shocks compared to the banking systems of other countries. Balance sheets free of distressed foreign assets, the strong level of capital and liquidity adequacy ratios of our banks will support the normalization of the Turkish credit markets earlier than its peers worldwide. The hikes in Turkey risk premium during the crisis lagged behind those of many other emerging market economies, and Turkey has shown significant resistance to the crisis at an extent more than implied by her credit rating. We note these developments as a natural outcome of the structural transformation that the country has undergone. Another factor that will facilitate a relatively faster recovery for the Turkish economy is the household indebtedness ratio, which is lower than those of many other emerging economies. Households have been affected relatively less by 5 exchange rate shocks owing to the significantly low share of FX-denominated and FX-indexed loans in consumer loans. Backed by the prudent monetary policy implemented since mid-2006, credit expansion in Turkey has been more moderate compared to other countries and this, in turn, has led households to defer their consumption demands. The increase of household consumption between the first quarter of 2006 and the last quarter of 2008 lagged behind the economic growth rate and the share of household consumption in the GDP declined from 72 percent to 69.7 percent. Therefore, we anticipate that the revival of economic activity in the short term will be mainly driven by the rebound in private consumption expenditures. Confidence indices and coincident indicators of demand expectations suggest that the economy may start to recover slightly by the second quarter of the year. However, I would like to underline once more that economic recovery is expected to be gradual and slow as opposed to the rapid recovery in economic activity after the 1994 and 2001 crises experienced in Turkey and that a significant acceleration in aggregate demand is not expected anytime soon. Persisting tightness in external financing conditions, lagged and gradual recovery in our primary export markets and the large share of durables and capital goods exports, which are sensitive to foreign demand, indicate that the recovery in the Turkish economy will be different from what we have experienced so far. Likewise, private sector investment expenditures, which are influential in overcoming crises, are not expected to display a rapid recovery in the forthcoming period. We think that the rise in unemployment rates will persist throughout 2009 and put further downward pressure on disposable income and unit labor costs for quite some time. Moreover, non-farm employment indicators will recover with a further lag compared to aggregate demand. Temporary tax reductions imposed on some goods in this period, by advancing future demand, have led to a slight improvement in expectations in the domestic market. Fiscal measures taken to mitigate the effects of global turmoil coupled with the reduction in tax revenues have recently led to a rise in budget deficit. Some easing in fiscal policy is understandable under the current conditions. The current debt structure of the public sector provides some room for maneuver, albeit limited, to implement a counter-cyclical fiscal policy. However, it should be kept in mind that the average maturity of public debt is still short and that financial depth is relatively low in Turkey. The significant and constant increase in public borrowing 6 coupled with the recovery of domestic demand might exert upward pressure on market rates and reduce the effectiveness of monetary policy. I would like to emphasize once more the importance of building a mechanism that will observe business cycles but will safeguard fiscal discipline in the medium term as well as the significance of supporting the short term fiscal easing with a concrete medium term fiscal framework. While concluding my remarks, I would like to extend my thanks to the members of the Finance Managers Trust of Turkey, who have organized this event and to those who have contributed to it. 7

Title: Speech of President Ylmaz on the Introduction of Financial Stability Report III
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: ON THE LAUNCH OF THE "FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT" Durmu YILMAZ 4 December 2006 Ankara Dear Guests, Dear Members of the Press, As it is known, the main objective of our Bank is to ensure and maintain price stability, and as a supporter of this goal, it is among the duties of our Bank to take measures to ensure stability in the financial system. Our Bank shares its assessments of financial stability with the public through the Financial Stability Report. In June, we shared with you the first issue of the Financial Stability Report, which is published twice a year, for 2006. Today, I am pleased to present to you the third issue of the Financial Stability Report, which was prepared specifically for the effects of the fluctuation in the May-June period. The report will also be published on our Bank's website as of today. A strong financial system that functions effectively helps to effectively implement monetary policy and provides the flexibility necessary to overcome external shocks. With this understanding, the Central Bank monitors the risk factors that threaten the financial system and the vulnerabilities of the system and draws attention to the issues it deems necessary by announcing its evaluations to the public. Dear Members of the Press, It is seen that the strict monetary and fiscal policy implementations, the ongoing structural reforms, the economic program implemented and the convergence process with the EU and the floating exchange rate regime policy make the Turkish economy more resistant to external shocks. Indeed, compared with previous experiences, the one that appeared in the period from May to June 2 The relatively limited effects of the fluctuation confirm this observation. In the first half of 2006, international developments such as the deterioration in global liquidity conditions and the decrease in the risk appetite of foreign investors for developing countries and the resulting uncertainty perceptions reflected negatively on our country's markets as well as other developing countries. The Central Bank decided to tighten monetary tightening in order to correct medium-term inflation expectations and increased policy interest rates. I would like to point out here that perhaps the most important thing a central bank needs to do to prevent financial instability is to provide a macroeconomic environment with low and stable inflation and sustainable economic growth. Therefore, these measures aimed to prevent the deterioration of macro balances in the medium and long term by adhering to the inflation target, thus contributing to the preservation of financial stability. As a matter of fact, the measures taken have started to show their effect since July and the volatility in the markets has decreased. The Central Bank does not see a contradiction between its ultimate goal of price stability and financial stability, which it considers as a complementary goal, and considers the stability of the financial system as a whole in its monetary policy decision-making process. On the other hand, in the event that threats to the entire financial system arise in the short term, the Central Bank has the power and determination to take the necessary measures without jeopardizing the price stability that it observes with a medium-term prediction. 3 Dear Members of the Press, Discipline in public finances remains important for maintaining financial stability. In 2006, the structure and level of public debt continued to improve. In the domestic debt composition of the public, the share of variable interest and foreign currency denominated debt stocks in Turkish currency decreased compared to the end of 2005, which shows that the Treasury's sensitivity to interest and exchange rate risk has decreased. The Undersecretariat's recent swap transaction in international markets indicates that the Treasury's borrowing costs have been minimally affected by the recent volatility. In addition to monetary discipline in the process of falling inflation, the importance of maintaining fiscal discipline and maintaining structural reforms without interruption is undoubtedly great. In this context, due to the continued possibility of global liquidity conditions turning against developing countries and the uncertainty brought about by the elections, the resolute maintenance of fiscal discipline and the achievement of non-interest rate surplus targets within this framework remain important for the preservation of financial stability. The ratio of household liabilities to financial assets also increased rapidly in the first half of 2006. However, in parallel with the rise in interest rates, the slowdown in the rate of increase of consumer loans since July has caused the rate to remain flat. Although household liabilities are increasing, the ratio to GDP is below the Eurozone average. Although the May-June fluctuation eliminated attractive interest rates for the use of new loans, the fact that consumer loans are fixed interest rates as required by the legislation so that households have a current 4 it has not increased the interest burden on its debts. However, although its share in consumer loans is decreasing, it is seen that the amount of foreign currency indexed loans of households has reached approximately 1.5 billion New Turkish Liras. Considering that the increase in exchange rates increases the debt burden of this segment, it is clear that the borrowing of households that do not earn foreign currency income carries a high risk and should be avoided. On the other hand, I would like to share with you a development that we see positively regarding credit cards. In my speech on the last issue of the report, I stated that it would be in favor of credit card holders who have short-term credit needs to meet these requirements with consumer loans instead of credit cards. I would like to express with pleasure that according to the data we have, the portion of the expenditures made with credit cards that are installments with interest decreases proportionally over time. Consumers continuing this trend and using credit cards as a means of payment will minimize grievances. Dear Members of the Press, In the period following the global fluctuation, the regain of the strong position of the New Turkish Lira, the dependence of increasing industrial production on imports of intermediate goods, and the high level in energy prices, although it tended to fall, led to the continuation of the upward trend of the ratio of the current account deficit to GDP compared to the end of 2005. The increasing current account deficit due to high economic growth needs to be closely monitored in terms of the economy and therefore financial stability. Short term, which has an important share in the financing of the current account deficit in the past 5 term portfolio investments are gradually decreasing and are being replaced by direct investments and long-term loans provided by the private sector. The borrowing of the companies that receive the largest share from the provided foreign resources in foreign currency increases their foreign currency position deficits. The depreciation of the national currency may increase the default risk of borrowers and cause the exchange rate risks carried by the companies to be reflected in the banking sector as credit risk. In this respect, real sector companies should be aware of currency risk management and use hedging tools widely, while banks should carefully evaluate the credit risks of companies with foreign currency open positions. As it is known, the financial statements of the companies operating in Turkey are arranged on the basis of the total amount of Turkish currency without distinction between Turkish currency and foreign currency, and therefore the foreign currency positions of the companies cannot be calculated on the balance sheets. Our Bank has been carrying out studies to determine the exchange rate risk of companies for some time. In this study, various statistical reports and balance of payments statistics made to our Bank and the information compiled from the "Locational Banking Statistics" database of the Undersecretariat of Treasury of the Prime Ministry of the Republic of Turkey and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) were utilized. In this issue of our report, we share the results of this study with you. Accordingly, the net foreign currency position deficit of the non-bank sector increased by 49 percent from USD 29 billion at the end of 2005 to USD 43 billion as of June 2006, and was realized at approximately the same level in September. 6 In particular, I would like to state that in the analyzes and evaluations made, the exchange rate risk of the real sector companies was discussed from a macro perspective. Therefore, considering that some companies may have open positions and some firms may have more positions, it should be taken into consideration that the vulnerability of the real sector to exchange rate risk should be evaluated only by analysis that can be made on a firm basis. In order to eliminate this drawback, our Report also examined the position deficits of 158 companies other than the financial sector whose shares are traded on the ISE as aggregated based on the information disclosed by the ISE. Dear Members of the Press, The banking sector, which constitutes the largest share in the financial sector, grew by 9.1 percent in real terms in the first nine months of 2006 despite the volatility in the markets, and the interest of foreign investors in the sector continued. The share of loans in the banking sector's balance sheets continues to increase. The growth in loan volume was mainly due to personal loans, especially housing loans. However, the increase in loan interest rates due to the fluctuations seen in the financial markets in the recent period has led to a slowdown in the growth rate of personal loans since June. The slowdown in the rate of credit volume growth is expected to continue in the coming period. Although 6 months have passed since the fluctuation in the May-June period, there is no deterioration in the rate of conversion of the banking sector's loans to overdue receivables. In addition, the continuation of the high reciprocity policy for overdue receivables in 2006 was positive in terms of credit risk. 7 evaluated. On the other hand, it is very positive that the BRSA has taken a prudent approach and doubled the overall reserve ratios for newly opened loans. Banks continued their tendency to balance their foreign currency net overall positions. Therefore, the effect of the increase in exchange rates since May on the profitability of the sector has been limited. The sector's capital adequacy ratio has declined since the end of 2005 due to the expansion and volatility in loans until July, and since then it has been on an upward trend and has been realized as 20.5 percent in September. According to the scenario analysis in our report, it is seen that the current equity structure of the sector is at a level that can meet possible losses. The fact that the decline in the Financial Robustness Index, which we monitor as an indicator of the soundness of the banking sector, is limited despite the fluctuations seen in May and June, shows that the sector is resistant to vulnerabilities. As a matter of fact, the Robustness Index, which was 117.2 at the end of 2005, decreased to 111.8 as of May 2006 and increased to 114.3 in September due to the decline of other sub-indices excluding asset quality. In addition to the ongoing prudent regulations, the strengthening of the supervision and supervision infrastructure and the development of a risk management culture in the banking sector have played a major role in the relatively limited impact of the volatility in the financial markets on the financial structures of the banks. In this context, the "target ratio" application introduced by the BRSA in order to encourage operating with a higher level of equity against possible market fluctuations is also evaluated positively. 8 In general, although it is seen that the effects of the volatility experienced in May and June on the banking sector are limited in the short term, it should be taken into consideration that some of its effects may occur belatedly. Dear Members of the Press, The publication dates of the Financial Stability Report, which is published twice a year, for the coming year will be announced with the announcement regarding the Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies for 2007 that we will make this month. 9

Title: Speech on "Price Stability", SBFKonferans
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: PRICE STABILITY I. WHAT IS PRICE STABILITY? Price stability, by a general definition, refers to a low rate of inflation to the extent that people do not need to take into account in their decisions regarding investment, consumption, and saving. Today, in developed countries, we see that inflation rates between 1 percent and 3 percent are considered low inflation rates. Therefore, price stability is not only about achieving a low inflation rate; it includes the maintenance of that rate. However, environments in which the low inflation rate is maintained for a certain period of time are considered as environments where price stability is ensured. In other words, the fact that inflation reaches low levels between 1 percent and 3 percent and then rises back to high levels, such as above 10 percent, does not mean that price stability has been achieved. In this context, it was previously desired to achieve price stability in our country and the inflation rate decreased to relatively low levels with the stabilization programs implemented in various periods; however, it was not possible to ensure price stability due to the fact that the programs implemented could not be continued. For this reason, in our country, there has not been a period in which price stability has been achieved in the last twenty-five years. 1 . What Happens If There Is No Price Stability? "Birtoplumutahrip etmeninen etk iliyolu,o toplumunparasn tahripetmektir." 1 Price stability is an indispensable condition for achieving economic and social stability. The failure to achieve price stability can affect a country's economy, political and 1 Lenin 'e atfen, W. Eucke n, Grundsatze der Wirtschaftspolitik, 2"d ed., Mohr, Tubingen, 1955, p.255. 1 The extent of the damage it has caused to its social structure, the situation our country has been in for the last twenty-five years and the experiences of other countries are clearly seen. For this reason, after all these crises, the fact that the only and ultimate goal of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey is price stability is emphasized both in the press releases of our Bank and in various reports published. At this point, revealing the problems encountered due to the inability to ensure price stability is very important in terms of understanding why price stability is given such importance all over the world. The effects of failure to ensure price stability are as follows: - In inflationary environments, firms and consumers, or in short, all units that make decisions in the economy, cannot easily distinguish relative price changes when making investment and consumption decisions and cannot have the necessary and sufficient information to make healthy decisions. Because stable money, in other words stable prices, is the cornerstone of a well-functioning market economy. - Inflation reduces the ability of financial markets to act efficiently as players in the market cannot predict the future and do not have the necessary knowledge. It reduces the efficiency of the financial intermediation system and therefore the volume of loans. - In environments of high and continuous inflation, investors demand a risk premium due to the uncertainty created by the inflation environment, especially in the rates of return on their long-term investments. As a result, real interest rates, which include a high risk premium, remain high. - High interest rates, which are the result of inflation, restrict the credit demands of the companies from the point of view of the producers, while from the point of view of consumers, it is directly related to social justice and long-term such as owning a house, which is a right. 2 It prevents the development of credit markets, which are prerequisites for expenditures that require financing, and prevents consumers from providing loans for long terms. - Inflation is a kind of tax burden on investments. Therefore, inflation, which means an additional cost for investors, creates variability in the rate of economic growth as it causes investments to fluctuate over periods. Accordingly, when we look at the long term, it is seen that the average growth rates are low in countries with high inflation. - Another negative impact of high inflation on growth is that investments efficiency. Economic units recover their savings from inflation areas such as non-productive foreign currency, real estate in order to protect and direct a large part of their resources to this area. Inflationary Due to the uncertainty created by the environment, the maturities of investments are shortened and the resources cannot return to productive areas in the economy. In other words, the country total in the economy Resources Consider when received, Country it causes it to produce a lower amount than it can perform. - High inflation also prevents the labor market from working effectively. In such an environment, job seekers and employers cannot see ahead in the medium and long term. In an unstable economic environment, those who want to work, especially if they are unskilled, find a job late and lose their jobs early. - The competitiveness of an economy experiencing high inflation in foreign markets weakens and access to foreign capital markets is restricted. In addition, as a result of the uncertainty experienced due to inflation, the inflow of long-term foreign capital into the country for use in productive areas decreases. The fact that the capital coming to the economy from abroad is largely short-term and speculative leads to the fact that the country's economy is fragile against external shocks. 3 - In the decision-making processes of individuals, habits of indexing to the past rather than looking to the future emerge, inflation gains inertia. - In countries with high inflation, economic policy practices are more likely to be changed, increasing uncertainty about the future. The skepticism created by this uncertainty creates a constraint on the success of policies. Therefore, a vicious circle is formed. - In inflationary environments, the transfer of resources cannot be ensured to be fair. In other words, inflation is a kind of corruption that takes place through the resources in the economy. However, the negative effects of the failure to achieve price stability are not limited to an economic framework. This includes: - Inflation undermines the sense of trust in society; It creates an environment of uncertainty and insecurity about people's present and future, and this destroys a society with all its segments and individuals at every stage of its life. There is also a sense of confidence in an environment of price stability. This sense of trust is when people trust in their own money, hence the values they have, the income they generate, and ultimately their future. - The consequences of the deterioration in the distribution of income and wealth due to inflation have the most impact on the social sphere. In these conditions, the pressure on the fixed-income segments, which have the least chance of protecting themselves financially, increases. To put it another way, the impoverishment of the country increases. - Inflation affects the behavior structure of the whole society as well as the investing. As a result of the uncertainty caused by high inflation, both economic 4 as well as short-term approaches and immoral behaviors increase in social and political relations and processes. As a result, the achievement of price stability confronts us not only as an economic phenomenon but also as a moral imperative. 2. Consequences of Failure to Ensure Price Stability in Turkey The consequences of not being able to ensure price stability, in other words, the attrition caused by inflation in economic and social fields, are also very clearly seen in our country. The leading reason for the distorted income distribution in our country is that price stability has not been achieved for many years. The distortion created by this distorted income distribution is strongly felt in social life. However, at this point, it is useful to clarify some concepts and to make a good diagnosis of the conditions of our country. In the World Bank definitions, less than 2 US dollars of daily income is expressed as poverty, and less than 1 US dollar is expressed as absolute poverty. If these definitions are respected, around 15 percent of our country earns less than 2 US dollars per day; that is, it is poor. Another definition of the World Bank is deprivation, which refers to the inability of people to participate in daily life. A much larger proportion of our people, including 15 percent at the poverty line, are unable to participate in daily life, benefit from adequate health services, receive quality education, or engage in cultural activities. Within the framework of these definitions, in our country, a very large part of people are both poor and deprived. 5 In addition, the segment that feels the corrosive effect of inflation the most is the one with the lowest income level. The reason for all this, poverty and deprivation, unfair income distribution is high inflation and the unstable environment it creates. The cost of living in a highly inflationary environment for many years to our country's economy is quite advanced. Driven by the inflationary environment to protect their savings, economic units have directed their savings largely to non-productive areas such as foreign currency and real estate, as has just been said. The damage caused to our country's economy by the money substitution created by this situation is significant. The share of foreign currency deposits, which is around 58 percent in total deposits, is indicative of the deterioration in the investment decisions of economic units against our own money. The reason for this is inflation. The maturity of the money and credit markets in our country is extremely short. The maturity of total Turkish lira deposits in banks is only 2.3 months. The maturity of more than 70 percent of the total loans is less than 1 year. As we mentioned earlier, inflation reduces the ability of financial markets to act efficiently as intermediaries. The most important indicator of this situation in our country is that the ratio of the total loans given by the banking sector to the non-financial sector to the Gross National Product has decreased to 18.1 percent. This rate has risen to just over 25 per cent in 1997-98 alone. When we look at the world examples, it is seen that this rate is above lOO in the European Union countries. As a result, the banking sector is unable to fulfill its expected task of providing resources to the economy. Due to inflation, due to the inability to absorb resources sufficiently into the system, financial markets are extremely shallow. In addition, the future of individuals 6 in futures markets that require long-term pricing due to their inability to predict operation cannot be done. Capital markets, which are extremely vital in terms of directing the resources in the economy to production, cannot be used by the private sector. Due to the fact that the public deficits, which have been the most important source of inflation in our country from the past to the present and which have been high for many years, are closed through borrowing, almost all of the stock of bonds and bills in the capital markets belongs to the public; and as a result, the private sector's ability to use these markets to fund production is extremely limited. In addition to the inability to use domestic resources efficiently and ensure their effective distribution, foreign capital inflows into the real economy, in other words production, are extremely low due to the uncertainty created by the high inflation environment. Especially since the beginning of the 1990s, our country has experienced many serious crises at more frequent intervals and has had to bear both economic and social costs. This is an indication of how fragile our economy has become due to inflation and how the macroeconomic balances have not been firmly established. Chronic inflation has harmed not only economic growth rates but also the nature of growth. Over time, there is an erosion created by inflation in the quality of the products produced, their marketing and the quality of the services provided. As a result of these conditions, as seen in the studies, our competitiveness in international markets has steadily declined in recent years, which cannot be explained only by economic dimensions such as the development of exchange rates and interest rates, and as seen in Chart l, our country ranked 69th among 80 countries as of 2002. 7 Chart 1. Finally, the instability in the economy has brought about political instability. When we look at our recent political history, it is seen that all elections in our country are early elections and the average election period is 3 years. i. Other Factors Fueling Inflation in Turkey Although it is not immediately noticeable among the consequences and / or causes of inflation in our country, during the long inflationary period we live in, certain elements that feed inflation and feed on inflation in a vicious circle also fuel the deterioration in the economy and society as a whole. These: 8 First of all, political instabilities, the constant electoral environment, as a result, short-term policy implementations in almost every field, especially in the economy, have created obstacles in the implementation of anti-inflation programs that require long-term implementation. Another factor that feeds inflation is the high pricing policies of the public sector to finance public deficits, especially in areas where there is a monopoly. application. In addition, fluctuations in raw material prices, especially crude oil prices, due to external developments and the fact that oil is an important input in production in our country is also an external factor that feeds inflation. In addition, the fact that high inflation has been experienced in our country for a long time has caused economic units to develop habits to continue their activities in such an environment. After all, the fact that it has been experienced with inflation for a long time leads economic units to expect that there will be inflation in the future, thus creating an inertia in inflation that stems from the habit of indexing to the past. Such a structure, due to the desire to maintain old habits, is a resistance to serious and comprehensive policy implementations aimed at combating inflation. form. This inertia, created by the behavior patterns acquired for many years, prolongs the duration of breaking the resistance of inflation despite all the structural changes and measures taken within the scope of the current program we are implementing as of today. 9 Therefore, one of the biggest reasons why inflation expectations within the framework of the current program carry a vulnerability that can be easily reversed is that such habits still persist in people's minds, although they have decreased. The biggest reason why these habits still persist is that there is no period in the last twenty-five or thirty years of our country's history where price stability has been achieved. Therefore, industrialists, exporters, workers, the financial sector and ordinary people, in short, all segments of society, have no experience in how and to what extent price stability will benefit them and to what extent it will raise their living standards. However, in countries where price stability is achieved, since the society feels all the effects of stability directly in its daily life, it reacts to the demands that may lead to the deterioration of this stability, regardless of which segment it comes from, and directly embraces the price stability themselves. In other words, on the contrary, an inertia has been formed. II. DuNYADAFYAT STKRARI 1. Development of Inflation in the WorldIn order to be successful in the struggle against inflation, which is extremely destructive both economically and socially, in our country today, it is extremely important to determine what has been done in the world and to what point it has reached. In this context, when we look at the history of inflation in the world, it is seen that countries have made very serious progress in price stability over the years. In the fight against inflation, countries have gone through many stages over time. Both developed and developing countries have faced serious inflation problems from time to time, and even for various reasons, the inflation rate is expressed in thousands. 10 they have also experienced periods of hyperinflation. In countries experiencing hyperinflation, it has been seen that price stability has been adopted as a common goal to be achieved by the whole society and even it has been suggested that provisions preventing inflation should be included in the constitution as an article. Especially after the abandonment of the Bretton-Woods system in the 1970s and the oil shocks that took place, inflation emerged as a major problem on a global basis. Then, the view that economic stability depends on price stability and that price stability is too important to be left to day-to-day politics is accepted by both economic theorists and policy practitioners. has seen. These developments have brought about structural changes in the competent institutions in the economy. In this context, inflation has come under the responsibility of central banks and the institutional structures and monetary policy designs of central banks have been aimed at reducing inflation to low levels and remaining at these levels, in other words, to ensure price stability. Institutional Structures of Central Banks and Price Stability Considering the experience of the country, the institutional structures of central banks; being independent, accountable and transparent seems to play an active role on the road to price stability. 15 i. Why an Independent Central Bank? Especially after the 1970s, there are some concepts that have been largely agreed upon in the economic literature regarding the structural features that central banks should have in terms of maintaining price stability and therefore economic stability. In this context, the first issue that comes to the fore in the institutional designs of central banks is that a central bank that adopts price stability as a main goal should be independent. As we have already mentioned, if price stability benefits all segments of society, and if it is a prerequisite for long-term prosperity and social justice, it is a need for society to create an independent institution that will stay away from everyday attrition and pursue this goal without distraction. The payoff for this need is a truly independent central bank. In this context, the central bank, which aims to ensure and maintain price stability, which is a prerequisite for the stability of the economy as a whole, must first have legal independence in order to pursue this goal. An independent central bank, whose purpose is clearly and implicitly determined by law, which is primarily price stability, is the greatest obstacle to the indiscriminate use of power at their disposal for the short-term purposes of political powers. Title: Developments in the Turkish Economy in the Light of Fighting Inflation
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: DEVELOPMENTS IN THE TURKISH ECONOMY IN THE LIGHT OF THE FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION Gazi Ercel B as an CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF TURKEY Washington September 1999 Two years ago, in the summer of 1997, the Asian crisis began to escalate. A year earlier, on August 17, 1998, the Russian crisis broke out, which seriously threatened not only the Russian economy but the entire international financial system. In terms of world economies, we can say that the summer of 1999 was calmer compared to last year. However, this did not apply to Turkey. The earthquake disaster that took place in our country on August 17, 1999 deeply wounded our country. The earthquake brought with it devastating consequences both in terms of human loss and physical infrastructure. Currently, the death toll is over 15,000 and the number of injured exceeds 25,000. In addition, more than 200,000 homes have been damaged or destroyed, leaving over half a million people homeless. Let me state at once that the voluntary and urgent aid from international circles and national sources has been our consolation both in terms of moral and reconstruction costs. I would like to thank those who contributed to the aid one by one. I would also like to emphasize that this tragic event will not lead to any change in our macroeconomic strategy and our difficult success in the fight against inflation will not be allowed to be jeopardized. As it is known, the macroeconomic imbalances in Turkey are underneath the inflation we have been living in for a long time. That is why we have been focusing our efforts on reducing inflation for some time. In early 1998, an anti-inflation program was introduced. This program aimed to gradually reduce inflation, which was 91 percent at the end of 1997, to single digits in the medium term. As we all know, there are three basic elements of the inflation reduction program. These are strong fiscal policies, structural reforms and nominal policies in line with this program. First, I want to touch on fiscal and nominal policies. Turkey has been living with inflation for a long time. Inflation in our country is mainly due to budget deficits and the way these deficits are financed. Therefore, fiscal policies form the backbone of Turkey's anti-inflation program. Calculations show that a non-interest budget surplus of around 4 or 5 percent to be created in the first two years of the program can alleviate the pressure on domestic demand and domestic borrowing. Such a development would also demonstrate the determination of the financial authorities to reduce inflation. By making it possible to implement a flexible monetary program in addition to a tight fiscal policy, it will facilitate our achievement of the goal of economic stability. First of all, I would like to state that the monetary program we have prepared is also consistent with the fiscal policies in question. We, as the Central Bank, have focused our attention on the Net Domestic Assets item since the second half of 1998 and have given two main messages. The first of these is; that public deficits will no longer be financed by Central Bank resources, the other being that; It is the fact that the Central Bank will increase its Turkish lira liabilities only to finance the increase in its net external assets. In addition to the significant decrease observed in the Short-Term Advance Account to the Treasury and Total Net Domestic Assets items, the significant increase recorded in the Net External Assets of the Central Bank is the result of these policies. Undoubtedly, it is necessary to take into account the negative effects of the Asian and Russian crises in this regard. The capital flight that occurred due to these crises led to a decrease in Net External Assets. In parallel, the Internal Assets item increased accordingly. However, the source of this increase has not been the loans to the public sector, but the Central Bank's funding of banks. Another aspect of the Central Bank's monetary program is linked to exchange rate policy. The exchange rate policy carried out in line with the inflation target has significant effects on inflationary expectations. The Central Bank first signaled to the market that it had approved the inflation target set by the government. Since public opinion monitors exchange rate movements on a daily basis, exchange rate policy that takes into account target inflation has become an important tool that affects public inflation expectations. Undoubtedly, the success of this policy depends on the realistic determination of the inflation target. This means that the inflation target is consistent with the budget balance. In addition to affecting inflation and inflationary expectations, exchange rate policy directly affects foreign trade. In this context, a stable real exchange rate policy puts the Central Bank in a neutral position. In this case, the Central Bank will not resort to exchange rate policy to support exports, nor will it resort to practices that will harm Turkey's long-term level of commercial competition. is not available. As a result of a stable real exchange rate policy implemented by the Central Bank, the current balance of payments of the economy is determined by real sector developments. There has been a decline in domestic demand in recent months. While imports decreased, a significant improvement was recorded in the foreign trade balance. As a result, Turkey closed 1998 with a current account balance surplus of 1871 million. In 1999, a low current account deficit is expected due to the expected increase in domestic demand in the second half of the year. The alignment between fiscal and monetary policies has led to a decrease in inflation from 91 percent in 1997 to 54 percent in 1998. As of August 1999, inflation, calculated according to the wholesale price index, maintained its level of 54 percent despite unexpected developments in oil prices and the relaxation in fiscal policy in the first half of the year. There is no doubt that the high inflation process that Turkey has been experiencing for a long time has brought about some attitudes and behaviors such as getting used to living with inflation. Breaking the inflationary resistance in the economy requires a high level of political determination. An indication of this determination is the success demonstrated in the field of structural reforms. There is no doubt that as the success in implementing reforms is achieved, the credibility of the programme will increase. Now, I want to touch on these reforms. Turkey has a positive record on structural issues. In the last two decades, the trade and capital movements items of the balance of payments have been liberalized. Our labour market is flexible. The high level of household savings is one of the important features of our economy. The market economy is another structural element of Turkey. There are currently four important structural reforms on Turkey's agenda. They are not only part of antiinflationary policies, but also important in terms of adapting to the changing global environment. These include reforms to the banking sector, the social security system, agricultural subsidy and privatization. Some of these reforms have passed through parliament, while others are in order. The new Banking Law passed by Parliament in June 1999 contains the following general objectives.  To close legal gaps,  To implement international banking supervision legislation,  To give the supervision of banks to an independent institution,  Some of the issues relating to the establishment and operation of banks carry out arrangements, Specifically, by BIS (Bank for International Settlements) in 1997 The "25 Main Principles for Effective Banking Supervision" were included in the new Banking Law. As a result, these regulations are in line with contemporary principles of banking supervision. I believe that the new law will enable the Turkish banking sector to quickly attain a healthier structure. This development is critical for effective monetary policy. The success of monetary authorities in ensuring price stability in the medium term depends not only on the support of appropriate fiscal policies, but also on the existence of a healthy banking system. The Banking Law, which has been approved by Parliament, is a great step forward. But there is still work to be done. Another important issue is the restructuring of public banks and the reduction of their role in the banking system. These banks not only operate in the highly competitive banking market, but also undertake transactions on behalf of the government, such as preferential lending to small and medium-sized enterprises and the agricultural sector. Since it is aimed to abolish preferential loans in the medium term, these banks can be privatized and given a commercial structure. Another reform that the government is addressing is the reform of social security. Now I would like to briefly touch on the issue of Turkey's social security system, which has led to significant budget problems in recent years. There are three pension institutions that make up the Turkish social security system. The Social Insurance Institution, which is the first and largest of these, is for employees with employee status. One of the other two organizations covers civil servants and the other covers the self-employed. These three organizations cover their pensions with premiums deducted from employees. In other words, pensions are not paid on the basis of the previous savings of pensioners, but with the contributions of the working population. The main reason for the increasing budget deficits in recent years is not the aging of the population, but early retirement. The deficit in the pension system has been growing rapidly since 1992, when the retirement age was lowered. The law prepared to correct this situation has been passed by the Parliament. When we consider the issue of privatization, we see that public institutions still play an important role in Turkey. We all now know that a strong privatization program would reduce the commercial and industrial activities undertaken by the state. As a result, the burden of subsidies on the budget will decrease, the depth of capital markets will increase, and the spread of capital to a wider base will become attractive. Since privatization is seen as a fundamental element of its policies aimed at improving the distribution of resources, Turkey needs to modernize its legal and institutional structure regarding privatization and bring them closer to the norms of the European Union and the economies of the former eastern bloc countries that have succeeded in this field. An adequate legal basis is the main element of such reforms. Important steps have been taken recently on this path. Blocking the privatization process the necessary amendment was made to the Constitution to eliminate legal obstacles. The long-awaited constitutional amendment to international arbitration to attract foreign investors interested in privatisation has passed through Parliament. The agricultural sector also has a special importance for Turkey. This sector has about 15 percent of Turkey's gross national income and 42 percent of employment. It is seen that the total support provided to agriculture in Turkey has more than doubled in the last decade. However, this figure is gradually decreasing in other western countries. The agricultural support system implemented in Turkey has a complex structure. The support is carried out through two channels: These are Ziraat Bank, which provides support based on the use of inputs through its product-based market support mechanism. Additional measures cover the cost of general services provided to agriculture and covered by the budget. It is not possible to abolish existing agricultural support arrangements overnight. Officials are currently working with the World Bank on projects aimed at transitioning to a direct revenue payment system in the future. Everyone in Turkey embraces the transition from the current support system to the direct support system. However, this change will take place gradually and will take some time. The new government, formed after the April general elections, appears determined to complete the reforms, as seen in the adoption of the Banking Law, International Arbitration and Social Security reform. Thanks to the environment of confidence that will increase with the completion of these reforms, I believe that Turkey's anti-inflation program will reach a new phase in early 2000. Significant progress has been made since last year's Close Monitoring Programme, and a new and comprehensive effort is now needed to eliminate inflation. A captive macroeconomic and fiscal program aims to reduce inflation to 10 percent by the end of 2001. I would like to emphasize that this time, the chances of the anti-inflation program succeeding are high for three reasons. The first is the consensus on the implementation of the policy of reducing inflation with the political stability that already exists. The second is that all segments of society see that there is no other option for solving our budget and debt problems. Third, the technical infrastructure is ready. These three factors underscore the importance of the new program. Accordingly, the inflation target for the year 2000 was set at 25 percent and for the year 2001 at 10 percent. The fiscal policy, which is expected to be consistent with these targets in the next two years, will be carried out with a broad-based approach that aims to improve all aspects of all expenditures and revenues of the public sector. To this end, monetary policy will continue to support fiscal policies. Money Although a radical change in policy implementation is not expected, it is clear that the monetary program to be implemented effectively will also contribute positively to fiscal policies. I would also like to underline once again Turkey's recent efforts to reduce inflation. As you know, in the 1980s, the Turkish economy managed to move from a closed economy to a market economy. With the recent efforts, Turkey aims to build its macroeconomic infrastructure in order to become a member of the global economy, where the financial and real sectors function healthily, low inflation and a sustainable growth rate are considered as minimum conditions. Finally, I would like to touch on an important issue. After the great earthquake, there was an opportunity for the Turkish economy to once again show its strength to overcome the difficulties encountered. Over the past two years, we have been able to overcome the crises of South Asia, Russia and Latin America, and especially the economic slowdown in the European Union region, where we trade significantly and where our financial and economic relations are intense. At the same time, the uncertainty experienced before the April 1999 general elections tested the resilience of the Turkish economy. I believe that we have successfully passed these exams and gained great experiences from them. As I always say, although we don't like it, we perform very well on bad days. The current situation and expectations are different. From now on, we will ensure that the Turkish economy shows the success it has achieved in bad times as well in good periods. The success of the program we have launched will affect at least the next 50 years of Turkey's economic and social life. I believe that these messages are clear enough and are correctly understood by our foreign friends. Thank you.

text: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey 77th SHAREHOLDERS ORDINARY GENERAL MEETING OPENING SPEECH DURMU YILMAZ GOVERNOR 14 April 2009, Ankara I. Introduction 1. Esteemed Shareholders, Distinguished Guests and Members of the Press, welcome to the 77th Shareholders Ordinary General Meeting of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. 2. I would like to start my presentation with a brief evaluation of the international financial crisis, which is not only deepening and growing more widespread, but also affecting real economies more seriously every day. Later on, I will summarize the key macroeconomic developments that took place in Turkey in 2008 and then I will share with you my evaluations pertaining to inflation developments and monetary policy implementations. II. Global Economic Developments 3. The global financial crisis that emerged in the US subprime mortgage market in August 2007, spread to the money and capital markets and became deeper following the bankruptcy of several large financial institutions in the US in September 2008 and the repercussions of the crisis on global financial markets still continue. Moreover, financial turmoil has started to adversely affect the corporate sector too and many countries especially developed countries went into recession, which resulted in economic slowdown becoming more evident globally. 4. While uncertainties regarding the magnitude and severity of the global economic downturn still persist, the liquidity crunch, which emerged as a result of the deterioration in risk perceptions and loss of confidence, was broadly remedied by the coordinated massive interventions of central banks and government authorities. The liquidity operations of the central banks of developed countries and especially the Federal Reserve continued with further expansion to cover new distressed assets. 5. Despite all the measures taken, the sharp drop in confidence driven by the global financial turmoil has started to dampen economic activity on a global scale leading to a significant decrease in growth rates. While the slowdown in global growth became more apparent in the third quarter, indicators related to 1 the fourth quarter suggest that the slowdown further intensified and developed countries generated negative growth rates. In the face of falling oil prices, OPEC decreased oil supply to counteract the decline in demand and thus, oil prices assumed a relatively stable course as of early2009. 9. Countries face major cutbacks in production amid slumping total demand and limited access to credit, due to the widening and deepening of the global financial crisis. Thus, it is essential that countries adopt strong fiscal rules that will reduce the adverse effects of the global financial crisis on production and help maintain sustainable economic growth in the medium term. For a counter-cyclical fiscal policy designed for times of economic contraction to be successful and generate a favorable impact on economic policy expectations, it needs to make strong commitments to maintain fiscal discipline in the medium-term. The gradually deepening global financial crisis has stood as a factor of uncertainty. On the other had, it exerted downward pressure on inflation through commodity prices accompanied with easing demand. In this context, the downtrend in inflation, which started in late 2008, lasted through early 2009 due to decreasing pressures on the demand and cost sides. Annual inflation became 7.89 percent in March. Recently released data indicate that the sluggish trend in domestic and foreign demand still persists. It is envisaged that the recovery in economic activities will take time and that the accumulated decreases in the prices of oil and other commodities will have a favorable effect on inflation through energy and food prices. These are predicted to lead to a further continuance of downward trend in inflation. Availing myself of this opportunity, I would like to remind you that we will provide the public with updated evaluations and forecasts regarding the medium term inflation outlook along with possible risks and policy measures in the Inflation Report to be published at the end this month. 17 44. The uncertainties regarding the global commodity and finance markets and risks related to their reflections on the inflation outlook required monetary policy to remain cautious until late 2008. Despite the slowdown in aggregate demand, the MPC decided to keep policy rates unchanged at the September and October meetings. Likewise, the central banks of developing countries adopted a cautious stance in the same period and maintained the monetary tightening trend launched in early 2008. In the following period, foreseeing that the marked deceleration in aggregate demand and the decline in commodity prices would adequately compensate for the pass-through from exchange rates to prices and that inflation would drop more than expected, the Central Bank launched a policy rate cut cycle as of November 2008. This cycle of policy rate cuts was accelerated as the released data indicated aggravation of the impacts of the global financial crisis on economic activities. It was also aimed at alleviating the effects of financial tightening thereby. In this period, the accuracy of the CBTs monetary policy decisions were confirmed by the inflation data. Moreover, market interest rates, backed by the improvement in risk perceptions, indicated a considerable decrease. All 18 these developments produced positive effects on inflation expectations. There was also a noteworthy improvement in medium-term inflation expectations. 46. At this point, it should be underlined that after the transition to the inflation targeting regime, the Central Bank responded differently to the sharp increases in exchange rates in two different periods. While the Central Bank had decided to exercise strong monetary tightening in May-June 2006 period following a global liquidity crisis, this time it opted for a controlled but rapid cycle of policy rate cuts. In contrast to the strong demand conditions observed in 2006, we are currently going through a process of relatively low levels of exchange rate pass-through under waning domestic and foreign demand conditions. This situation, accompanied by tight credit conditions, declining import prices and improving inflation expectations, facilitated non-inflationist policy rate cuts to be made. 47. In this environment of global financial crisis, the Central Bank, in order to prevent setbacks in international credit markets and the global economy from adversely affecting the functioning and stability of the financial system in Turkey and the countrys economy in general, has taken the necessary measures in advance. The measures taken by the Central Bank are as follows: 48. Firstly, the Central Bank resumed its activities as an intermediary in the foreign exchange deposit markets in Foreign Exchange and Banknotes Markets on 9 October 2008. Considering the level of the banks balance sheet aggregates, transaction limits in the said markets were revised as of 14 October and doubled as of 24 October, increasing to USD 10.8 billion in total. The announcement of such measures has raised confidence in the market and averted potential problems to be observed in foreign exchange liquidity flow. 49. Secondly, with a view to strengthening foreign currency positions of the banks, foreign exchange buying auctions were suspended as of 16 October 2008. Thus, the liquidity withdrawn from the foreign exchange market was kept within the system. In the following days, the loss of confidence in the international finance sector adversely affected global liquidity flow; particularly the demand for US dollar liquidity increased. This development led to the emergence of speculative price behaviors in Turkeys foreign exchange markets as well. Against this background, foreign exchange selling auctions were launched on 24 October 2008, the daily sales volume of which was USD 19 50 million. The said auctions were suspended on account of the favorable developments in the global markets on 30 October 2008. In this period, two auctions were held, through which a total of USD 100 million was sold. Accordingly, in view of ailing price movements in the foreign exchange market, foreign exchange selling auctions were resumed on 10 March 2009. The Central Bank suspended these auctions on 3 April 2009 as a result of easing concerns pertaining to the depth of the foreign exchange market, which was also facilitated by favorable developments in the global markets. In this period during which 18 auctions were held, a total of USD 900 million was sold. 50. Thus, net USD 7.5 billion was bought via buying and selling auctions throughout 2008. The Central Bank gross foreign exchange reserves became USD 71 billion by end-2008.
