Title: Speech on "The Role of Finance in Sustainable Development and Participation" at the International Conference on Islamic Economics and Finance
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: President Murat Uysal's Speech on "The Role of Finance in Sustainable Development and Participation" Istanbul Sabahattin Zaim University 14 June 2020 Dear participants, I wish that this conference, which was held in an environment where economic and financial problems were discussed in depth with their structural elements all over the world during the coronavirus outbreak, would be beneficial and productive for all stakeholders and our country. Before I start my speech, I would like to commemorate in your presence our recently departed professor Prof. Dr. Sabri Orman, with whom I had the chance to work and benefit from his experience during his time as a member of the Bank Council at our Bank. I wish the deceased the mercy of Allah and my condolences to his relatives. As Mr. Orman mentioned, "Islamic economics studies require an Islamic Science and Economics equipment." I am pleased to see that this program we are in today has been prepared in this spirit, and I would like to thank those who contributed to the organization of the conference for bringing together such a distinguished participant profile within a program that includes important agenda items for the sector. 1 In my speech, I will first briefly talk about the role of Islamic finance in the global financial system. Then, after summarizing the development of the participation finance system in our country, I will make a brief assessment about the importance of Islamic finance in the context of sustainable development and some of the studies that can be done by referring to the studies carried out by our Bank on the subject. In the last part of my speech, I will evaluate the monetary measures we have taken to reduce the effects of the coronavirus outbreak on the Turkish economy. Dear participants, Although significant capital inflows into developing countries in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis, there are still financing-related challenges for these countries in achieving sustainable growth and development. This has led to the acceleration of the search for a sustainable and long-term financing model that can be an alternative to the financial system based on borrowing and leverage. Ideally, financing sources should increase production and employment by financing both infrastructure and private investments, and encourage new sources of public finance, thus contributing to social policies as well. Islamic finance is based on risk sharing with its asset-based financing structure. In addition, a sound financial infrastructure, reduction of income inequality and its contribution to financing issues that are sensitive to environmental problems bring Islamic finance to the forefront. The global Islamic finance sector, which consists of Islamic banking, capital markets, takaful and fund management markets, has shown remarkable growth over the past decade. 2 As of 2019, it reached an asset size of USD 2.44 trillion. However, considering that its share in the global financial sector is only around 1 percent, it is seen that the sector still has a significant growth potential. On the other hand, the Islamic finance sector is largely based on banking, with the share of capital markets being below 30 percent and the share of takaful being only 1 percent. In addition, the geographical distribution has been largely limited to certain regions such as Gulf Cooperation Organization (GCC) countries and Malaysia. This points to the need to increase inclusivity and product diversity in the Islamic finance sector. Dear Guests, In our country, we observe that important studies are carried out for the development of the Islamic finance sector, especially participation finance institutions. The participation finance sector, which dates back 30 years, failed to make progress in terms of asset size and product diversity before 2005 due to the effects of economic crises and legislative deficiencies. In 2005, Private Finance Institutions, as it was known at that time, started to develop with the necessary legislative arrangements. In 2013, the Bank and all stakeholders of the sector, especially the regulatory and supervisory institutions of our country, contributed to the Workshop on Interest-Free Finance and Participation Finance System, and recommendations that would contribute to strategy and action plans were put forward. Released in December 2014 3 Within the scope of the Tenth Development Plan, the development of the participation finance system was included as the 7th component in the Action Plan of the Istanbul International Finance Center Program and increasing the variety of interest-free finance products and services was determined as the state policy. In 2020, the number of participation financial institutions in our country reached 6 with the entry of public participation financial institutions into the sector. It is seen that participation financial institutions increased their weight between 2005 and 2019 by achieving a growth above the banking sector average. It is seen that the asset share, which was around 2 percent in 2005, increased by more than 20 percent in the last two years with the establishment of public participation financial institutions and reached 6.5 percent as of March 2020. The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey also contributes to the development of the participation finance sector in parallel with the increasing importance of interest-free finance within the framework of the duties assigned to it by the Law. Since 2009, the Central Bank has been making arrangements for the participation finance sector in various areas such as liquidity management, deposits, reserve requirements and rediscount, taking into account the demands of stakeholders. After the announcement of lease certificates issued in 2010, the Central Bank started to provide liquidity to participation financial institutions through open market operations in 2013. With the subsequent studies, participation financial institutions were provided with smooth access to the Central Bank's liquidity facilities and in line with the working principles of the sector. In this way, participation finance 4 institutions have been facilitated to manage liquidity risk, thus strengthening the system against possible liquidity shocks and eliminating a significant deficiency in terms of the participation finance system. Participation financial institutions, which have recently started to take a more active role in the foreign exchange and effective markets within the Central Bank, have started to increase their swap transactions, especially with our Bank. In this context; The transaction limits of participation financial institutions in the gold swap market for foreign currency and Turkish lira were increased. These institutions also make intensive use of gold trading and swap opportunities in exchange for foreign currency. In December 2019, a separate implementation instruction was put into effect for these institutions in order to enable participation financial institutions to mediate in export and foreign exchange earning services rediscount credit transactions. In February 2020, the necessary communique was amended to ensure that participation financial institutions comply with the basic principles of the Islamic finance system in accepting deposits. In addition to these, the Central Bank closely follows and contributes to the global scale studies by becoming a member of international organizations working in the field of Islamic finance in order to support the development of the sector. 5 Our Bank has been one of the founding partners of the International Islamic Liquidity Management Organization (IILM) since 2010. IILM was established by nine central banks and an international organization to issue sukuk, which is considered a high-quality, short-term and liquid asset. The sukuks issued by the IILM are used as collateral in interbank borrowing transactions, traded in the secondary market and accepted as collateral in short-term financing within the scope of open market operations. It is seen that the establishment of the IILM has accelerated the arrangements for liquidity management for interest-free finance in many countries. Active in the field of international regulation, the Central Bank has been a member of the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), a standard-setting organization in the field of Islamic finance including participation financial institutions, since 2009. 6 Dear participants, The participation finance system supports participatory and inclusive growth by emphasizing partnership agreements and risk sharing. On the other hand, this system prioritizes financing real economic activities, limiting overly speculative financial transactions and not allowing highly leveraged transactions; it is very important for providing a more sustainable financing model and financial stability. In this context, it is useful to carry out various studies in order to increase the awareness of the system and to better benefit from its potential. First of all, the dissemination and encouragement of training and information activities in order to raise awareness about the place, functioning and distinctive features of participation financial institutions in the financial system will contribute to the better promotion of the sector. With the increase in financial literacy in the field of participation finance, more investments and savings will be brought to the financial system and financial markets will be able to deepen. In this direction, I would like to express that the timely implementation of a comprehensive communication strategy to be prepared to raise awareness in the field of participation finance and to strengthen confidence in the sector can further increase the momentum gained by the sector. Considering all aspects of partnership-based financing, working together with the requirements of banking legislation and the infrastructure required by partnership-based products, which are the basis of the participation finance system, 7 If necessary, the separate and holistic handling of partnership-based financing will be able to make a difference and minimize the disruptive or criticized aspects of the system. In this respect, it is beneficial to consider the participation finance legislation in a holistic manner with all relevant regulatory institutions and stakeholders. I would like to state that the studies needed for the development of the financial sector should also be carried out by academicians, and that we attach importance to dialogue and cooperation between academicians, sector representatives and regulatory institutions. The increase in the interest of academics in Islamic finance will also make a significant contribution to the development of the sector. This conference sets a good example in this respect. One of the important conditions for making progress in the field of participation finance and becoming one of the leading centers in this field is the development of institutional capacity and human resources infrastructure. In this context, the timely actions of public institutions in their institutional structuring will increase the human resource capacity that can contribute to the growth of the sector. The training of experts and researchers who will work on participation finance in the fields of banking, capital markets and insurance will support the long-term growth of the sector. 8 Dear guests, In this part of my speech, I would like to make a brief assessment of the extraordinary period we are going through and the monetary measures we have taken during this period. The rapid spread of the epidemic across the globe has led to a marked slowdown in global trade and economic activity. The high uncertainty surrounding the economic effects of the pandemic and the normalization process significantly weakened the global growth outlook. In this process, central banks all over the world have taken extraordinary expansionary policy measures such as interest rate cuts, asset purchases, liquidity steps and credit support programs. In the normalization period we are going through, it is important to ensure a rapid recovery all over the world and to minimize the costs on different segments by supporting the households and companies most affected by the epidemic. The fact that the epidemic affects economies through many different channels points to the critical importance of macro-scale monetary and fiscal policies, as well as multifaceted, micro-policy implementations that directly target economic units in need and take into account sectoral interactions. Depending on the determination of the damage to be caused to the economies in the coming period and the rate of normalization, there are serious uncertainties regarding the duration and size of the supportive policies. Packages of unprecedented measures in developed and developing countries 9 The announcement points to a view that budget deficits will expand in the post-pandemic period, public and private sector indebtedness will increase, and global interest rates will remain low for a long time. In this process, it is of great importance that the policy steps are targeted and temporary with an understanding of effective resource management, limiting the negative effects of the epidemic and preventing the possible side effects of expansionary policies. As the Central Bank, the policies we have implemented in this period should be evaluated within this framework. The monetary measures we have taken recently aim to support production and financial stability in the economy and to overcome this period with the least damage. In order to limit the negative effects of the developments related to the coronavirus, it is important that the financial markets, the credit channel and the cash flow of the companies continue to operate uninterruptedly and healthily. In line with these objectives, we have taken timely, target-oriented and predictable steps to meet the increasing liquidity needs of the system by closely monitoring this process and its effects and to ensure the uninterrupted continuation of the credit flow to the real sector. With the interest rate cut decision we took at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting on 17 March 2020, we shared with the public the first package of measures we put into practice to limit the economic effects of the epidemic. This was followed by additional measures we announced on March 31 and April 17, 2020, as well as policy rate cuts in April and May. 10 In this period, in order to provide flexibility in Turkish lira and foreign currency liquidity management, we have committed to provide financial institutions with all the liquidity they need within the framework of ready-made opportunities in intraday and overnight maturities. In order to ensure the uninterrupted flow of credit to the real sector, we provided targeted additional liquidity opportunities to financial institutions. In addition, we have taken steps to support liquidity in the DIBS market within the limits we have set in this process. In addition, by including Asset-Based Securities and Mortgage Secured Securities in the collateral pool, we aimed to deepen the capital markets and diversify the liquidity opportunities that financial institutions can use by bringing quality collateral. We also offered the rediscount credits we provided to support exporter companies within certain limits and against collateral. In the last period, we have seen that the credit need for working capital has been effectively met by the banking system. For this reason, we have recently announced to the public that we will extend 20 billion Turkish liras of the facility allocated for Turkish lira denominated rediscount loans as advance loans with investment commitments in a more efficient manner in order to support investments in selective sectors that are critical for our country within the framework of our Bank's legislation. With this step, we aimed to encourage investments that are highly productive, reduce imports and support exports, reduce foreign dependency and the current account deficit problem, and support sustainable growth. 11 In summary, we aimed to support financial stability and the post-pandemic recovery process by providing the financial system and the real sector with the liquidity they need under favorable conditions. Thus, we aimed to minimize the damages that the effects arising from the temporary epidemic environment may cause to production and employment in the long term. As a matter of fact, we observe that the measures aimed at overcoming this period with the least damage by supporting production and financial stability in the economy support the liquidity and credit conditions of the financial sector and maintain the effectiveness of the monetary transmission mechanism. Dear guests, In the coming period, we will continue to take the decisions that our country and our economy will need quickly and to implement the decisions taken effectively. As the Central Bank, we have a wide and powerful set of tools at our disposal to minimize the negative effects of the epidemic. In this period, we will continue to determine our monetary stance in a way to ensure the continuity of the decline in inflation and to use all the tools at our disposal for price stability and financial stability purposes with a data-oriented approach. As we have repeatedly emphasized, price stability contributes to sustainable growth by supporting the growth potential of the economy by reducing uncertainties in the economy, while healthy and inclusive growth strengthens the sustainability of price stability. 12 While concluding my speech here, I would like to express my gratitude to all the participants and those who contributed to the organization of the event, especially to Sabahattin Zaim University, and hope that this meeting will benefit the discussions and studies on the participation finance system. 13

Title: CBRT 82.Speech at the Ordinary General Assembly Meeting
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: 82nd Ordinary General Assembly Opening Speech Erdem BAcI President 17 April 2014, Ankara 1 Dear shareholders, today I would like to share with you my views on the results we have achieved last year in the fields of inflation, monetary policy, growth and employment and what they look like in the future. The primary purpose of the Central Bank, given to it by law, is to ensure price stability, to maintain the purchasing power of the Turkish Lira, especially against goods and services, and to keep inflation as low and predictable as possible. Turkey has experienced a 35-year period of high and fluctuating inflation, which has had significant costs on the Turkish economy. The most important of these costs is that real interest rates are extremely high; During the periods when inflation remained between 20 percent and 100 percent, real interest rates in Turkey remained between 20 percent and 30 percent for a long time and followed a very fluctuating course. There is a fluctuating and unpredictable real interest rate in the period in question, and its objectionable effects on investments and employment have had a real cost to Turkey. Therefore, reducing inflation in Turkey has been an important gain in this sense; Thanks to a significant structural reform, inflation has fallen to at least single-digit levels and has remained there for a long time. The most important reason for inflation is budget deficits, the fact that the Governments of those times have moved away from fiscal discipline and the budget deficits are met from the Central Bank resources. For this reason, it was necessary to take steps in two areas. The first of these is to ensure fiscal discipline and reduce budget deficits, thus reducing the public's need for financing. The second is to cut the direct relationship between the Central Bank and the Treasury and to make it impossible to finance budget deficits from the Central Bank's resources. To this end, in 2001 2 With the amendment of the law, the Central Bank's relationship with the Treasury was severed in that sense, the Bank could only buy and sell bonds for monetary policy purposes and only from the secondary market, it could not buy bonds directly, it could not give short-term advances or loans to the public under any name. Fiscal discipline is crucial to ensuring credibility, which has quickly brought budget deficits from double-digit levels to single-digit levels. As a result of the steps taken in these important areas, inflation has reached single-digit levels since 2004-2005 and Turkey has first implemented an implicit inflation targeting regime and then an open inflation targeting regime. Inflation targets are set by the Central Bank together with the Government; The Bank strives to bring inflation to levels close to the target by using the tools at its disposal. Then, if he fails to achieve this goal, he explains to you, our esteemed shareholders, why he has not achieved this goal, but at the same time he writes an open letter to the government at the end of the year; The open letter in question specifies the measures to be taken and the letter is shared with the public. There is a transition process in Turkey; Although inflation has fallen to single digits, it has not yet reached levels that can be called price stability. Our inflation targets for the next three years have been set and announced with the government as 5 percent together with the Government. Apart from this, the 10th Amendment adopted by the Turkish Grand National Assembly In the Five-Year Development Plan, the inflation target for 2018 is foreseen as 4.5 percent. Although the level of price stability has not yet been reached, in the following years 3 reducing inflation to 4.5 percent and reducing it to a level below 4.5 percent in 2023 will be more consistent with price stability. A low inflation that our citizens no longer take into account and neglect in their decisions is called price stability. When the inflation targeting regime was implicitly introduced in 2002, targets were set not only on short-term interest rates, but also on monetary quantities. Our shareholders, who are sensitive about this issue, have spoken in the past that "inflation is a monetary phenomenon, so if you supply money too much, then prices will increase". This is indeed true; those goals were also tried to be met; Since we come from very high rates such as 70 percent, the initial inflation target was set at 35 percent, and in 2002 it was 29.7 percent. In 2003, 20 percent was targeted, 18.4 percent was realized; In 2004, the target of 12 percent was 9.3 percent; In 2005, 8 percent was targeted and 7.7 percent was realized. Until 2005, there was always a falling target, a falling inflation and a realization below the target every year. In 2006, there was a significant transition to inflation from the depreciation of the Turkish lira of about 30 percent due to an external shock. The U.S. Federal Reserve (FED) tightened its monetary tightening at that time, gradually increasing interest rates from 1 percent to 5.25 percent over a period of about 1.5-2 years; While approaching this level, sales and portfolio outflows were in question in developing countries, the depreciation was prevented thanks to the measures taken that year, the Turkish lira started to appreciate again, but inflation was well above the target. In this period, inflation was targeted at 5 percent for 2006, realization 4 9.7 percent, and in 2007 it was 8.4 percent against the 4 percent target. The period before the Lehman crisis in 2008 was a period in which oil prices approached 200, the volumes of credit in the world were increasing tremendously, and the price of all kinds of commodities was rising. In that period, while inflation was targeted at 4 percent, it was realized as 10.1 percent, the targets were gradually revised, and the targets of 7.5 percent in 2009, 6.5 percent in 2010 and 5.5 percent in 2011 were realized as 6.5 percent, 6.4 percent and 10.4 percent, respectively. Later, a target of 5 percent was announced from 2012; At the end of 2012, when this target was the closest, inflation in Turkey was 6.2 percent. This is known as the lowest year-end inflation in 44 years, but it is necessary to come further down and approach 5 percent. In 2013, the realization was 7.4 percent, and since it was over 7 percent, an open letter was written to the Government and this letter containing the reasons for the deviation and the measures to be taken was shared with the public. An upward trajectory in inflation continued for some time; the reason behind this is mainly exchange rate developments. The gradual depreciation of the Turkish lira since May 2013 and the continuation of this depreciation in December have significantly affected inflation. Inflation expectations are very important; How people expect inflation in the future and how they behave accordingly in both leases and wages is a very important variable. The deterioration here has been limited; There has been some deterioration in inflation expectations, whereas the Central Bank has been in monetary policy in two stages. 5 implemented the measure: the first stage; is the measure implemented in the summer months, with the liquidity policy predominantly an upward adjustment in interest rates. Then, secondly, an adjustment in interest rates was made in January, thus preventing the deterioration in inflation expectations and the depreciation of the exchange rate. If the situation continues in this way, the effects on inflation from the exchange rate are considered to be temporary; Inflation, which will be announced next month, is expected to rise slightly, most likely to peak in May, followed by a downward trend in June. However, it will be well above our target of 5 percent at the end of the year. Since an Inflation Report will be shared with the public at the end of April, I cannot give you an exact figure today without an assessment of a new forecast by the Board. However, it will be seen in 2015 that the effect of the exchange rate is temporary. Inflation will be observed gradually approaching 5 percent, especially in the middle of the year, in the summer and then in the third quarter. The Central Bank has taken the necessary measures in a timely manner and will continue to do so. In terms of monetary policy, another variable that the Central Bank is trying to influence is the growth rate of loans. The Bank has instruments related to short-term interest rates. When the Bank increases or decreases interest rates, it can affect the growth rate of total loans, both commercial and consumer loans. In previous periods, the Central Bank could only look at the growth rate of total loans. Different effects on consumer loans, different effects on commercial loans, even different from housing loans within consumer loans, non-housing consumer loans 6 a number of different instruments with different effects were not in the hands of the Bank. These instruments are in the hands of the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency, so the Financial Stability Committee established in June 2011 is of great importance. In the Financial Stability Committee, under the chairmanship of our Deputy Prime Minister, the Central Bank, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency, the Capital Markets Board, the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund and the Undersecretariat of Treasury come together and the measures that can be taken are coordinated together. Then, each institution takes the necessary measures by making a situation assessment within itself. The measures taken by the BRSA in the recent period are very appropriate and selective measures. Important measures have been taken mainly in credit cards and consumer loans except for housing. An advantage was provided in the loans given to enterprises especially for exports and SMEs. The most recent decisions came into force in February and the impact was immediately observed; While the growth rate of consumer loans has decreased to more reasonable levels, it has also fallen below the growth rate of corporate loans. In retrospect, this has rarely happened in Turkey, for the first time the loans given to companies exhibit a faster increase process than the loans given to consumers. This has two benefits: the first has to do with inflation, if policies support production, control consumption somewhat, then a lowering effect on inflation will be seen over time. The second benefit is related to the external balance, the current account deficit, savings: A significant part of the savings in Turkey comes from the public. The most important reason behind the low savings rates in the private sector is the extremely fast growth of loans. This is rather the consumer 7 it determines the loans. The fact that the growth rate of consumer loans has slowed down in this way also shows a corrective and reducing effect on the current account deficit, and this effect will continue in the future. The overall growth rate of loans is also getting closer to the benchmark value of 15 percent every week, in line with macro targets that are seen as sustainable. An important variable that will summarize the savings developments in the public sector is the ratio of the central government budget deficit to the gross domestic product, in other words, how much budget deficit the state gives according to the total value of the goods and services produced by Turkey in a year. In 2001 and 2002, budget deficits of around 11.5 percent were observed at double-digit levels. Then, thanks to fiscal discipline, the budget deficit gradually fell below 3 percent, and the last time it was 1.2 percent in 2013 with great success. This means that the state establishes the public income-expenditure balance and contributes positively to savings. There is some deficit in the public sector, but it is at a manageable and sustainable level, and is below the European Union benchmark of 3 percent. As a result, the debt burden of the public decreases; In gross terms, public debt in gross terms decreased from 74 percent in 2012 to 36 percent in 2013 and to 12 percent in net terms. This decline is projected to continue; this will have a positive impact on both the current account deficit and inflation; The continuation of fiscal discipline in terms of inflation is also extremely important. When we compare it with other countries, although our public debt burden is low compared to developed countries, Turkey is in a middle place compared to other developing countries. Turkey on fiscal discipline 8 it has entered a very healthy and sustainable trend. The problem that Turkey is currently solving is to improve the savings of the private sector. The problem of saving in the public sector has been solved to a great extent. All kinds of measures to increase the savings of the private sector, prevention of excessive borrowing and similar measures will definitely be beneficial. It is also necessary to mention the private pension reform here. This reform also has the effect of increasing savings. In the 10th Five-Year Development Plan, the Turkish Grand National Assembly has considered increasing savings as a priority area. There is a study in this direction in the Ministry of Development and on the part of the Government, it would be useful to translate this into an action plan and to announce to the public how the structural reforms that need to be made will be carried out within which timetable. The most important tool of the Central Bank is short-term interest rates. The most important of the short-term interest rates is the weighted average cost of the fund provided to banks by the Central Bank. The Central Bank currently lends to banks and can influence the interest rate generated in the interbank market by adjusting the amount of it. These are short-term interest rates, and they are two instruments that have a direct impact on other short-term interest rates as well. The Central Bank adjusted to the upside when conditions required the upward adjustment of short-term interest rates and to the downside when it needed to be adjusted to the downside. The most striking move in this area was made during the Lehman crisis by lowering the policy rate by close to 10 points, and then it was seen that this decision was necessary and beneficial. The Lehman crisis completely lost its effects in Turkey as a result of two quarters, and the developments turned positive with the measures taken afterwards. Measures taken not only in the field of monetary policy, but also in the field of financial sector policies and fiscal policy 9 Thanks to Turkey, Turkey experienced that great shock for only 6 months; then there was a rapid recovery. The Central Bank did not raise interest rates much in the following period. This is due to the low interest rate environment in the world. The US Federal Reserve Board (FED), the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan and the Bank of England have brought their interest rates to a place very close to zero in the Lehman crisis, kept it at levels close to zero so far, and have announced additional quantitative expansion packages. These countries, according to them, have tried to give an additional incentive to the economy by increasing their central bank balance sheets through the purchase of long-term bonds or other methods. They could not turn negative because they did not have much room to move like we have; It may be possible to make the nominal interest rate negative, but it is not very desirable. Therefore, they go to quantitative easing by using the tool called the money base. The Fed has done this in three stages; The first quantitative easing, the second quantitative easing and the latest third quantitative easing are still ongoing, with its pace gradually decreasing. There was a very serious uncertainty at this point, and this uncertainty had some effects on us and other developing countries in May, June, July and August, then in December and January. Within the framework of the latest announced program, it has been explained that this will continue to decrease gradually and that the size of the balance sheet will be kept stable again in the autumn months, that there will be plenty of money in the market again, but that there will be no additional expansion, the uncertainty has been eliminated and this situation has now been reflected in the prices. Unless there is a very important change, the FED will continue this policy until September, October, November. 10 and after that he announced that he would no longer make any further expansions; thus, the sensitivity to data has been eliminated. The question that is currently being debated and communicated in the US is: In the current situation where the recovery is better than in Europe, if the short-term interest rates that the Fed keeps at zero are increased, when will the increase start and how long will it continue? Officials say they are looking at the labor market and inflation, and since inflation in the U.S. is at 1.5 percent, below the 2 percent target, they will not rush to do so unless there is an excessive increase here and there are no signs of warming in the labor market, and the market is trying to make a forecast about the interest rate increase. Since the signals are largely given at the moment, Fed officials are both more or less predicting where it will stop and giving an idea of when it will start; therefore, uncertainty has also been partially reduced and the negative effects arising from uncertainty have eased somewhat. In Europe, there is a different picture: inflation is 0.5 percent and the target is 2 percent. Inflation is very low and they do not want it to remain low for a long time, or even to fall to negative. Rather, there is a debate in the European Central Bank about whether we can give additional monetary support to the economy. There is talk that this can be done in two ways: nominal interest rates can be reduced slightly to negative, or large-scale bond purchases can be used. There has been no explanation yet that they can do both, we are monitoring the data, we can use them if necessary. Growth in Europe appears to be slower than in the US; Growth in Europe is expected to be below 1 percent, while in the U.S. it is expected to grow slightly below 3 percent, so the situation in the U.S. looks a little better. 11 These developments can be summarized as some reduction in risks related to growth. It is understood that monetary tightening will not be too hasty; it is clear that there is a need for a very good communication policy at this point, and the authorities continue to do so. In the summer of 2013 and then in December 2013 and January 2014, the Central Bank used its foreign exchange reserves against excessive currency volatility, while reinforcing its foreign exchange reserves thanks to the returns of rediscount loans given to exporters through Turk Eximbank. They can be used especially in periods of extreme volatility, as it is known, our foreign exchange reserves have increased significantly since 2002, but they follow a more horizontal course due to the use in the recent period. Gross reserves stood at USD 125.2 billion as of April 4, 2014, including the latest data gold. Some of this 20 billion is gold, and some of that is gold that is taken from banks as a mandatory provision. The mandatory reserves they deposit in foreign currency or gold or the reserve options they voluntarily deposit are opportunities that banks can always use. These are also among the available reserves. Banks will be able to use them easily if any problems arise or if they suffer from a borrowing problem. A discount can be made if necessary in the compulsory ones, and those who volunteer can use them themselves if they wish. At the moment, there is no need for both. 12 Looking at the growth and employment side, it is seen that Europe has turned from a growth close to zero or even a negative growth, albeit a little slow, to a positive growth of less than 1 percent, while in the US there is a slightly stronger growth course. Therefore, while growth from developed countries tends to increase somewhat in the world, there is a slower growth in developing countries compared to their own past. When you look at the selected countries, before the Lehman crisis, there was an average growth of 8 percent in these countries, but now there is a growth rate slightly above this 4 percent. Therefore, this growth is below the growth before the Lehman crisis, but above that of the developed countries. Developing countries are growing faster than developed countries, including Turkey, and their growth rate will continue in this way for a long time; because there is a gap that needs to be bridged, and they are gradually closing that gap. In terms of unemployment rates, it is seen that the Eurozone is lagging behind. Recovery has been very slow and there is still an unemployment rate close to 12 percent. Some areas have much higher unemployment rates. Therefore, it can be seen from this that Europe needs an additional monetary stimulus. However, the US and UK are seeing some improvement in unemployment rates. When we look at Turkey's growth, it is seen that our growth rate was higher before the Lehman crisis, but now we have entered a growth trend of around 4 percent. Last year, growth was 4 percent in real terms for the whole year. 13 What is remarkable at this point is that a very important global shock such as the Lehman crisis has been experienced and has really had a very serious impact on us. However, Turkey has shown a rapid "V" shaped recovery after a period of 6 months. Gross domestic product has reached pre-crisis levels and even surpassed this level after that recovery was completed. However, there is some slowdown in the growth rate. Turkey's growth throughout the history of the Republic has been 5 percent, which currently seems to be hovering around a trend of 4 percent. What will be Turkey's growth in 2014 is the most talked about issue these days. So far there are signs that growth will be slightly below 4 percent. When we look at both the leading indicators and the realizations, growth seems to be in line with a trend of 4 percent and slightly below, but in general, markets and international organizations have revised this rate a little lower. However, it is necessary to wait a little and see the developments. At the moment, we don't see any justification for a downward revision on the growth side. However, we cannot say that this will be a very rapid growth. At the moment, the post-crisis trend continues in line with developments in the world. Unemployment rates are declining thanks to strong growth in employment; this is a very remarkable development. Because it is seen that our unemployment rate is below the levels before the Lehman crisis. When we look at seasonally adjusted unemployment rates, while the non-farm unemployment rate was above 12 percent before the Lehman crisis, it is now below 12. Before the Lehman crisis, the overall unemployment rate was also above 10 percent, and now the latest data is 9.1 percent. 14 On the employment side, there has been a remarkable improvement, mainly due to non-agricultural employment. Non-agricultural employment in Turkey continues to increase quite rapidly. In agricultural employment, there is a more horizontal course. Since 2007, there has been an average annual employment growth of over 3.5 percent; When we compare this with other countries, it is observed that we have an average employment growth well above the developed countries. This is an employment growth that developed countries cannot even imagine. In this regard, Turkey is also at the forefront among developing countries. In terms of employment growth, Colombia, Chile and Turkey come to the forefront. When we look at the 100 level of 2007, it is seen how positively the level of employment in Turkey has developed compared to developed countries. We observe that there have been losses in employment in countries that are experiencing crises, especially in countries with public debt problems such as Greece, Spain, Ireland, Portugal and Italy. This shows that fiscal discipline yields beneficial results in this area as well. When we look at the external balance side, it is seen that global developments have been very effective in the recent period. Since there is a low interest rate environment in the world, savings have fallen in developing countries, borrowing has increased and current account deficits have been given especially in 5 major developing countries. However, while in this low interest rate environment, there has been an adjustment in long-term interest rates since mid-2013. After the Fed announced its exit strategy in May and June 2013, there was uncertainty, and then long-term interest rates were expected to be 15 We see that their value starts to fluctuate between 2.5 and 3 percent. Previously, this rate was between 1.5 and 2 percent. In order to understand how this change is effective in other countries, it is necessary to look at the market interest rates of the countries. If we look at the long-term domestic currency denominated interest rates, it is seen that there is a significant change in Poland, Russia and India, while in Hungary this is limited. In Turkey, South Africa, Brazil and Indonesia, there has been a significant increase in long-term interest rates in domestic currency. It is seen that the effect of the 1 point increase in the US is much more than 1 point in us. Although pricing is more established than before, it is seen that some shocks arising from both domestic and geopolitical developments may come. Although some more fluctuation is observed as a result of the shocks, it is seen that the pricing is about to settle to a large extent. In addition, if these additional shocks are put aside, the impact from the Fed has also decreased recently. The U.S. bonds' own volatility index has fallen, and there has been some improvement in our bonds' volatility indices in recent months. Leaving aside other developments, it is observed that geopolitical developments and some internal risks can also have an impact from time to time, but what is important at this point is that the impact from America is seen to be alleviated. A similar comparison can be made here on foreign currency borrowing rates. The Turkish Treasury can borrow in both dollars and euros. The difference in interest it pays in borrowing in dollars, in other words, how much more than what the US Treasury pays, 16 it is an important indicator that it can borrow. For the private sector, this is actually an important reference point. In the Lehman crisis, there was a very serious increase in this difference. Later, this gap widened during the Eurozone debt crisis. Although there was some increase after the Fed's exit signal, the amount of increase remained limited. Here, too, the Turkish Treasury can borrow at an additional cost of slightly over 2 percent. Therefore, the effect here has been less than the costs of borrowing in domestic currency. When we look at the history of interest rates in Turkish Lira, it is seen that the interest rate of the benchmark bond has reached 70 percent in the period of high inflation. However, as you know, the maturities of the benchmark bond at that time are also very short. The Treasury could only borrow with a maturity of 3 months. As of today, the Treasury can borrow at a nominal cost of around 10 percent in Turkish Lira with a maturity of 10 years. The interest rate of the 10-year term asset in Turkey is an extremely important variable. This interest rate is set in the market because the Central Bank does not intervene directly or indirectly. There are 2 determinants of this: the first is Turkey's country risk premium, in other words, the part of the Treasury related to borrowing costs, every improvement and every positive step taken in fiscal discipline brings down the risk premium here. Therefore, there has been a resulting decrease in interest rates in recent years. The second is inflation expectations. The Central Bank, together with the Government, has decided on the inflation target at 5 percent, but the market is pricing in 6.5-7 percent as an inflation expectation; When 3 points of real interest is put on top of this, the interest rate is reached 10 percent. There are additional reductions in Turkey's risk premium, so the real interest rate of 3 points has fallen slightly and inflation 17 In a scenario where expectations reach the inflation target of 5 percent, long-term interest rates may also reach very low levels. Therefore, we need to convince both our citizens living in Turkey and the international public opinion that we will succeed in the fight against inflation and ensure price stability. So what we're going to do is continue to be transparent about communication and speak our minds. It is also, of course, necessary to make the most appropriate use of all the policy tools at our disposal. We need to pay special attention to the issue of external balance. International and domestic analysts and the press drew attention to why Turkey was affected along with 5 other countries in the summer months. After the exit signal of the Fed, it was stated that there may be a need for adjustment in the current account deficit countries. The need for adjustment can also be observed in interest rates and exchange rates. Therefore, in all these five countries, there has been an adjustment in both variables and a tendency to recover after an observed improvement in the external balance. At this point, the question of what we should do to prevent our country from being affected so much by such external shocks comes to mind in the future. Savings must be increased in Turkey. We should not over-borrow, we should borrow in proportion to our income and increase our savings as much as possible. There are a number of ways to do this, both short-term and medium- and long-term. One of the short-term ways is to adjust prices. However, we want steps to continue to be taken on the medium and long-term structural side and thus to bring Turkey's income-expenditure balance to a positive point more easily. 18 When our expenditures rise above our income and the gap opens, this gap is somehow closed later as a requirement of market conditions or thanks to the policies implemented. A very rare positive point in Turkey's history is that this gap is closed through implemented policies. These policies began in late 2010 and mostly used banking instruments without raising interest rates too much. Total expenditures did not increase much, but revenue continued to increase with the contribution of exports. The current account deficit fell from 10 percent to 6 percent, but then in 2013, a revival in domestic demand was observed and some upward movement was observed in the current account deficit again. Looking ahead to the year, we expect gross domestic product to continue to grow despite the fact that total spending has followed a more horizontal course and slower growth since the first quarter. There is only one way to do this: to increase exports. We think that it will be a very healthy development for Turkey to continue to grow through export growth. It is recalled that in 2012, growth in Turkey was around 2.2 percent. While expectations are reduced to 2.5 and 2 percent, it is generally thought that the period is remembered and the situation of that period is repeated. Unlike that period, we think that growth in this period may be a little more positive, because there is a serious recovery in Europe and a transition from negative growth to plus growth. There is a demand from there. Compared to the 2012 period, our exports are slightly better, so growth may be a little faster. There will be no slowdown in domestic demand big enough to be worried about. 19 we think. Therefore, growth will be slightly closer to 4 percent this year. There is a very clear stabilization in quantity indices. While exports are upwards, imports follow a horizontal course; Looking at the data, excluding gold, it seems to be going down slightly. The ratio of exports to imports says a lot here. In Turkey, this ratio has remained around 64-65 for many years and Turkey has given a continuous external deficit. However, there has been a very serious deterioration here since the end of 2010. There has been a decrease of up to 56 percent in the ratio of exports to imports, and in 2011 our current account deficit was 10 percent compared to GDP. As a result of the measures taken since then, the gradual coverage rate has progressed towards 65 percent and above again. This is the 12-month sliding window, but when we look at the current trend, it is currently hovering above 65 percent. This line is moving towards a level of around 66 percent, so that the external balance will reach a more positive point in 2014. We expect a significant improvement in the current account balance this year. In particular, last year's high imports of gold are not observed this year. Again, when we look at it in terms of gold, there will be a significant improvement in the current account balance. We think that this year we will probably encounter a better external balance than the medium-term program projections. So, when we look at the triad of inflation, growth and current account deficit here, we see that inflation is above 5 percent and the current account balance is close to 5 percent, maybe depending on developments. 20 We expect it to be somewhere between 5 and 6 percent. Growth is also likely to be slightly below 4 percent at the moment. This is our expectation for these three variables this year. Thank you for listening to me and for your interest. I salute you all on behalf of myself and my institution. 21

Title: Speech by Governor Erdem Ba at the CBRT Governor - Handover Meeting
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: CBRT PRESIDENCY DELEGATE OF DUTIES - DELIVERY MEETING Erdem BAcI 19 April 2016, Ankara Esteemed Chairman of the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency, esteemed Undersecretary of the Treasury, Esteemed Chairman of the Capital Markets Board, Esteemed Central Bankers, Distinguished Members of our Press; all of you are welcome to this handover meeting. I have served at the Central Bank for more than 12 years, including the last 5 years as the President. Today, I am completing my 5-year term of office and handing over this important task to our new President Mr. Murat cetinkaya with peace of mind. I am very happy about this, because I guess I am the first Chairman in the history of the Central Bank to start this business with a handover meeting and then hand over with the handover, which gives me great happiness. Along with the extraordinary challenges I've faced over the past 12 years, there have been developments of extraordinary beauty. For example, it was during this period that inflation was permanently reduced to single-digit levels after a 35-year hiatus. As a natural consequence of the decline in inflation, 6 zeros were eliminated from our money in this 12-year period. Our Turkish Lira attained its symbol in this period, was adopted by our citizens and began to be widely used. Again, a development that makes me very happy is that Turkey's G20 Presidency was successfully concluded in this period, that is, last year. The global economic crisis that began in 2008 affected our country for a short time and to a limited extent. In the coming period, under the presidency of our new President Mr. cetinkaya, it has become possible for inflation to fall permanently to low single-digit levels. We can summarize the reasons for this as follows: During the exit period from the global crisis, our current account deficit increased to 75 billion US dollars and approached double digit levels compared to gross product. With the contribution of the measures taken in the last four years, the current account deficit has decreased to 30.5 billion US dollars and around 4.5 percent compared to gross domestic product. The other obstacle to reducing inflation was food inflation. Food inflation also fell to single digit levels with the measures taken as of today after being at double-digit levels for a long time. Inflation, on the other hand, decreased to 7.5 percent as of the latest data as a result of the measures taken. We expect the decline in inflation to continue in the short term. 2 As a result of all these, while the internal and external balancing continued, our economy continued to grow uninterruptedly in the last 6 years. These successful results are the product of a team work, a collective effort. First of all, I would like to thank our esteemed ministers, prime ministers and presidents who have entrusted me and our other colleagues in the management of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey with these important duties. In addition, due to their valuable and effective contributions to the healthy financing structure of the private sector, our Financial Stability Committee member institutions, especially the BRSA, CMB, SDIF and Undersecretariat of Treasury; To our Undersecretariat of Treasury, Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Development for their valuable and effective contributions to the healthy financing of the public sector; To the member institutions of the Food Committee due to the diagnosis and treatment recommendations related to food inflation; I would like to especially thank the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Livestock for the structural and cyclical measures being taken. Dear guests; At the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, I would like to thank all my colleagues at the Central Bank, from our researchers to our Chief Economist, from our assistant experts to our vice presidents, from our officers to our branch managers, from our branch managers to our general managers, from our Supervisory Board members to our Bank Council members, for their sense of duty, diligence and dedication. We also have employees in dozens of title groups that I have not counted here, and I thank them separately. Continuity and change are the two basic elements behind success. Institutionalization ensures continuity, while continuity reduces uncertainty by providing predictability, and in this way increases stability and confidence. Change is essential for progress, for making progress and for adapting to new circumstances. Institutional structures that can establish the right balance of continuity and change can achieve a sustainable success. In the last 15 years, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey has set a good example of this. Continuity and change are in our eyes as a relay race 3 we can revive it. There is both continuity and change in relay racing. Mr. Murat cetinkaya, our President, made significant contributions to the development of the institutional capacity of our bank during his term as Vice President. In addition, together with our other vice presidents, he made very important contributions to the design and implementation of the roadmap we published on August 18, 2015. I strongly believe that in the next 5 years, under the leadership of our President cetinkaya, our economy will significantly approach its 2023 targets. I wish them ease and success and hand over this precious flag with peace of mind. Best regards. 4

Burada saymadm onlarca unvan grubundaki alanlarmz da var, onlara da ayr ayr teekkr ediyorum. Sreklilik ve deiim baarnn ardnda yatan iki temel unsurdur. Title: Speech by Governor Murat etinkaya at the CBRT Presidency Handover Meeting
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: CBRT PRESIDENCY DELEGATE OF DUTIES - DELIVERY MEETING Murat cETNKAYA 19 April 2016, Ankara Mr. President, distinguished guests, esteemed colleagues; This last day of our President's 5-year term of office has been spent with an intense pace of work and now we are in this hall for the handover program. I think that even today's work alone shows the Central Bank's corporate culture, business style and understanding of continuity. Chairman, the institutionalization and continuity you mentioned is a reassuring element for all of us for the coming period. From my point of view, it shows the extent of the responsibility I have taken over. Mr. President, I have had the opportunity to work with you for four years of your five-year tenure. I would like to express that this is a very valuable experience for me. Our term in office was perhaps one of the most extraordinary periods of the last century for central banks. We have experienced a period in which risks are being redefined on a global scale and new and different solutions are needed. Our dynamic approach has made invaluable contributions to bringing the ship to safe havens in stormy waters caused by global risks. While trying to design and implement new vehicles with a view specific to our country, we did not leave the caution behind. We have shown that it is possible for a central bank to be cautious while expanding its toolkit. In particular, the macroprudential tools we have used have gained general acceptance in the world. Another important element that shaped the period in which we worked together was the efforts to develop common sense. Your disciplined approach to solving problems is one of the defining factors of your presidency. I would like to put special emphasis on common sense. Coordination of different opinions and policy proposals around a common goal in our Bank's decision-making processes will be one of the basic building blocks of the next period. The raison d'etre of central banks, as is known, is to support economic stability. The most effective tool on this path is reputation. The most important components of reputation are technical capacity and quality communication. It is important to analyze global and local dynamics competently, to formulate policy preferences with the same competence and to communicate all these with stakeholders. In this context, the Republic of Turkey 2 As the Central Bank, I believe that taking steps to further strengthen communication with stakeholders in the coming period will provide significant benefits. It will be among our priorities that our Bank's policies are understandable as we always work and that the policy instruments we use can further increase their effectiveness. In the coming period, we will be determined to achieve the goal of ensuring price stability permanently with transparent and predictable policies. We will act with a holistic approach that also takes into account macroeconomic balances and their interaction with monetary policy. While aiming to keep inflation at levels consistent with the target, we will continue to observe financial stability. Believing in the necessity of joint efforts to achieve all these goals, I believe that we will exhibit successful examples in the coming period in terms of cooperation with the relevant institutions. These policies will be the main factors that strengthen our hand in consolidating economic stability and reducing trade-offs. In the coming period, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey will continue to determine its policies dynamically, taking into account both the conditions of the day and the expectations for the future; In this direction, it will strive for continuous development and self-renewal. Further strengthening the institutional identity of the Central Bank and increasing its technical competence and communication capacity are among our primary goals. Mr. President, In concluding my speech here, I would like to thank you again on behalf of all our employees, myself and our Bank for the services you have rendered to the Central Bank so far. I wish you great success in the new period of your next working life. May your path always be clear. Yours truly. 3

Before moving on to the agenda items to be discussed in the General Assembly, I would like to dwell on some of the issues that I consider important. First of all, by referring to the recent macroeconomic developments, I will try to summarize how monetary policy is shaped in this context. Global growth maintained its weak course in 2016, which it had maintained since the global financial crisis. In the last five years, when growth in developing countries was weak, the Turkish economy showed a relatively good performance (Chart 1). As the Central Bank, we maintained our policy stance in 2016 that was tight against the inflation outlook, stabilizing foreign exchange liquidity and supporting financial stability. In November 2016, ongoing uncertainties regarding global economic policies and the upward update of U.S. policy rate expectations led to volatility in financial markets and a rise in the exchange rate in Turkey, as in other developing countries. Dear Guests, We define our current policies as a tight stance to offset risks to inflation. I find it useful to remind you that we take into account the medium-term inflation outlook when making monetary policy decisions. Therefore, we will maintain our tight stance on monetary policy until there is a significant improvement in the inflation outlook. 6 Dear Guests, Monetary policy will continue to support the long-term potential growth of the economy through its contribution to combating inflation and balanced growth. On the other hand, advances in structural reforms will provide additional support to the fight against inflation by increasing the growth potential of our country. In this context, steps towards human capital and labor markets, the creation of a structure that supports technology and innovation, and the increase of savings stand out as the main areas of structural reform. In this part of my speech, I would like to inform you about the strategy we have created as the Central Bank to ensure price stability and its reflections on the structuring and activities of our Bank. As you know, the main purpose of our Bank, which is determined by law, is to ensure and maintain price stability. The fact that the aim of ensuring price stability is given by law clearly reveals the importance of the issue. As a matter of fact, there is a consensus in the economic literature on the direct contribution of price stability to social welfare in the medium and long term. Accordingly, the permanent stabilization of price stability increases predictability in the economy; provides a favorable environment for the improvement of investment and financing conditions. Central banks have a primary role to play in ensuring price stability. The CBRT is already actively using its monetary policy instruments in line with its purpose set out by law. Past experience indicates that in order to ensure price stability permanently, the fight against inflation must be supported by a holistic effort and a structural approach. In order to keep trade-offs at a minimum level and to achieve permanent results, it is of great importance that all relevant institutions and stakeholders in the economy contribute to the process. Another issue is the progress on structural issues that increase inflation rigidity. 2016 was a period in which we strengthened our focus on price stability and took important steps in communication policy. In the light of the experience of the past decade, we have designed a holistic strategy to achieve price stability permanently and communicated with the public. This strategy envisages a holistic structure based on joint efforts with stakeholders by raising awareness of structural elements, in addition to a framework in which the Central Bank uses monetary policy tools to combat inflation when and to the extent necessary. We have taken important steps last year in order to contribute to solution proposals in structural areas and to create a common discussion platform. Again within the CBRT 7 We established our Structural Economic Research unit. In this way, we have established an institutional capacity to develop solutions in structural areas in the fight against inflation in close communication with the real sector. This new unit of ours is active in two important areas in addition to its efforts to support the policy-making process and the research it carries out. The first of these consists of activities within the scope of the Food and Agricultural Product Markets Monitoring and Evaluation Committee (Food Committee). The other includes studies on the compilation of regional and sectoral field information on the real sector. I would like to touch briefly on these two important issues in order. The Food Committee, which was established to carry out studies on food prices, which lead to high volatility in inflation, gained a new structure in 2016 and its secretariat was given to the CBRT. In the coming period, it is planned to take the necessary steps to expand the joint institutional effort exhibited in the Food Committee and to implement it in other structural areas related to price stability. I mentioned the importance of supporting structural efforts with a holistic approach in order to achieve price stability permanently. In this context, in recent years, we have sought to strengthen our efforts to closely monitor and understand the real sector. By expanding the scope of the company meetings we have held in order to follow the current developments in the economy and to strengthen our communication network with the real sector, we have made the necessary arrangements in the Bank's organizational structure in order to manage the process more effectively. As the Central Bank, we regularly visit companies in different cities of our country. In these meetings, on the one hand, we receive evaluations of the activities and expectations of the companies, and on the other hand, we strive to identify structural problems. In order to increase the effectiveness of all these efforts and public awareness, we have made some innovations over the past year to strengthen communication with the public. In this direction, regular meetings were first held with real sector representatives and financial institutions. Subsequently, technical meetings with investors and analysts were increased and expanded. By closely following the current technological developments in the field of communication, we started to use social media tools more actively. In addition, in order for our Bank's employees to share their views with the public, to open them to discussion and to contribute to the economic agenda in a timely manner, the blog titled "Diary of the Center" 8 site. With our new communication activities, we have greatly improved our practices to meet the information needs of different target groups. In summary, the Turkish economy has demonstrated a strong performance in recent years. Recent macroeconomic developments have confirmed the resilience of the Turkish economy. With the contribution of fiscal policy and the supportive stance of macroprudential policies, economic activity has entered a recovery trend. On the other hand, monetary policy is used effectively to ensure price stability. We believe that the steps to be taken in the structural areas in the coming period will contribute to the permanent achievement of price stability. Dear Guests, Within the framework of the duty assigned to it by law, our Bank continues to contribute to the balanced and sustainable growth process of the Turkish economy by considering financial stability in line with its price stability target. As we go through a period of low predictability on a global scale, our most important task is to move forward in line with our basic goals. At the end of my speech, I would like to remind you again that our Bank has left its 85th year behind. The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey is one of the most important economic institutions of our country with its deep-rooted history and corporate culture. Today, as in the past, our Bank continues its activities with the aim of contributing to economic stability and the welfare of the country. As I conclude my speech here, I would like to thank you once again for your interest and offer my respects. 9

text: 2014 JULY INFLATION REPORT INFORMATION MEETING Erdem BACI 24 July 2014, Ankara Dear Guests, Welcome to the information meeting where we will share the main messages of the July 2014 Inflation Report with you. I would like to present to you an overview of the Report, which will be published on our website in a moment. In the Report, as always, we share our assessments of macroeconomic developments with the economic outlook that form the basis for monetary policy decisions and present our medium-term inflation forecasts and monetary policy stance updated in line with the developments in the last three months. In addition to the main sections of the Report, we have included seven boxes on various topics. These boxes contain analyses of current and interesting topics. For example, there are boxes in the Report that examine the sensitivity of inflation to business cycles and examine direct and indirect purification approaches for national income data. In addition, there are boxes related to real and current account balancing in Turkish foreign trade, examining the relationship between current balance and loans in a wide group of countries, analyzing the relationship between consumer and commercial loans in Turkey and the current account deficit, examining liquidity policy and the relevance of Turkish lira loans, and access to credit for companies in Turkey. You see the titles of the boxes on the mirror. Each of them sheds light on important issues related to the Turkish economy. I recommend you to read these studies, which will be published on our website within the scope of the Inflation Report in a moment. Dear Guests, I will begin by referring to the global economic outlook, which continues to play an important role in our policies. In the second quarter of the year, after prolonged global uncertainties, financial volatility decreased and liquidity conditions improved. In this period, we observed that risk appetite remained positive and the weakening trend in portfolio flows to developing countries reversed (Chart 1). Recently, the Federal Reserve (Fed) lowered its long-term interest rate expectations by announcing that it would continue its supportive policies for a long time. In addition, the European Central Bank (ECB) lowered policy interest rates and announced a new quantitative easing program. We can count these developments as important factors that have a remedial effect on global liquidity conditions. We expect the moderate global growth outlook and the positive trend in risk appetite to continue to support capital flows to developing countries in the coming period. 2 Chart 1. Monetary Policy Practices and Monetary Conditions Dear Guests, At the end of 2013 and the beginning of 2014, with the significant increase in uncertainties in domestic and foreign markets, we observed a significant depreciation of the Turkish lira compared to other developing countries and a significant increase in risk premium indicators (Chart 2 and Chart 7). As the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey (CBRT), we organized an interim Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting on January 28 in order to control the deterioration in inflation expectations and pricing behaviors and to protect macroeconomic and financial stability. At this meeting, we went for a strong and front-loading monetary tightening (Chart 3). In addition, we started to simplify the operational framework and started to provide CBRT funding mainly through a one-week repo auction (Chart 4). The conditions that led to our strong and front-loading monetary tightening on January 28 have improved significantly in the time frame from the April Inflation Report to this period. The reduction of internal and external uncertainties and the recent decisions of the Fed and the ECB have been important factors in this recovery. In its June statement, the Fed stated that it would continue its low interest rate policy in the medium term. In addition, Fed members lowered their long-term interest rate expectations from 4 percent to 3.75 percent. During the same period, the ECB lowered the borrowing interest rate to negative and announced a new quantitative easing program that will start from September. As a result of these developments, we observed improvements in global liquidity conditions. Capital flows to developing countries showed some recovery. On the other hand, in addition to the developments in financial indicators, the deterioration in the inflation trend in the first quarter has stopped, and a significant decline in the inflation trend excluding food has been observed in recent months. Dear Guests, As you know, the monetary tightening we did on January 28 was strong and front-loaded. In the period since January 28, there have been decreases in risk premiums, improvements in global liquidity conditions and improvements in the inflation trend.
