While reductions were made in the upper band of the interest rate corridor especially in the first half of the year, a conventional tightening step was taken in November for the first time since 2008. In January 2017, we implemented a tightening framework that included dynamic and different liquidity instruments in the face of the excessive activity observed in the foreign exchange market, although the macro framework and economic fundamentals were unchanged. While a simple policy framework increases the effectiveness of the transmission mechanism, it does not exclude such dynamic responses. In this context, since January 12, 2017, we have suspended repo auctions with a maturity of 1 week; As of 16 January, due to the limitation of marginal funding, we meet part of the system's funding needs at the late liquidity window lending interest rate on the days deemed necessary (Chart 4). With the effect of these practices, a significant increase was observed in our weighted average funding rate and BIST Interbank overnight repo rate (Chart 3). In addition, in order to increase the flexibility and instrument diversity in the management of Turkish Lira and foreign currency liquidity, we opened the Foreign Exchange Deposits market for Turkish Lira Deposits on January 17. At the PPK meeting on January 24, we decided to strengthen monetary tightening in order to limit the deterioration that may occur in the inflation outlook due to the excessive mobility observed in exchange rates. Against this backdrop, we raised the marginal funding rate by 75 basis points to 9.25 percent and the late liquidity window lending rate by 100 basis points to 11 percent. We closely follow the reflections of the policies we implement on the markets. Monetary policy decisions in the coming period will depend on the inflation outlook. We will be able to closely monitor developments in inflation expectations, pricing behavior and other factors affecting inflation and make additional monetary tightening if necessary. In addition, in the event that unhealthy price formations that are not compatible with economic fundamentals are observed in the foreign exchange market, we will take the necessary measures with liquidity instruments. Dear Guests, Thanks to the macroprudential policies supporting the financial system, the delayed effects of the liquidity measures we have taken and the public incentives, a moderate upward trend was observed in the last quarter of 2016 in the annual growth rate of loans extended to the non-financial sector (Chart 7). When we look at the sub-items of the loans, we see that commercial loans increased at a limited rate due to Turkish lira loans in the said period; With the partial recovery in consumer confidence and the delayed effects of the adjustments, we see that the upward trend in consumer loans continues to strengthen. When we look at the sub-items of consumer loans, it is seen that the increase is generalized. The downward trend in loan and deposit rates in the previous periods paused in the last quarter of 2016 due to the tightening in domestic and international financing conditions and the tightness in credit conditions continued. On the other hand, TL loan rates to small and medium-sized enterprises declined in the last quarter of the year due to the effect of supportive public policies (Chart 8). 6 Figure 7. Source: CBRT. 2. Macroeconomic Developments and Basic Assumptions Dear Guests, In this part of my talk, I will touch on the macroeconomic outlook and assumptions that form the basis of our forecasts. First of all, I would like to summarize the recent inflation developments. Then, I will talk about the domestic and international demand outlook that we base our forecasts on in the base scenario. Consumer inflation, which showed a gradual slowdown trend after July 2016, was 7 percent in November, close to the lower band of the October Inflation Report forecasts. However, inflation in December increased significantly due to the volatility in unprocessed food prices and tobacco price adjustments, and finished the year above the forecast upper band with 8.53 percent (Chart 9). The increase in inflation outside of unprocessed food and tobacco was more limited (Chart 10). In this development, the depreciation of the Turkish lira and the impact of tax adjustments came to the fore. 7 Figure 9. In addition to this effect, energy inflation increased rapidly with the rise in crude oil prices (Chart 11). The increase in the exchange rate also adversely affected basic goods group inflation, and goods group inflation, which showed a steady slowdown trend until November, rose in the last month of the year with the effect of tax increases. Recent tax adjustments, particularly on tobacco products, have had a significant upward impact on inflation. In November, Special Consumption Tax (SCT) regulation was made on automobiles; In December, the excise duty rate on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products was raised for the second time after the tax increase in January 2016 (Chart 11). Thus, in 2016, tax adjustments and the contribution of managed/directed prices to inflation were well above historical averages. Food inflation moderated until November, making a relatively limited contribution to inflation compared to past years. In December, food inflation increased with the depreciation of the Turkish lira and the effect of adverse weather conditions (Chart 11). Despite this rise, food inflation ended the year at a historically low level of 5.65 percent with the effect of both the contraction in the tourism sector and the measures taken. In the last quarter of the year, basic goods group prices differed on the basis of subgroups; While inflation slowed down in groups such as clothing and furniture, an upward trend was recorded in sectors where domestic sales were relatively strong. Despite the moderate outlook for food inflation and the weak course of demand conditions, service inflation remained high due to real unit labor costs and the increase in rents, especially in Istanbul. Towards the end of the year, the pressures from producer prices became evident, especially in December, the tendency to increase prices according to the spread indices strengthened. Under this outlook, the main trend of the core indicators followed an upward trend with the month of December (Chart 12). In summary, despite the limiting effect of economic activity, the inflation outlook in the near term has deteriorated as a result of tax increases, strengthening cost-side pressures and a partial rise in food prices. Dear Guests, In the third quarter of 2016, a significant slowdown in economic activity was observed. In this period, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) decreased by 2.7 percent compared to the previous quarter and by 1.8 percent compared to the same period of the previous year (Chart 13). We have seen that the loss of momentum in economic activity due to the decline in tourism revenues has deepened with the negative effects of the developments in July on domestic demand (Chart 14). The modest outlook in the construction sector, with a strong 23.8 percent year-on-year increase in public consumption spending, mitigated the effects of the decline in other components of domestic demand on growth. In addition, the negative effects of the extended Eid holidays and the loss of working days due to the negativities in mid-July were also observed on the activity. Therefore, although the main trend in economic activity is in the direction of slowing down, it is not as weak as the data imply. 9 evaluate. Excluding the effects of these business day losses in addition to the normal calendar effects, we estimate that economic activity in the third quarter recorded limited growth rather than contraction on an annual basis. Indicators for the last quarter of 2016 indicate a moderate growth in economic activity, with the exception of a technical recovery due to the compensation of working day losses in the third quarter. In addition to the increased use of credit due to the measures taken and the incentives put into practice, expectations that tax and exchange rate increases will be reflected in prices stimulated the demand for durable consumer goods. However, demand for products other than durable goods remained weak, and the sectoral spread of the recovery in private consumption demand in the last quarter was limited. The recovery in investments was slower than consumption expenditures. In the light of this information, we anticipate a moderate year-on-year increase in domestic demand in the last quarter. Although we expect the ongoing positive impact of foreign trade terms on the current account deficit to decrease in the coming period, we assess that the normalization of relations with Russia and the support of the depreciation of the Turkish lira to net exports will support the periodic recovery (Chart 15). In the upcoming period, although there is no significant improvement signal in the tourism outlook, we expect the trend of moderate recovery in economic activity to continue with the contribution of the supportive incentives and measures taken. However, the recent depreciation of the Turkish lira and the rise in the perception of uncertainty as a result of other domestic and external developments are likely to limit domestic demand through both consumption and investment channels. The global growth outlook and uncertainties regarding the monetary policies of developed countries, the weak course of capital flows and geopolitical developments pose downside risks to growth in 2017 as well as in the near term. On the other hand, the incentives and measures taken in the recent period are likely to be 10 we can specify the delayed effects as an upside risk factor. On the current account balance side, we expect the improvement to continue. In response to the increase in commodity prices, we anticipate that the moderate outlook in growth will limit import growth in the coming period. We anticipate that the current account balance will improve in 2017 with the positive effects of normalizing relations with neighboring countries, the continuation of the increase in demand from European Union countries and the flexibility of export market diversification despite the limiting effects of geopolitical developments. Under a tight policy stance focused on reducing inflation, we estimate that inflation will gradually converge to the 5 percent target in the medium term. In this context, inflation will be 8 percent in 2017; After declining to 6 percent in 2018, we anticipate that it will stabilize at the level of 5 percent in 2019. Title: Understanding Turkey's Market Opportunities
Subtitle: THE CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF TURKEY ON THE OCCASION OF THE CONFERENCE OF "PRIVATE PROVISION OF INFRASTRUCTURE IN TURKEY"
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Remarks by GAZ ERcEL GOVERNOR ON THE OCCASION OF THE CONFERENCE OF "PRIVATE PROVISION OF INFRASTRUCTURE IN TURKEY" cIRAAN PALACE STANBUL APRIL 3, 1997 UNDERSTANDING TURKEY'S MARKET OPPORTUNITIES For a comprehensive understanding of the opportunities offered by Turkey's market, I should stress the implications of our journey toward liberalisation. In 1980, with world conditions changing and the domestic economy in crisis, Turkey launched a structural adjustment program based on free market principles and an outward-looking economic policy. Since then, a series of liberalisation measures have been taken. The most significant accomplishment of the Turkish liberalisation process is that it has restructured economic relations. Both the financial system and the foreign exchange system have been liberalised. Before discussing Turkey's economic performance, I would like to describe some features of our foreign exchange system and financial system. Let me begin with the foreign exchange system. Efforts to liberalise Turkey's balance of payments go all the way back to the Great Depression, and ever since the 1930's, the issue has been whether to liberalise the current account or the capital account. Now these questions have been settled. Let me summarise the state of the foreign exchange regime under five headings: 1. Residents are permitted to buy, sell, and use foreign exchange freely. 2. Residents are also allowed to purchase, through authorised financial institutions, shares quoted on foreign stock markets, and are permitted to transfer foreign exchange abroad to pay for purchases of such securities. 3. By the same token, non-residents are allowed to buy and sell Turkish securities quoted on the Turkish stock market. They are also allowed to buy and sell Turkish government securities through intermediary institutions operating in Turkey. 4. A substantial part of the controls on capital movements were removed, greatly easing inflows and outflows of credit. Turkey has accepted the provisions of Article VIII of the Articles of Agreement. 5. To avoid excessive risks for the banks, new regulations were adopted governing the foreign exchange position of the commercial banks. The banks are free to set their own rates for buying and selling foreign exchange. Our foreign exchange system, described above, is very convenient for foreign capital flows. Now let me describe the main characteristics of our financial system. Even though our efforts to liberalise the financial system did not begin until 1980, the Istanbul Exchange Market has existed and operated since 1858. It grew out of the activities of Non-Muslim bankers in the Galata district of Istanbul. These operators, mostly Levantines, Jews, Armenians, and Greeks, used to risk their own capital by extending credit to the government, secured by pledges of future tax collections. Even though during the early years of the Exchange Market's operation in the 1860's, the amount of foreign direct investment in Turkey was negligible, foreign capital was being encouraged to form joint stock companies. Up until the beginning of the 20th century, the Market helped the government find funds to finance its obligations. In 1906, the Istanbul Exchange Market was re-organised and once more became a source of new capital for young private ventures. Without giving the whole history of the Istanbul Exchange Market, I want to emphasise that Turkey's experience with free markets did not begin in 1980 but goes back more than a century before. What the reforms of 1980 did accomplish was to institutionalise the markets and put them on a solid legal footing. Besides liberalisation, the structural reforms begun in 1980 included measures providing investment and tax incentives. I would like to review these issues briefly. The aims of these incentives were to encourage activities that would earn foreign exchange on the one hand, and to help foreign sources of capital finance investments in Turkey on the other. It can be said that by liberalising its capital account and introducing structural tax changes to improve investment returns, Turkey issued an invitation to foreign capital. Under these new arrangements, the tax incentives aimed at deepening the securities market and encouraging investment in it are of two kinds:  Double taxation of dividends was prevented by raising the corporate income tax rate and making it the only tax on dividend income. In addition, the income tax rate for small shareholders was lowered.  For residents, capital gains on shares became exempt from taxation if the security was listed on an exchange. Capital gains from the sale of through licensed intermediaries were made tax free. Premiums from the issuance of stock are also tax free for stocks listed on a stock exchange that does not distribute dividends to shareholders. There are also tax facilities for government securities. Privatization is an important part of our modernisation and liberalisation effort. Turkey embarked on a privatization program in the 1980s. Turkey's telecommunications and energy sectors are great targets for global partnership. Despite extensive exemptions from the program, by 1994 total proceeds derived from privatization since it began in 1986 had reached US2.4 billion, which is not so bad. Moreover, 25 percent of this total came from sales on the Istanbul Stock Exchange. More than 60 percent of the sales were direct sales to domestic and international buyers. The main purpose of privatization is to get the government out of the business of business and increase the efficiency of the privatised enterprises. Let me follow this account of the general framework of regulation governing financial investments denominated in foreign exchange with a description of the structure, strengths and weaknesses of our economy. The basic economic features of our country are attractive. A liberal trade and exchange rate regime, a modern and competitive private sector, abundant and vigorous consumer demand, and extremely attractive investment opportunities. This rosy picture is clouded by three economic problems that can be solved by a firm commitment to macroeconomic discipline. These three problems--high and persistent inflation, high public sector deficits, and large current account imbalances--are interrelated. Persistent high inflation has been Turkey's main economic problem for the last two decades. Its main cause lies in the sizeable public deficit. Its other causes include entrenched inflationary expectations, exchange rate movements, monetary developments, interest rates, and price increases initiated by public enterprises. Under conditions of an open capital account, large public deficits can generate imbalances in the current account. Turkey's current account tends to be volatile. For this reason, what Turkey really needs is to accept fiscal discipline. A sustainable and consistent fiscal policy is evidently the key to solving other economic problems. Achieving fiscal discipline will require political will as well as persistence. Even though we have economic problems, we unquestionably also have the ability to overcome them. Turkey needs to make use of this potential. I therefore now wish to draw your attention to the considerable strengths of our economy. For purposes of this discussion, I will split our economy in two--the real economy and the financial economy. Let me begin my explanation of the present structure of the economy with real variables.  The Turkish economy is a continuously growing, dynamic economy. Its long-term average annual growth rate is over 4 percent and its average annual productivity increase is around 2 percent. In each of the last two years, GNP has increased by around 7 percent, well above most OECD countries. Along with this rapid growth, the composition of the gross domestic product (GDP) has shifted during the last two decades, toward the industrial and services sectors, while the GDP share of agriculture has greatly declined. The share of the public sector in industrial output has also decreased.  Spending on investments has been increasing since the first quarter of 1995. Normally, periods of investment aimed at increasing production capacity last for about 20 months, but the increase in investment activity spending remained focused on increasing production capacity throughout 1995 and 1996. The Economic Trend Analysis of the Central Bank of Turkey shows that no earlier period of expectation of rising investments has ever lasted longer.  Official records show that Turkey's unemployment rate has been holding fairly constant at around 7 or 8 percent, which is very low compared to the other OECD countries. In April 1996, total employment rose by 2.6 percent and unemployment fell to 6.3 percent. The urban and rural unemployment rates were estimated at 9.3 percent and 3.8 percent respectively. In addition, Turkey was among the top ten countries in terms of improving its score on the United Nations' human resource development index, which is based on a country's literacy rate, per capita income, and life expectancy. Of course, such a nation-wide measurement takes no account of the wide differences between urban and rural conditions. Be that as it may, the strong growth of the working age population, the high degree of urbanisation, and increased numbers of well-educated young workers are all favourable to strong growth in labor productivity.  Turkey has a strong, dynamic and competitive private sector. The non-agricultural private sector recovered quickly from the financial crises in spite of unsettled political conditions and extremely high interest rates. In addition, it is the private sector that has been mainly responsible for capital formation.  There have been interesting developments connected with Turkey's foreign exchange earnings. Even though the official trade account and current account figures reflect sizeable deficits, I would like to emphasise that the level of merchandise exports is significantly understated due to its omission of rapidly growing but unrecorded "shuttle" trade with neighbouring countries. We are on the verge of being able to include these activities in our balance of payments figures. In addition, there has been serious underreporting of the value of transactions connected with some of Turkey's foreign direct investments, a problem that the Central Bank is working to resolve. Now let me touch briefly on Turkey's financial system. Turkey's financial sector is still dominated by the banking sector. In other words, most financial savings are channelled through the banking sector. The banking sector's total assets amount to a 66 percent of GNP. The reformation of the financial sector had the effect of reinforcing the privileged position of the banks. Turkey has a universal banking system, which is another way of saying that Turkish banks are allowed to participate directly in all forms of financial activity except insurance. The Banking Act of 1985 governs the establishment of banks, their capital structure, branch banking, foreign banking, credits, deposit insurance, and all other activities related to banking. Today our banking sector is highly competitive and efficient. It is integrated with the international financial markets. Its strength is based on an up-to-date technical infrastructure, a well-educated work force and experienced, and a well-qualified management. The banking sector's adaptability, shown by its rapid introduction into the system of new financial instruments, has increased the available range of financing sources. Financial reform has increased the efficiency and competitiveness of our banking sector. The Istanbul Stock Exchange is one of the best performing of all the emerging markets. Its total market capitalisation in increasing, both in nominal terms and as a percentage of GNP, which indicates that it is playing an increasing role in the transmission of domestic financial savings. The GNP share of market capitalisation has increased to 22 percent, while the GNP share of M2y, which is the total of financial savings held in the banking sector, is around 40 percent. In addition, the return of the Istanbul Stock Exchange, though volatile, increased substantially this year. Market volatility creates liquidity and great trading opportunities. When I talk about money markets I mean the Turkish lira money market and the foreign exchange cash and deposit market, open market operations, and government securities auction markets. These markets, which were introduced as a part of the financial sector reforms, have increased the effectiveness of the central bank's control over the liquidity in the financial system, and increased the role of market mechanisms in money management. When market mechanisms began to play a larger part in the allocation of resources, the responsibilities and instruments of the central bank also changed, bringing the issue of central bank autonomy onto the agenda of the Turkish economy. Turkey now has a well established and efficient system of financial markets. The main obstacle at present to the functioning of the financial markets is our large public sector borrowing requirement, which crowds out other demands for financing. The inability of domestic resources to cover the financing needs of the public sector has kept real interest rates very high for over a decade. Bold privatization efforts, broadening the tax base, and reforming the social security system are the best ways to correct this situation, and I may say that they are all under way. Macroeconomic stability and political stability are the keys to achieving sustainable growth in a low inflation environment.

Title: Press Interview
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: INTERVIEW OF PRESIDENT SuREYYA SERDENGEcT ON 26 - 27 AUGUST 2002 - Is it possible that the stability program implemented with IMF support will be affected by election policies? As far as I can see, it is not possible to implement electoral economics as in the past. There are several reasons for this. First, public banks are no longer in their former positions. Governance was ensured in these banks, they became rationally managed. Second, the Treasury has today come up with a new and transparent legal framework. They are already pursuing a principled and stabilization policy in cash management. Therefore, in my opinion, it is not possible to implement electoral economics through the Treasury. Moreover, whenever bond/bond yields rise, it is not possible to increase public expenditures beyond what the program allows in an economy where the sustainability of the domestic debt is discussed. Only the Central Bank remains. As you know, it is not possible for it to open loans to the government or public institutions in any way that is autonomous, and it is already following a policy that is in line with the task of price stability. - Postponement of elections is currently being discussed in Turkey along with election chaos. In this case, what are the chances and risks of implementing Turkey's economic program? We continue our program as it is. Because, in our opinion, this program is the right program because it will bring the longed-for economic stability. Since we have exhausted alternatives in the past, there is no alternative for today and a lot of progress has been made in the program. Last year, there was talk of hyperinflation in public opinion. Now, we see that the inflation expectations of the public opinion have reached the same level as the inflation target of the Government and the Central Bank. And this is happening for the first time in 25-30 years. There have been discussions about whether growth will happen or not, in my opinion, that are not based on knowledge. It was said that without growth, the program would not work. However, according to the data and forecasts we had, we had no doubts about growth. It is possible to move to positive growth by the second half of the year and it is understood that we will reach a growth of over 3 percent by the end of the year. The Central Bank's goal is to restore price stability in Turkey, which has not existed for 25 to 30 years, and it is not possible to change this regardless of political developments, because inflation is at the source of all our problems. And finally, another stability that we cannot give up is financial stability: the process of restoring the health of the banking system must continue without a hitch. If the program does not continue after the election... I don't even want to think about it. First, the inflation process of 25-30 years has not only destroyed stability in the economic field, but has also caused serious damage in the social and political fields. The deterioration of income distribution or the short-term perspective of politics and the fact that almost all elections are early elections are just two examples. Needless to say, if the program does not continue, it will be worse? Secondly, what will you do if you do not continue the program? Will you implement loose fiscal policy and distribute non-existent resources, or will you loosen monetary policy and go to hyperinflation? I am not saying in vain that we have exhausted alternatives in the past. - Is growth or inflation a priority in terms of the policies implemented by the Central Bank? The goal of any government in the world or in Turkey is to achieve growth and employment growth. The goal of modern central banks in the world or in Turkey is to ensure and maintain price stability. Do they contradict each other? No, it doesn't contradict in the long run. The Central Bank, which tends to ensure price stability, must necessarily get the support of the Government. As a matter of fact, this is the legal framework in our country today. On the other hand, if price stability does not conflict with its mandate, the Central Bank will support the Government's growth and employment policies. Therefore, the Government and the Central Bank need to work together in both areas. If you ask why, the reason is very clear. What is needed is sustainable growth. As in the past, we do not have very high growth, followed by crisis and contraction. The prerequisite for achieving sustainable growth is price stability. Since price stability is a prerequisite, tight fiscal and tight monetary policies have been implemented in this program since the beginning. I would also like to point out this here. When we reach the 35 percent target at the end of this year, we will not have solved the inflation problem. Inflation in Turkey will still be one of the highest in the world. We still have a long way to go in this regard, everyone needs to be patient, determined and long-term. - Will inflation targeting be introduced at the end of the year? As we announced in the letter of intent, our preparations are expected to be complete by the end of the year and to switch to this regime. For this, very intensive studies are being carried out in our Research and Statistics departments and these will be completed. In addition, the Central Bank has developed its communication strategy and we are starting to see the results of this. Therefore, we will be in a position to switch to inflation targeting. On the other hand, apart from the Central Bank, the discipline in public finances needs to be maintained and it must be shown that it will continue in 2003. Unless there is an unusual, unexpected development outside of us, the inflation targeting regime will be introduced. And the economy will have a solid anchor: the anchor of inflation. - July figures show that inflation has turned its direction upwards. There hasn't been much of an increase in the exchange rate in the last month, but it still has a strong impact on inflation. In this case, what kind of measures do you think to prevent this effect of sudden exchange rate fluctuations on inflation, which may also be caused by political developments in the coming period? As you said, in the recent past, in the process of political uncertainty, the excessive depreciation of the Turkish Lira, as well as the fact that this year's public price hikes have been significantly squeezed into the last two to three months, have had a negative impact on inflation. Public price hikes and the depreciation of the Turkish Lira will have an impact for a while, but on the other hand, when we look at the expectations related to inflation, we see that they are adversely affected for the short term, but not for the long term. Therefore, in our opinion, there is no reason to worry about the year-end inflation target. The effect of the exchange rate on inflation is of course very important: But, in the floating exchange rate regime, we see that this effect is now beginning to weaken. - What do you expect for the coming months? We see the effect of public price hikes and the excessive depreciation of the TL to some extent in August and September as well as in June and July. - Have you benefited from the free floating exchange rate regime in an environment of political uncertainty? We have benefited greatly because we know from past experience that if we had been caught up in this recent perception of political uncertainty while we were in a fixed or predictable exchange rate regime, we would have lost our reserves to defend the exchange rate level and bond/bond yields would have risen to much higher levels. When you look at the periods in 1998 and 1999 when we were affected by the crises in Russia and Brazil, you can see them. In the floating exchange rate regime, the exchange rate is not a policy tool, but as a result of all the policies and expectations implemented. This is also a very important difference. The pressure of negative developments is now not on TL liquidity due to foreign exchange reserves, but on the exchange rate. - The Central Bank was made an independent institution by law. Is the Central Bank also independent of the IMF, which imposes certain limitations? The limitations you mentioned in the program are the restrictions imposed in order to move towards macroeconomic stability in Turkey. This is our program, and we have introduced these limitations. Even if we did not have an agreement with the IMF, I think we would still have to implement such a program, and there would be limitations in it. There would be tight fiscal policy again to settle the domestic debt problem. If the Central Bank was doing monetary targeting, there would be a number of targets. If it switched to inflation targeting, there would be another set of limitations, and the Central Bank would not give credit to the government again. - Will the Central Bank, which is defined as the bank of banks, fund banks that have been hit hard by crises and have difficulty in lending to the real sector? What you say is true because the crises we experienced in 2000 and 2001 were essentially a banking crisis. As you know, efforts to restore the banking system to health are continuing with the support of the Banking Supreme Council and other institutions. The banking sector will be able to finance the real sector again. In the meantime, what we can do for the real sector as the Central Bank is; to ensure macroeconomic stability and for this the most important component, price stability. In addition, financial stability needs to be ensured. When we look at today, we see in the markets that there is not much need for us to provide a fund except in extraordinary cases. There is already a surplus of liquidity in the market. In 2001, the Turkish economy shrank by a record 9.5 percent, while almost all companies reported losses. The Central Bank announced a significant profit. And this has led to significant criticism. What is your view on these reviews? All the central banks in the world make a profit. The main reason why they make a profit is that they get zero-interest resources by putting banknotes in circulation, they make a profit on it. Contrary to its examples in the world, our Central Bank does not make as much profit because the emission (banknotes in circulation) are not very high in Turkey in the environment of chronic inflation. So what happened last year that we saw a high profit? This has a direct relevance to post-crisis operations. Our profit consisted largely of the income we earned from the interest income of the government domestic debt securities we received through our operations after the crisis and the repos we gave them as a result of the liquidity operations we carried out with the public and fund banks within the framework of the banking reform. This year, it's the opposite. This year, the Central Bank is losing money because there is too much liquidity in the markets. And when you withdraw it, the interest expense of the Central Bank is incurred. In our Annual Report, all these issues were included in detail. And although the Annual Report is open to the public, I leave it to your discretion that it has been dealt with with false ideas that are not based on information. The fact that the Central Bank is subject to external supervision is also criticized by some circles. What are your views on this? The Central Bank has historically had both internal and external supervision. Internal audit is carried out with the General Assembly, the Supervisory Board or the Inspection Board. In external audit, the Central Bank is subject to the supervision of the Prime Ministry or may also be subject to the supervision of the Ministry of Finance because it is a taxpayer. Since 2000, our Central Bank has also had an external audit of accounting. This type of external audit is not a transaction audit, but a determination of whether accounting information is accurate and in accordance with international standards. It is present in almost all central banks in the world. So much so that it is in the Law of the European Central Bank, in relation to the national central banks that are members of the system. Finally, it is enough to look at the publicly available risk management principles of the Bank for International Settlements, the central bank of central banks, to get the right idea on this issue. It takes a little effort to get to all this information, just a little bit of effort. It's like calling the General Secretariat of the Central Bank by phone. - Has the management approach changed with you at the Central Bank? I saw the advantages of being trained from the inside and knowing the institution well. Perhaps in this way, it was possible to reflect the real central banker understanding to the outside. In my view, the nature of their jobs does not require central bank governors to be sympathetic. For example, when the economy is growing and warming, and everyone is happy because of it, most don't like a president raising interest rates, but the real central bank governor has to do it. This is also the case all over the world. I think we've come a long way because we've approached things with honesty and seriousness, and we've told the truth to the public clearly. In this new era, there is no longer any need to distribute blue beads to everyone or to give sherbet according to the pulse. And we see the benefit of that. So, sir, what was the communication between the bankers and the Central Bank when the tension was very high? Naturally, the Central Bank needs to have constant communication with bankers at all levels. I can say that we were in constant communication with public and private sector banks during the crisis. After the abandonment of the monetary board-like regime that did not allow liquidity and the exchange rate commitment that was an integral part of it, many of the operations we carried out since February 26, 2001 were aimed at the recovery of public banks, including the granting of liquidity to one-eighth of the national income, and the restoration of the liquidity and foreign exchange situation of private banks, which had entered a severe crisis. Let me give you just one example; After switching to a floating exchange rate regime last year, we sold over 7 billion in foreign currency to banks. Notice I'm not talking about the 5 billion that is in court. We did this even though we did not have a currency commitment in the new period. It is still not well understood, but this alone was a very important contribution to the restoration of the situation of the banks. Finally, it should be remembered here that we established a crisis desk an hour after the events of September 11 and organized liquidity operations. - The banking sector now has a Supreme Council, but it is not possible to deny the Central Bank's presence in the sector in terms of supervision. What kind of cooperation do you have with the BRSA in this area? The relations between the managers and other employees of the two institutions are constantly improving, but we need to take more distance. The exchange of information was regulated by a protocol. The BRSA is responsible for supervision, but the Central Bank also has important information gathering functions according to the Law. Comparison of information and exchange of ideas are of great benefit to both institutions. This will become increasingly important in the European Union process. - Is there any conflict in any practice until this process is settled? Working in harmony, there is no conflict. But let me broach one topic. The objective functions of both institutions are different from each other. Monetary policy may at a certain moment contradict the policy towards the banking system. This is one reason why the Central Bank and the BRSA are autonomous institutions. This does not mean that one cannot work in harmony and come together around a program that reconciles contradictions. Just as it applies to governments and central banks in the developed world. In our country, unfortunately, whenever two people have different opinions on something, how they work together, there is no harmony between them. The influence of the monophonic tradition is probably the effect. - The biggest problem of the Treasury at the moment is that its borrowing has reached very large figures in foreign currency. Since the free exchange rate is applied in our country, do you have a common policy with the Treasury on this issue? We work with the Treasury on a constant, almost daily basis to coordinate monetary policy and borrowing policy. In our opinion, significant progress has already been made in terms of the diversity and maturity structure of borrowing in Treasury borrowing. When we look at who owns the debt, in our opinion, there is no problem in terms of maintaining the debt. This is the first one. Secondly, the Treasury's foreign currency borrowing has contributed to the settlement of the open position problem of banks last year. This was important for exchange rate stability in the floating exchange rate regime. As long as we ensure exchange rate stability with as little central bank intervention as possible in the floating exchange rate regime, which is very important for inflation targeting, and we saw this in the period November 2001-May 2002, we will be able to better assess the exchange rate risk assumed by the Treasury. - Markets are wondering when the Central Bank will cut interest rates. When will there be a new rate cut? As the Central Bank, we make our interest rate decisions by looking at future inflation. Looking at future inflation, we can make a decision in any direction at any time. We explain this to the public and the markets with short and long announcements we make every time. These announcements and others, which are written with honesty and whose content is clear, should be read and understood very well and no other thoughts should be sought behind them.

CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: PART ONE GROWTH PERFORMANCE IN 2002; INFLUENCES AND EXPECTATIONS FOR THE FUTURE Mr. President, I thank you and those who have brought this conference to this day. Dear participants, Here the other day we talked about post-crisis monetary policy and operations, which in our opinion is still an under-understood issue. Today, we will first look at what information we have about growth, and then we will reconsider what we are telling the public these days about price stability and the relationship between growth. Introduction: The Turkish economy entered the growth process again in 2002 after the rapid contraction in 2001. The stability and positive expectations and structural adjustments provided by the monetary and fiscal policies implemented after the crisis in the goods and financial markets contributed to the start of the growth process in all sectors of the economy, especially in the industrial sector. In the 2002 program, GDP growth was projected at 3 percent. At the beginning of the year, there were serious doubts that the economy could reach the projected growth rate. However, as the Central Bank, we have made public that this growth forecast is achievable both in our press releases and in the Monetary Policy Reports. In these statements, the following factors that will positively affect growth were emphasized. These are; 1. The competitiveness gained by the economy in 2001 has a positive impact on exports and growth, 2. The reasons leading to reverse currency substitution, in particular the stabilization of the exchange rate, stimulate domestic demand, 3. Stability in financial markets stimulates deferred investment and consumption spending, 4. Strengthening of the banking system and increase in the volume of loans, 5. Stocks that were rapidly decreasing in 2001 started to increase again, 6. Expectation of an increase in agricultural production . was highlighted as. Excluding the credit volume, it is observed that the above-mentioned factors were effective in the rapid growth in the first half of 2002. Evaluation of 2002 Growth Performance in terms of Production: It was announced by SIS that the GNP growth rate was 0.3 percent in the first quarter of 2002 and 8.8 percent in the second quarter. While the contribution of net external world factor revenues to GDP growth was negative in the first quarter of the year, it was positive in the second quarter. In the second quarter, the industrial sector grew by 12.2 percent and the commercial sector by 10.1 percent. As a result of stabilization in financial markets, the decline in exchange rates and interest rates positively affected the expectations of companies regarding production and demand, and provided a rapid revival in industrial production, especially since March. In parallel with industrial production, the increase in agricultural production positively affected growth in the second quarter of 2002. Agricultural value added, which declined by 2.9 percent in the second quarter of last year, increased by 2.3 percent in the same period of this year due to the increase in cereals and pulses production. Evaluation of 2002 Growth Performance in terms of Demand: As it is known, SIS calculates the GNP and GDP series by using sectoral production realizations and forecasts. Demand elements are obtained by using the GDP series calculated in terms of production. When the developments in demand factors in 2002 are examined, it is seen that the highest contribution to growth in both quarters came from stock accumulation. In 2001, domestic and foreign demand was largely met from inventories, which adversely affected production and GDP growth. Considering this situation, it was expected that stock accumulation would have a positive contribution to growth in 2002. The contribution of inventory accumulation to GDP growth was 5.9 points in the first quarter of the year and 10.9 points in the second quarter. In this development, the negative contribution of stock accumulation to GDP growth in 2001 was also decisive. Stock accumulation Its contribution to GDP growth was negative 5.3 points in the first quarter of 2001 and negative 8.6 points in the second quarter. Similar trends have been observed in past crisis periods. As a matter of fact, the same situation occurred in the first half of 1994 and 1995. In the second period of 1994, while the contribution of stocks to GDP growth was negative 7.5 points, the contribution of stocks in the same period of 1995 increased to 6.5 positive points. In response to the relative revival in the industry, insufficient domestic demand and the continuation of the decline in imports led to an increase in the stocks of manufactured goods. However, in the second quarter of the year, with the rapid increase in industrial production, especially the increase in imports of non-oil intermediate goods, indicates that raw material stocks have increased. Considering the slowdown in imports since June, it is estimated that imported raw material stocks were effective in the stock increase in the second quarter. An important contribution to growth in terms of demand is also due to the increase in exports of goods and services. Exports of goods and services increased by 9.1 percent in the first quarter of the year and by 4.2 percent in the second quarter. The continuation of the decline in other invisible incomes and the slowdown in tourism revenues limited the increase in exports of goods and services. Nominally, exports of goods increased by 4.6 percent in the first quarter of the year and by 2.3 percent in the second quarter of the year. This is expected to have a negative impact on the growth of non-agricultural sectors. As a matter of fact, while a slowdown in imports has been observed since June, production expectations for August indicate that manufacturing industry production will lose some momentum. Uncertainties in financial markets will also cause a partial slowdown in investment and consumption demand. The CBRT Economic Orientation Survey's data for the next three months also show that the vitality in demand and production will lose momentum. However, the expected increase in agricultural production is seen as a fundamental factor that will positively affect growth in terms of production and demand in the second half of the year. In addition, according to the records of the Exporters' Associations, the momentum gained by exports since July is considered as a factor that will positively affect growth. Likewise, the completion of the recapitalization process of the banking system will ultimately be a factor that will support growth. Conclusion: Dear participants, This is the information about growth and the expectations. There are positive and negative aspects. When forming an opinion on this issue, it is useful to consider the information as a whole. This is the first one. Second; The data obtained at the Central Bank since the beginning of the year and the forecasts made have never shown that the 3% growth foreseen by the Program will not be achieved. It still doesn't show it today. This has been repeatedly confirmed in our presentations to the Parliament, the Government and the public since the beginning of the year. Third; Since the beginning of the year, we are curious about the information on which the discourse "there will be no growth in this program, and the program cannot work without growth", which has been frequently reflected in the visual and written press, is based on. But we have clues. We know from the experience of other countries that the serious fight against inflation, which is a form of corruption, has started to disturb some segments of society. Fourth; Growth and inflation figures and calculation methods can always be discussed. That's right. We can argue too. What's surprising is that these discussions weren't made when growth  8 and inflation were above the 70s. Yet the methods were the same. Finally, the fifth; It is a fact that the program and the Central Bank's serious orientation towards price stability increase confidence in society. This also has a very important share in the recovery in the economy. PART TWO PRICE STABILITY AND GROWTH

text: ) CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF TURKEY MONETARY POLICY PRACTICES MACROECONOMIC OUTLOOK AND EXPECTATIONS JANUARY 2003 ANKARA PARAPOLITICAL PRACTICES - IMACROECONOMIC OUTLOOK AND EXPECTATIONS I. PARAPOL?T?KASI UYGULAMALARI I.1- General Framework of Monetary Policy and Exchange Rate Regime 1. The chosen exchange rate regime in any economy is the main determinant in monetary policy implementation. In other words, the monetary policy practices of central banks differ depending on the chosen exchange rate regime. 2. In Turkey, too, the exchange rate regime is determined by a joint decision of the Government and the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey in accordance with the Law. In addition to the basic economic policy priorities, the current structure of the economy also plays an important role when deciding on the choice of the regime. 3. When we look at the recent evolution of exchange rate regimes and monetary policies in the world and in Turkey, it is possible to make the following determinations: In economies that are closed or open to international capital movements to a limited extent, central banks can play a decisive role on both exchange rate level and interest rates due to this feature of the economy. As a matter of fact, as in almost all developing countries until the beginning of the 1980s, the practice of "fixed exchange rate, controlled interest" in Turkey formed the basis of monetary policy. 4. However, by the years 1980'1, inward-looking import substitution and controlled foreign trade policies all over the world had been replaced by liberal policies that were open to the outside. In parallel with these general trends in the world, the infrastructure of an open liberal economy has been tried to be established in Turkey for 80'1 years, and in addition to the liberalization of trade, money, foreign exchange and securities markets have been established and developed. In this period when capital movements are still low, Turkey 1 The Central Bank of the Republic has directed control of the exchange rate in its monetary policy practices, but continues to control interest rates. ettirebilmi?tir. 5. In the 1990s, however, the crises that occurred as a result of the further liberalization and parallel acceleration of international capital movements, and the consequent sudden and large capital inflows and outflows, especially in developing countries, were the main causes of the world economic conjuncture. lines. 6. The common feature of this period in terms of the monetary policies of developing countries is that the exchange rate is still fixed or predictable, but the effects of central banks on domestic interest rates remain extremely limited due to the fact that economies are even more open to foreign countries. In this practice, central banks try to maintain the level of exchange rate they commit to, while monetary sizes and interest rates are determined largely depending on the inflow or outflow of foreign capital. In other words, the control of central banks over monetary quantities during this period is extremely limited. In this practice, the predictability of the exchange rate can accelerate capital inflows for speculative purposes as long as the belief that the regime can be sustained continues; However, with the deterioration of the expectations, the capital in question leaves the country abruptly and these outflows cause very serious crises. As a matter of fact, these sudden capital outflows have been the trigger of the crises in some Far East Asian and Latin American countries as well as Turkey. 7. At the point reached today, the basic approach to the exchange rate regime, which is gaining weight in the world, is the "floating exchange rate regime". In other words, central banks are moving towards a more active monetary policy, especially trying to control short-term interest rates and adopting the approach of determining the exchange rate level under market conditions. In this system, the exchange rate is now rated anchor 2 Since it cannot be used as an anchor, inflation itself is chosen as an anchor, especially for the purpose of directing expectations, and central banks shape their practices only within the framework of targeted inflation. 8. As a result, there are three main policy options and when these options are evaluated from Turkey's point of view: i. pre-1980 and partly in the period 1980-1990: Control of interest rates and fixed or predictable exchange rate regime in an environment where capital movements are restricted; ii. In the period 1990 - 2001: Freedom of capital movements and fixed or predictable exchange rate regime, i.e. passive monetary policy; iii. After 2001: Freedom of capital movements, control of interest rates and active monetary policy were preferred and implemented within this framework. 9. In the light of this information, when we look more closely at the period from 2000 to the present day in terms of monetary policy and exchange rate regime implementations, there are two separate periods in which the conditions taken as data in practice are different, although their ultimate objectives are the same. The first of these is the implementation of an exchange rate-based stabilization program implemented at the beginning of 2000 with a predictable incremental fixed exchange rate regime at the center, and the other is the ongoing stabilization program in May 2001, which is based on the strengthening of the structural elements of the previous program under the name of "Transition to a Strong Economy", but in which the exchange rate has lost its anchor character and the implementation of the floating exchange rate regime is valid. application. 10. In these two periods, when the application of the exchange rate regime was different, the objectives of monetary policy were the same and price stability, while their practices and the reflection of these practices on the market were different. Since the exchange rate was used as an anchor in the 2000 program, the effect of monetary policy implementation on short-term interest rates is negligible. During this period, the Central Bank made a commitment to exchange rates. 3 it assumed the exchange rate risk, but left the interest rate risk directly to the market. With the transition to the floating exchange rate regime, in other words, with the exchange rate acquiring the character of an external variable, monetary policy has been placed in a framework that increases the determinant of the Central Bank on short-term interest rates. In this period, short-term interest rates have become the main instrument of monetary policy implementation. In current practice, it is essential that the level of the exchange rate is formed in the market under the conditions of supply and demand. The Central Bank has no commitment to the level of the exchange rate. Thus, exchange rate risk has become an important variable that market players must directly consider. 11. The selection of the different exchange rate regimes in these two periods was made in accordance with the conditions in which they exist, the objectives and characteristics of the programme implemented. At this point, it is worth reminding one thing: The floating exchange rate regime that is currently being implemented was the exchange rate regime that the previous program ultimately targeted. However, this regime must be passed before the foundations of the economy are consolidated and after a crisis. remained. 12When we look at these regimes, it is seen that both exchange rate regimes have advantages and disadvantages. Fixed or predictable exchange rate regime; Due to the fact that it is understandable and easily followed by the public, it can be an effective anchor in directing expectations in economies where fiscal policy is implemented in line with the exchange rate regime and where a healthy banking system is available. In addition, the fact that the exchange rate has a strong interaction with inflation, especially in developing countries, makes it possible to use the exchange rate as an effective tool against inflation as long as it is sustainable. However, in addition to these advantages, such a regime obliges central banks to maintain high levels of international foreign exchange reserves because it requires the defense of the exchange rate. In addition to high reserves, additional foreign exchange reserve facilities are also provided to ensure that the level of exchange rate pledged for crisis periods is maintained. 4 must be found. In addition to these, the fixed or predictable incremental exchange rate system may have some other disadvantages, such as having almost no flexibility against external shocks and leading to an increase in short-term speculative capital movements. 13. In the floating exchange rate regime, as seen in the example of our country, a new anchor is needed due to the loss of the anchor feature of the exchange rate and inflation itself generally assumes this role within the framework of a monetary policy regime under the name of inflation targeting. Since no exchange rate level is targeted under this regime, the need to keep foreign exchange reserves as high as before in order to defend the exchange rate is weakening; however, it is considered that a reserve at certain levels should be kept in order for the external debt service to be carried out smoothly, to ensure and maintain the element of trust and to establish exchange rate stability as a result, as seen in similar country examples. The floating exchange rate regime is a regime with high flexibility against external shocks. In the event of such shocks, changes in the level of the exchange rate will bring the supply and demand of foreign currency in the markets back into equilibrium within the framework of the current conditions. Similarly, such a regime has a limiting feature of speculative capital movements, also called "hot money", because it releases the level of the exchange rate directly to the market, in other words, because the exchange rate risk remains in the market. Under such a regime, market players are now forced to consider the behavior of all players in the market towards the exchange rate, as in the case of a predictable incremental exchange rate regime, only by considering whether the institution that has committed to the exchange rate level can maintain this level. On the one hand, this structure directs all market players to be much more careful and helps to limit short-term and speculative capital movements (hot money), and on the other hand, it contributes to the stability of the exchange rate by preventing large rate movements in the exchange rate. 5 14. In this regime, important factors determining the level of exchange rate in the short term: changes in the preferences of domestic residents and non-residents for domestic currency - foreign currency portfolios depending on the difference and expectation of domestic and international interest rates; domestic and foreign political and economic developments, balance of payments realizations and expectations for the balance of payments. In the case of our country, frequent political instability or political decisions that are incompatible with the requirements of the economy and that give the impression of deviation from the economic program being implemented, the fact that the foreign exchange and futures markets have not developed sufficiently and the culture of exchange rate risk management is not sufficiently established in both the financial and real sectors cause fluctuations in the level of exchange rates and emerge as an important factor in the formation of the exchange rate level. In determining the level of exchange rates in the long term, differences in domestic and international inflation rates also gain importance. This is discussed in detail in paragraphs 99, 100 and 101. 15. As regards the view that the floating exchange rate regime increases the uncertainty in the economy and therefore the risk premium on debt instruments; In international academic studies, it has not been concluded that countries that adopt the floating exchange rate system pay more risk premiums when borrowing than countries that adopt a fixed or predictable exchange rate system1. 16Similarly, the application of floating exchange rates is a regime that can be followed by everyone and is very visible because it does not involve any commitment to the exchange rate and leaves the determination of the level of the exchange rate to the market. Therefore, the positive or negative effects of other policy implementations are directly reflected in the exchange rate. Therefore, under the application of floating exchange rates, fiscal and monetary discipline can be achieved more effectively, as seen in Latin American countries. 1 Felipe Larrain B., Velasco A., April 2001 , "Exchange Rate Policy in Developing Countries: The Case of a Floating Exchange Rate". 6 17. Another advantage of floating exchange rate regimes is that they motivate economic units to keep the risk they are burdened with at a level that they can control by carrying an open position in foreign currency because exchange rate risk is left to the market. In parallel, considering that the main reason for the large amount of declines in production that occur as a result of the sharp impact on the cash flows and balance sheets of the economic units due to the jump in the exchange rate after the crises is that the economic units carry a high amount of open positions, the importance of the floating exchange rate regime providing more control over the amount of open positions than fixed or predictable exchange rate regimes, is better understood. 18. The success of our monetary policy implementations established under the implementation of the floating exchange rate regime depends on the existence of certain factors. These are; maintaining the effective functioning of the floating exchange rate regime towards price stability, which is the ultimate goal of monetary policy, without compromise, maintaining the non-interest surplus within the framework of the targets in order to reduce the public debt stock, concluding the restructuring process of the banking system; the permanent functioning of the financial sector real sector fund transfer channel and the strengthening of the role of the private sector in the economy. 19. At the point we have reached today, it is not possible to return to fixed or predictable incremental exchange rate systems. The failure of past practices and their results in crisis have destroyed trust in such regimes. Title: Speech on Money, Payment Systems and Communication
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: "Money, Payment Systems and Communication" Erdem BACI 18 September 2013, Istanbul Vegetable Oil Industrialists' Association, Istanbul Distinguished Guests and Distinguished Members of the Press, As I begin my speech, I respectfully greet all the esteemed participants and guests on behalf of myself and the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. Today I will share with you my views on two main areas. The first of these is the catalytic effect of money on economic life and the change in our commercial life and financial relations with the development of payment systems. The second is the catalytic effect of the communication policies of Central Banks in the world on their monetary policy implementation. Dear listeners; In the first part of my speech, I would like to briefly talk about emission activity and payment systems, which are among the most important areas of responsibility of Central Banks all over the world. The historical development of money must be considered together with its physical and technological development. Money, which has a history of about five thousand years, began to be used in paper form in the XI century. Nowadays, with the development of technology, we all observe in our daily lives that money expresses a numerical value on your computer screens and that the change of hands is with a key that you will touch on your keyboard. With the transformation of money from a tool of use that physically changes hands to a recorded value on our screen; In parallel with this development, the development of new tools, technological systems and legal regulations has been inevitable. 2 At this point, I would like to draw your attention to the similarity between vegetable oil and money. Just as vegetable oil acts as an indispensable catalyst for food to achieve the desired flavor, money is an integral element of commodity exchange. In other words, we can say that money is the most important catalyst that greases the wheels of the economy. The increase in demand and demand for the Turkish lira in recent years is a result of the increase in confidence in our money. In the 90s, when inflation was in double digits, the ratio of emission volume to gross national product was only around 2 percent, while this rate has risen above 4 percent in recent years when inflation has fallen to single-digit levels. The increase in the utilization rate is also a direct reflection of the increase in the reputation of our money. In recent years, it has been observed that the number of transactions and amounts have increased with the effect of the rapid development of payment systems and the diversification of payment services. For example, it is seen that approximately 33 trillion Turkish Liras worth of transactions were carried out in the EFT System, which is one of the most important payment systems of our country, in the whole of 2012 and that this transaction amount corresponds to approximately 24 times the Gross Domestic Product of our country in the same period. However, a new payment system for retail payments has been established and started to serve at the Central Bank using our own human resources. The most important advantage of the new system has been the safer and faster end-to-end realization of fund transfers. 3 As the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, we carry out numerous activities in order to ensure the smooth operation of the payment and securities settlement systems in our country. These activities can sometimes be in the form of establishing and operating the system itself, as in electronic fund transfer systems, or through the supervision of systems created by other institutions. Recent developments regarding checks, which are an important means of payment, are also noteworthy. As a result of an intensive work carried out by the Risk Center established under the roof of the Banks Association of Turkey through the Credit Registration Bureau, an infrastructure has been established in which the creditworthiness and payment adequacy of companies and individuals can be monitored. Thanks to this infrastructure, financial institutions and companies will be able to follow the credit history of the people they deal with in their commercial relations with the consent of the other party and commercial relations will have a safer functioning. With the Law No. 6493 adopted by the Turkish Grand National Assembly on June 20, 2013, "Payment institutions" and "Electronic money institutions" are legally defined for the first time in our country. These organizations are established in Turkey as a Joint Stock Company and it is ensured that they have a certain amount of assets and it is possible for them to operate by obtaining the necessary permissions from the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency by regulating issues such as licensing, field of activity and supervision related to the aforementioned organizations. I believe that all these developments will contribute to the more effective and efficient execution of payment transactions by you, the representatives of the real sector, who are indispensable elements of our economy. 4 Dear Guests; In recent years, we see that Central Banks have intensified their efforts to inform them about the policy tools they have, in which time period, for what purpose and how to use them. I would like to share with you my views on this policy dimension, which we call communication policies, in this speech. Central Banks, which preferred less communication with the public in the past, have started to inform the public more by adopting the principles of openness and transparency since the early 1990s. An increasing number of central banks in the world, notably the Central Banks of the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, New Zealand, Sweden and Norway, are already using verbal guidance on policy objectives and instruments as an effective means of communication. The European Central Bank has recently adopted and started to use this method. On top of that, the Central Bank of the Czech Republic, for example, continues to use verbal guidance as one of its active communication strategies by publishing the exchange rate assumptions underlying inflation forecasts. In my speech on August 27, 2013, my public sharing with the public the assumption of the exchange rate behind the inflation forecast of 6.2 percent in our Bank's July Inflation Report can be considered as a step in a similar direction. 5 Again, the Bank of England has declared that as long as inflation does not deviate from the target in an upward direction, it will not change interest rates until the unemployment rate in the country falls sufficiently and will not go to monetary tightening by reducing its stock of assets.1 A mode of communication in this direction with the markets has begun to be preferred by many Central Banks in the world. Similarly, in its latest Monetary Policy Committee decision, our Bank stated that the cautious stance in monetary policy will be maintained until the inflation outlook is in line with medium-term targets. Since our first Inflation Report in January 2006, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey has been sharing more and more information about the monetary policy stance behind the inflation forecast in the report. Thus, it is ensured that the values that can be referenced regarding the basic variables that directly affect price stability, such as credit growth rate and exchange rates, and the policy instruments that can have an impact on them are shared with the public in a more transparent manner. In this context, we can also use the same analogy that we used for money and payment systems for communication policy and verbal guidance tool. Communication policy acts as a catalyst that increases the power of influence of the policy instruments in the hands of the central bank and lubricates the transmission mechanism. 1 Bank of England, (2013), Monetary policy trade-offs and forward guidance, Austos gforwardguidance.pdf 6 The Central Bank will continue its efforts both to ensure and maintain price stability and to contribute to financial stability in its field of duty. While performing this duty, it will further develop its communication policies and use them in the most effective way. Thank you for listening to me and offer my regards. 7
