As I mentioned earlier, we revised our end-2019 inflation forecast down by 1.9 points. We expect the year-end inflation forecast to face a downward effect of 1.1 points from the impending fall in the underlying trend of inflation and the third quarters consumer inflation that came in 1.5 points lower than the July forecast. Moreover, we estimate the downward revision to assumptions for TL-denominated import prices will drive the inflation forecast down by 0.3 points. In addition, the revision to the food inflation forecast for end-2019 led to a 1.2-point decline in the inflation forecast. However, the largerthan-expected hike in tobacco prices drives the end-2019 inflation forecast up by 0.6 points. Furthermore, the slightly wider-than-expected output gap adds 0.1 points to the consumer inflation forecast. We kept the inflation forecast for 2020 unchanged at 8.2%. We estimate that the improved underlying trend of inflation and revisions to assumptions for oil and import prices will bring inflation down by 0.3 and 0.2 points, respectively, in 2020. However, being revised upward from the previous reporting period, the output gap drives the end-2020 forecast up by 0.5 points, offsetting these disinflationary effects. The above-mentioned forecasts are based on a framework in which global financial conditions will follow a moderate course and the recent gradual improvement in perceived uncertainty will continue into the upcoming period. Projections rely on an outlook in which the extent of monetary tightness will be determined in a way to ensure that the ongoing disinflation is consistent with the targeted path. Additionally, we assume that the fiscal policy stance will be determined in coordination with the monetary policy with a focus on price stability and macroeconomic rebalancing. In the last part of my speech, I would like to share my views on our monetary policy approach for the upcoming period. As I mentioned earlier, we take into account indicators regarding the underlying trend of inflation when determining the monetary stance. Following the policy rate cuts at the Monetary Policy Committee Meetings in July and September, we communicated that the monetary stance was, to a large part, consistent with the projected disinflation path. In the meantime, the data flow following the September MPC Meeting pointed out a significant improvement in the underlying trend of inflation. Moreover, more expansionary monetary policies at a global scale and the announcement of the medium-term macro policy framework on the domestic front led to a notable downward revision compared to the July projections. In this respect, we made an additional cut in the policy rate. 9 I would like to re-emphasize that we establish our monetary stance in a way to deliver a reasonable real interest rate on the underlying trend of inflation. Accordingly, we monitor inflation expectations closely, while our inflation forecasts and the underlying trends that they imply also play an important role in our decision-making process. As for other factors affecting inflation outlook, our output gap forecasts, an important indicator of aggregate demand conditions, suggest that developments regarding economic activity and labor market have a downside effect on inflation. Meanwhile, import prices and the improvement in macrofinancial outlook due to developments in external-balance also support the disinflation process. In sum, demand and cost factors imply that the underlying trend of inflation is on a downward track. We evaluate that the current monetary policy stance, to a large part, is consistent with the projected disinflation path. I would like to emphasize that, as of where we stand, we have used a significant part of the room for easing, and the timing and size of the additional steps that we might take will be based on the data flow as well as developments in inflation outlook. Our focus is to pull inflation down permanently to singledigit levels in the shortest time possible and to reduce it to the 5% target, which is our ultimate target. In this respect, we will continue to determine the extent of the monetary tightness by considering the indicators of the underlying inflation trend to ensure the continuation of the disinflation process. At this point, I would like to underline that price stability and financial stability are inseparable. We have followed an approach in which we closely monitor the interaction between financial sector and real sector with an aim to bring inflation down and to ensure healthy functioning of the financial system to make disinflation permanent. Recently, we have effectively used our instrument set, reserve requirements in particular, to support financial stability and enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy transmission mechanism. We believe that these steps will contribute to the convergence of the economy towards a healthy and sustainable growth path in the medium and long run. The envisaged moderate recovery in credit and economic activity is consistent with an economic framework that would ensure that the gains in internal and external macro balances will be maintained. I would like to conclude my remarks by thanking all my colleagues who contributed to the Report, primarily those at the Research and Monetary Policy Department as well as the members of the Monetary Policy Committee. I also would like to thank every one of you for your participation. 10

Title: OpeningSpeech on "Reflections on the February 2001 Crisis: Lessons to be Learned from the Central Bank  Perspective", METU Conference
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF TURKEY Opening Speech of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey Governor Sureyya Serdengecti "Reflections on the February 2001 Crisis: Lessons to be Learned from the Central Bank's Perspective" erc/METU VI. International Economic Conference Ankara, 11 September 2002 9.30-10.30 I am very happy to be here with you today at the METU Economic Conference, where some of the basic problems faced by all the world's central banks will be discussed. In today's speech, instead of talking to you about inflation forecasts or market developments, I would like to share with you the basic elements of the Central Bank's efforts to overcome the February 2001 Crisis. I believe that discussing our experiences with crisis management will be enlightening for the majority of respondents in order to improve our understanding of the practical key elements of financial crises, which we have followed from numerous literature. As a preliminary information, I would like to make a brief assessment of the February crisis before moving on to the key elements of our crisis management strategies that contributed to the prevention of hyperinflation with the significant amount of liquidity withdrawn in record time resulting from the bank restructuring operation. Taking advantage of looking back at things and commenting, I will end my speech by touching on the lessons we can draw from our experiences. A BRIEF ASSESSMENT OF THE FEBRUARY CRISIS Aiming to stabilize its economy, which is experiencing problems due to chronic inflation, high real interest rates and deteriorating debt dynamics, Turkey initiated a stabilization program based on the exchange rate supported by international financial institutions in December 1999. Other periods of stabilization programs suggest that this decision was the right one. Countries that have included a fixed exchange rate in their stability packages and, of course, frozen Central Bank loans  which is an integral feature of exchange rate-based stabilization programs  have been found to be more successful in combating inflation and maintaining fiscal discipline. In addition, countries that adopted exchange rate-based stabilization programs (DKDP) achieved a faster improvement in yield than countries that adopted stabilization programs based on monetary magnitudes (Table 1). Despite its effectiveness as a nominal anchor in reducing inflation, the adoption of the DKDP brings with it a number of dangers that end with the collapse of the fixed exchange rate regime depending on the basic characteristics of the country. Looking at the data obtained to date, at least four main factors have been identified that could lead to the collapse of the program: (i) inconsistent fiscal policy; (ii) weak banking system; (iii) the absence of a pre-announced release date or strategy; (iv) negative shocks in which raising the exchange rate becomes a welfare booster, such as negative terms of trade shocks. At first glance, the DKDP, which started to be implemented in Turkey, does not seem to lack an exit strategy as it foresees the transition to an exchange rate band that will expand 18 months after the implementation of the program. However, it is now seen that a soft exit from the exchange rate anchor depends on positive global economic conditions and the local economic program on track. Unfortunately, as I will elaborate later, these conditions did not exist in Turkey. The other factors I have referred to have had a more pronounced impact on the program's collapse to varying degrees. Now, with your permission, I would like to return to the issue of the main reasons behind the collapse of the DKDP in Turkey. First of all, as in many DKDP, Turkey witnessed a large amount of capital inflow after the implementation of the program (Figure 1). While most of these inflows consisted of loans taken from outside by banks and the private sector, the contribution of foreign direct investments was limited. These developments also supported to some extent the much-discussed problem of moral damage, which suggested that the anchored exchange rate would implicitly guarantee those who wanted to borrow in foreign currency. Officials generally insist that there is no possibility of this changing in order to maintain the anchor. In this way, the government gives the private sector a guarantee regarding exchange rate changes. In this case, there is an inflow of capital, but the economy becomes more vulnerable to external shocks. [1] Fig il 1. As is known, credit increases contribute to the decline in the quality of banks' assets for at least three reasons, causing financial weakness. First, banks' capacity to evaluate projects is limited. Second, regulatory bodies have limited supervisory capacities and resources. Third, the number of "good" projects with high expected returns relative to their variance is small. The consumption-based credit growth experienced by Turkey  as can be seen from the remarkable increase in consumer loans (Figure 3)  has been an important factor affecting the large current account deficit (Figures 4 and 5). Second, since the stabilization of banks and the protection of the currency anchor are conflicting objectives, the weak and insufficiently controlled banking sector are the main factors that cause the collapse of fixed exchange rate regimes. The situation was no different in Turkey; As can be clearly seen from the figure, the banking sector was not adequately controlled for various reasons and banks became vulnerable to negative shocks. All this points to the fact that these weaknesses must have been rectified before the transition to the DKDP in Turkey. In this context, the weaknesses of the banking sector have also affected the sustainability of the regime in a way that has been overlooked until now. At first glance, fiscal policies were quite tight in 2000,[2] while tacit aid guarantees and possible deficits to the increasingly deteriorating banking sector raised serious concerns about the sustainability of the anchor. The expectation that at least some of these future deficits could be financed by inflation tax on the seigniorage revenues or the nominal debt stock contributed to the collapse of the anchor in Turkey. Thirdly, the least controversial of the factors affecting the February crisis is the apparent trade shock to which the country has been exposed. As a result of the large increase in oil prices, among other factors, the terms of trade fell by 8.4 percent compared with 1999, thus worsening the already large current account deficit (Figure 7). In order to restore the balance of current accounts, the real exchange rate would have to rise, which would require a decrease in the level of domestic prices if no adjustment was made to the nominal exchange rate. Since there was no adjustment of both types in the exchange rate, the trade terms shock raised concerns about the sustainability of the anchor. Fig il 7. Change in Trade Rates (Change in Percentage) Fourthly, the lack of an additional source of financing at the beginning of the stabilization program has been detrimental to the sustainability of the programme, given the possibility that the availability of such financing could prevent the occurrence of a possible liquidity crisis. Furthermore, negative external developments  especially those in the Argentine economy  have not been in our favor because investors are putting these two emerging economies on the same level, despite their different characteristics. The resulting capital flight has also jeopardized the sustainability of the anchor. I now want to go back to the key elements of our crisis management strategy. TEM EL OPERATIONS CARRIED OUT BY M-ERKEZ BANK DURING THE FEBRUARY CRISIS The main objective of the Central Bank after the February crisis was to restore financial stability and prevent hyperinflation. In the face of excessively rising interest rates in the first days following the collapse of the anchor due to the increased liquidity needs of public banks and fund banks and the escalation of demand for foreign currency The Central Bank entered the money markets by announcing the buying and selling rates to ensure the integrity of the payment system and to restabilize the financial markets. The collapse of the anchor and the transition to a floating exchange rate regime allowed the Central Bank to lift the restriction on domestic loans. As a result, interest rates fell to more reasonable levels (Figure 8). Figure 8: TCM B's Interest Rate Quotations in Money Markets, IM KB RepoReverse Repo Markets and Average Rates of Bond and Bond Markets (Compound) In contrast to the liquidity crisis of November 2000, when only foreigners' demand for foreign currency increased, it is seen that the demand for foreign currency of the residents also increased during the February 2001 crisis. In addition to the high amount of foreign exchange demands from customers, banks faced the problem of foreign currency liquidity as their access to international markets was also restricted due to the reduction of international investors' risks in Turkey. In order for local banks to fulfill their responsibilities in foreign currency, the Central Bank has introduced one-week foreign currency deposits to banks. Furthermore, the Central Bank intervened in the money market to eliminate excessive volatility in foreign exchange markets. For this purpose, the Central Bank sold USD 2 billion as of March 2001. Considering the increase in the domestic debt stock and the negative effects it has had on monetary policy, the banking sector liquidity operation constituted the most important policy measure. From the perspective of state-owned banks, the banking sector restructuring process involved the establishment of two important boards of directors: one for public banks and the other for fund banks, the first of which was aimed at improving the fund management functions of public banks based on the principle of zero new duty losses and drawing up an action plan for the merging or sale of fund banks. In order to make the banking system healthier for private banks, the main principle is to transfer all problematic or bankrupt private banks to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund. At this point, I would like to mention three points in relation to this issue. The first is the banking restructuring operation; the second is the withdrawal of the surplus liquidity resulting from the banking restructuring operation and the prevention of hyperinflation; the third is the internal debt swap and its consequences. Liquidity Operations in Public Banks and F-on Banks Even before the November crisis, public banks and fund banks met their liquidity needs by borrowing from other banks and the Central Bank in the money markets. The unequal distribution of Turkish lira liquidity among banks increased both the level and volatility of interest rates, reducing the effectiveness of the exchange rate anchor and Turkish lira liquidity management after the November crisis. This caused the confidence in the markets to be shaken and started a trend towards foreign currency. After the November crisis, the maturities of all transactions within the Turkish financial system, including depositors' deposits, were significantly shortened. As a result, state-owned and fund banks entered the February crisis with accumulated short-term liabilities, mostly overnight, which made banks extremely vulnerable to risks in relation to interest rates. The payments system collapsed because these banks did not have access to the liquidity they needed during the crisis. Due to competition between public banks and fund banks, these banks began to give higher deposit rates than other private banks. In addition, the borrowing rates of these banks in the interbank market varied greatly. For example, during the crisis, one public bank's borrowing rate was 850 percent, while the same interest rate was 2,200 percent for another public bank. As a result of these developments, the very high level of liquidity needs of these banks have become one of the most important reasons that constitute an obstacle to the implementation of monetary policy. Market interest rates were determined in line with the liquidity needs of banks instead of the Central Bank's liquidity management strategy. The overnight borrowing requirements of public banks and fund banks reached TL 21.8 quadrillion as of March 16, 2001, up from TL 15 quadrillion on February 26, 2001. Public banks and fund banks are not able to finance their overnight liabilities, which reach large amounts, and that their obligations are due to be monetized. it was very clear that they could not extend it without damaging their markets. For this reason, we had to urgently solve the liquidity problems of these banks in the immediate aftermath of the February crisis. The aim of the actions taken by the Central Bank to solve this problem was to keep the surplus liquidity in the market under control in order to prevent hyperinflation, to support financial stability and to minimize the financial burden of the operation. To this end, the Central Bank and the Treasury worked closely together to follow the strategy that I will briefly explain to you in a moment (Figure 9). Figure 9. Liquidity Deck Operation for Public Banks and Banks Transferred to TM SF At the beginning of the operation, the Treasury issued government domestic debt securities to cover the duty losses of public banks and intervened in the banks' negative capital balances. The coupon rates of these securities were indexed to the repo rates of the Central Bank. With this transaction, indirect public debt was transformed into direct public debt and there was no change in net public debt. In the next step, the Central Bank directly purchased the 14 quadrillion bonds issued by the Treasury. The Central Bank also provided repo facilities to these banks in the amount of TL 7 quadrillion with 7 days and 14 days maturities. The total amount of liquidity provided by the Central Bank to these banks reached 21 quadrillion. In addition, in order to prevent competition between the aforementioned banks, the Central Bank coordinated the maturity and interest rates between the banks on a daily basis. The Central Bank ensured that these banks closed almost all overnight borrowing and deposits as of May 2001. As of June 2001, the authority of these banks to borrow overnight and accept overnight deposits was abolished. The next step in the liquidity operation was aimed at eliminating the obligations of public and fund banks to their customers and private banks, which resulted in the introduction of a significant amount of liquidity into the market. In order to keep the excess liquidity in the market under control, the Central Bank has tried to attract liquidity in the hands of private banks and the public through open market operations. To this end, the Central Bank has begun announcing borrowing quotations in two organized markets in Turkey. The excess liquidity in the markets was withdrawn through reverse repo transactions on the Istanbul Stock Exchange and overnight, one-week, two-week and one-month deposits on the Central Bank Interbank Money Market. Since the liquidity surplus in the markets is large, interest rates in the money market have been equalized to the interest rates announced by the Central Bank and the rates announced by the Central Bank have become reference values. Meanwhile, the Treasury withdrew part of its liquidity surplus by borrowing from the market as much as market conditions allowed. The Treasury then made early redemptions for the securities in the Central Bank's portfolio in order to keep the Central Bank's balance sheet under control. Table 2. The Central Bank continued to provide the repo facility it offered to these banks as long as it remained within the 7 quadrillion limits. The amount of repos used by these banks decreased as their liquid positions improved. The repo obligations of the Fund's banks amounting to 3.6 quadrillion Turkish Liras were paid in February 2001 using an IMF loan. On the other hand, the liquidity operation was completed when public banks paid their repo debts in April 2002 (Figure 10). With the end of the liquidity operation, public banks have been forced to take advantage of the Central Bank's TL liquidity facility. and fund banks began to be treated equally with other banks. Figure 10. Total TCM B Liquidity Support Provided to Public and TM SF Banks (Repo Stock Direct Purchases, Trillion TL) Use of IMF Credit In addition to the liquidity operation, another factor that increased the liquidity in the market in 2001 was the IMF loan, which the Treasury used through the Central Bank to finance the budget. Of the 9.9 billion loan the Central Bank received from the IMF, 9.6 billion was used by the Treasury for budget financing. The Treasury used most of the IMF loan to make payments in Turkish lira in the domestic market. Thus, a significant amount of liquidity was provided to the markets. Clearly, it was not easy to withdraw such a high volume of liquidity without putting extra pressure on the exchange rate. There were other factors that affected the exchange rate. These were: increased money substitution, capital flights, and open positions of banks and corporations. Therefore, monetary policy in 2001 envisaged sterilizing the surplus liquidity by selling large amounts of foreign currency in order to reduce the pressure on the exchange rate as much as possible. After the February crisis, the Central Bank used the direct foreign exchange sales method since the end of March. However, after March 2001, the Central Bank started to use the tender method in foreign exchange sales in a way that would not contradict the floating exchange rate policy. (Figure 11). Thus, while the Central Bank's foreign exchange sales provided a more effective sterilization, on the other hand, it met the need for foreign currency in the banking sector without disrupting the functioning of the floating exchange rate regime (Figure 12). Repo Stock-Reverse Repo-Interbank Withdrawals (Trillion TL) Domestic Debt Swap Another important operation after the February crisis was the internal debt swapping process. The purpose of the domestic debt swap transactions, which took place in mid-June 2001, was to reduce the risk of government debt not being converted, to facilitate the lowering of interest rates, and to help banks close their open foreign exchange positions. The swap included the exchange of treasury bonds, longer-term fixed and variable-rate bonds with a package of bonds indexed to the U.S. dollar and Turkish lira-denominated bonds. The swap resulted in significant cash flow savings by increasing the debt service structure to an average of 6 months for formerly cleared bonds and 37.5 months for new bonds (Table 3). Prior to the swap, open foreign exchange positions on the balance sheets of private banks were US7.6 billion. When the banks in question bought the bulk of the new bonds indexed to this dollar, the swap led to a significant reduction in their open positions on the balance sheet. As a result of the swap, the stock of public debt denominated in foreign currency (or indexed to foreign currency) increased by only 13 percent, thus limiting the increase in the Treasury's vulnerability to exchange rate risk. POLTKA cIKARIMLARI I've heard that the Chinese word crisis also means opportunity, and I think that applies to public policy as well. The crisis can be an opportunity to do things better. In this context, I think that our experience is a good example of this. The rational fiscal and monetary policies put into practice after the February crisis, along with the deep-rooted structural reforms that were most needed, not only made the Turkish economy more resilient to negative shocks and less vulnerable to crises, but also increased the possibilities of achieving sustainable development. With these in mind, I would like to summarize the lessons that can be learned from the financial crisis in Turkey. In addition, in order to keep my speech short and concise, I will underline some points that I did not mention during my speech. Still, I believe these considerations and their implications from a policy standpoint are clear enough. First of all, based on our experience, I would like to emphasize the importance of the urgency of the policy response and the close cooperation between the central bank and other institutions. As we have seen in other countries, the inflationary effects of restructuring operations in the banking sector can be very important policy problems. In our case, the Central Bank worked closely with the Treasury and the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BRSA) to prevent excess liquidity in the market. Without the additional measures taken by the Treasury and the BRSA, the measures taken by the Central Bank to control excess liquidity alone would have been much less effective. Secondly, as we have observed, the transparency of transactions carried out during crisis management; it is extremely important for the market to perceive the possible financial risks, especially related to the recapitalization of banks. If this is achieved, the reliability of transactions in the eyes of market makers and the public increases. Third, the February crisis has once again shown how sensitive a role banks play in times of crisis. The strict banking rules that have been promulgated are rarely enforced, such as the prohibition of bankruptcy bailouts. Therefore, banking debts are largely unsettled public debts. As a result, a banking crisis can cause a currency crisis due to large public deficits that can occur due to implicit bailout guarantees given to bankrupt banks. As long as market participants expect that at least part of their future deficit will be financed through higher seigniorage revenues, future monetary policy will be perceived as inconsistent with the fixed exchange rate. This, in turn, will create a currency crisis before the deficits begin to be monetized. In this respect, government guarantees are the main factors that cause real shocks to turn a banking crisis into a monetary collapse. Fourthly, during the implementation of the DKDP in Turkey, it was observed that capital markets tended to quickly forget about positive structural reforms, immediately noticed even the smallest deficiencies in structural reforms and overreacted to short-term financial shocks. Even in cases where capital inflow is highly persistent, the gain from capital inflow remains significantly below the cost of capital flight. As a result, it is better to err by underestimating the persistence of capital flows than by overestimating it, and in any case, it is better to help policymakers they are advised to keep their cool and rein in investor morale during capital inflow periods. The above points explain why a positive financial balance should be maintained during periods of capital inflow. This would be advantageous both in terms of cooling the economy and creating public sector savings that could be used to increase total government spending during periods of capital outflow. These extra savings will be especially important if the country breaks away from the capital market during these periods. Fifth, as we have experienced in recent crises, governments tend to take temporary measures to correct their liquidity positions. As we have seen in the case of Turkey, governments tend to react by imposing new taxes that are easy to collect in the short term but can adversely affect production. However, I do not think that such measures show the necessary benefit. Therefore, temporary measures themselves can also cause payment crises. Based on our own experience in fiscal policy, I would like to draw attention to the importance of debt maturity and currency as a characteristic of public debt instruments. The fact that the maturity structure is excessively prolonged from time to time often causes countries to choose short-term public debt. In addition, countries sometimes drift toward short-termism as they try to meet ambitious price stability targets. For example, officials can announce fiscal policies that can be sustained by short-term debt tied to low interest rates. It is a fact that extending the term of the debt may not be a very easy process and can bring high costs. These costs are a sign to policymakers that credibility is poor. Ultimately, the first thing to do is to restore confidence through a tighter (but effective) fiscal policy. As can be seen, Turkey's experience with an exchange rate-based stabilization program highlights the complementary relationship between macroeconomic stability, financial stability, and the satisfactory progress achieved through proposed structural reforms. None of this alone is enough. Based on the experience of other emerging economies, it is clear that showing indecision in one of them increases the risk of not paying enough attention to the others as well. Thank you. [2] A particularly objectionable point in this estimate is that the financial situation should have tightened given the growing current account deficit in 2000.

Title: Speech on "YTL" at Istanbul "IMI"
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey
text: Dear Guests, As it is known, as of January 1, 2005, 6 zeros will be thrown out of our currency and our new currency "New Turkish Lira" will be passed. In this context, I would like to give brief information about the reasons, benefits, timing and meaning of the transition to the new currency for our country. High inflation, which started in the 1970s and became chronic over time, also had a negative effect on banknote sizes and monetary values, causing some economic values to be expressed in quadrillion today. Again, as a natural and inevitable consequence of high inflation, since 1981, a total of 11 new clippings have been circulated at the top value, on average 1 time every 2 years, in order to meet the increasing need for emissions. As of today, the world's largest denomination banknote, the 20.000.000 TL banknote, is used only in Turkey. This, of course, has not only reduced the reputation of our currency, but also negatively affected some of the monetary functions of the Turkish Lira, such as being a means of exchange and storage of value. Influenced. The difficulties created by the numbers with abundant zeros are not limited to these. Every new zero added to our money; It has caused various problems in writing and expressing monetary values, teller transactions, accounting and statistical records, information processing programs, payment systems and many areas in daily life. In this case, to put it briefly, the removal of 6 zeros from our money is seen as both a psychological and a technical need. At this point, I find it useful to make an assessment of the timing of the operation. As it is known, the "Law on the Currency of the Republic of Turkey" on the removal of six zeros from the Turkish lira was published in the Official Gazette on January 31, 2004. was published and entered into force. The fact that the date of transition to YTL was determined as January 1, 2005 is not a date that was decided by chance. When the experiences of countries carrying out monetary reform are examined, it is seen that the transition to the new currency usually comes up with a stabilization program and zero is thrown at different inflation rates. In some countries where the stabilization program has been successfully concluded (e.g. in Israel), monetary reform is carried out shortly after the program is started, while in some countries (such as in Poland, Bolivia, and Bulgaria) such a practice is implemented after the positive effects of the stabilization program on inflation are revealed. In cases where stabilization programs fail, it is noteworthy that after a while the need to throw zero out of money again arises, in other words, with the relaxation of financial measures, the zero-throwing operation loses its effect and loses its function after a while. When we look at the studies in our country, we see that since the beginning of the 1990s, the day has been projects that foresee the disposal of 3 zeros or 5 zeros, according to their conditions; structural economic problems the inability to be resolved, the failure to sustain the fight against inflation for various reasons, inflation of Both inflation bekleyilerinin appropriate to levels . .. nmesnn it has not been realized to date due to its inability to be provided. However, the concrete emergence of the positive effects of the recent economic stabilization program on inflation and the rapid downward trend in inflation in recent years have prepared a favorable environment for monetary reform. The rate of consumer price growth, which was 30% in 2002, declined to 18% in 2003. As of today, there is no serious risk to reach the 2004 target of 12% CPI. In 2005 and beyond, our goal is to ensure permanent price stability in single digits. In this context, it was decided to carry out the operation in 2005 as an indication of both the struggle to ensure economic stability and the distance taken and the determination to reduce inflation to single digits and to ensure permanent price stability. Dear guests, In the next part of my speech, I would like to give some information about the operational part of the transition process to YTL. The phrase "Lira", which was traditionally used when determining the name of the new currency, which was the only currency of the Republican period and which was identified with our country in international markets, was retained. It is seen that this method is mostly used in other country applications and the phrase "New" is introduced at the beginning of national currencies. In countries that experience hyperinflation and have to throw zero out of their money many times, it is seen that different names are used to avoid causing confusion between currencies when switching to new currencies. Since it will not be necessary to throw zero from our money in the long term with the continuity of economic stability, the first method applied in many countries has been chosen. In the second phase of the operation, which will be carried out at a later date, the phrase "New" placed at the beginning of the Turkish Lira will be removed and the transition to the Turkish Lira will be made again. When determining the composition of banknotes and coin clippings, country experiences were examined and in many countries no more than 6 or 7 banknote clippings were preferred; when a larger number of clippings were printed, some clippings were found to be out of use. As a result of the evaluations, 2 new banknote clippings, 50 YTL and 100 YTL clippings at the top value were added to the banknote clipping composition currently in circulation; In addition, it was decided that 1 New Turkish Lira banknotes would be circulated together with 1 New Lira coins. The images and security features of the YTL banknotes will be announced in the second phase of the promotional campaign in October. However, in order to make banknotes more easily recognized in the transition to YTL and not to cause confusion, clippings with the same purchasing power were produced in similar colors and designs for both TL and YTL. As it is known, the Law stipulates that TL and YTL banknotes will be in circulation together for 1 year as of January 1, 2005 in order to make the transition to the new currency smoothly. Therefore, our citizens do not need to rush for change. During this time, they will be able to use both currencies in their purchases and the conversion will take place in the normal course of transactions. Due to the upward rolling of prices during the transition period, the operation is not expected to have a lasting impact on inflation. Since it is a legal obligation to show the prices of goods and services in both TL and YTL on all labels and price lists as of January 1, 2005, our citizens will have the opportunity to control prices with this application and therefore the inflationary effect arising from the upward rounding of prices during the transition period can be minimized. In addition, the rounding effect in this operation based only on zero throwing can be felt less due to the rolling effect that already exists in our country due to the effect of the clippings removed from circulation in an environment of high inflation and the loss of the habit of using coins, with the introduction of 1 New Kurus, which is not currently in circulation and will have the same purchasing power as 10,000 TL, the existing rolling effect is even more it is thought that it will decrease. Another issue that needs to be mentioned regarding the inflationary effect of the operation is the cost of switching retailers to YTL to consumers or pennies! that their price rounding in order to take advantage of the illusion will not be continuous, so they are not expected to have an impact on inflation. In some sectors that have already prepared labels and price lists, it is observed that price reductions have been made due to high competition and this situation is expected to continue in 2005. The fact that price increases that may arise during this operation due to other economic reasons are not attributed to this operation and that individual increases that may arise in the prices of some goods and services are not considered as a general price increase is an important point to be taken into consideration when assessing the inflationary effect of the operation. In other words, in order to accurately analyze the impact of price increases, all the factors that may cause these increases must be taken into account. On the other hand, zero is thrown out of our money; It will not affect interest rates, which are mainly shaped according to expectations depending on the fundamentals of the economy and developments in the stabilization program, budget discipline, structural reform process and developments in inflation. Regarding exchange rates, there is no effect other than the psychological effect of writing and expressing monetary values by removing zero from our money. Dear guests, Although the operation to throw zero from the Turkish Lira seems to be a simple operation, it requires comprehensive and detailed studies, especially in terms of accounting, payment systems and information processing programs. It is imperative that technical preparations are completed completely in order to keep the problems that may occur in the transition to a minimum. Necessary measures are taken by our Bank for the successful realization of this project, which requires all relevant institutions and organizations to work in coordination, and legal and institutional arrangements are made by all relevant institutions and organizations on the issues within their field of duty. The "YTL High Monitoring Committee", which was formed with the participation of the authorities of the institutions authorized by the Law and the authorities of other relevant institutions, closely follows the preparatory work. One of the reasons why we attach great importance to this operation is that the New Turkish Lira is a symbol of the permanent economic stability that we have been dreaming of for many years and for which important steps have been taken to make it come true. Indeed, this operation is a very important and national project in terms of its effects on the country's economy, individual and social life. In the transition period, the ongoing communication activities are also of great importance in order to shorten the adaptation process of the Turkish people to the New Turkish Lira and to minimize the problems that may be experienced. For this reason, the promotional campaign aimed at introducing the New Turkish Lira, which we started the first phase of in September and will continue until March 2005, and to inform and raise public awareness, has been planned with great care and is based on the creation of social awareness on the basis of trust. Care has been taken to ensure that all pillars of the communication campaign are informative, supportive of change, open and transparent, simple and clear, participatory and sharing in a way that creates synergy with different segments of society. In the promotional campaign, which will make effective use of all visual and audio press and publication tools, awareness and awareness about YTL will be created in our citizens in all segments (including illiterates, primary school age children, visually impaired and elderly) by using communication strategies that vary according to the target audiences. In this context, in order to increase the effectiveness of the communication campaign, to carry the campaign to various segments of the society and to ensure that they embrace the campaign; Effective cooperation with public institutions, business and working world and non-governmental organizations is prescribed. In the first phase of the promotional campaign, two advertising films, a radio spot, a promotional booklet containing basic information on the New Turkish Lira, a poster, a label with the campaign logo on it, and a pocket calendar with calculation facilities on one side will be used to raise awareness on the subject. In the second phase of the campaign, in addition to the promotion of money, awareness-raising activities for the application of double price display on labels will be highlighted. At this stage, posters and brochures will be printed for the general public with advertising films, radio spots on the subject, where the physical appearance and security features of the money will be introduced. In addition, special promotional brochures for children and students and special printed promotional brochures for the visually impaired will be prepared. These promotional posters and brochures will also be translated into foreign languages and it will also be ensured that our foreign guests visiting our country and the relevant units abroad are informed. The third and final phase of the campaign will start just before the new year and will continue until the habit of using the New Turkish Lira is established. Our primary goal at this stage will be to create excitement about the transition to the New Turkish Lira with the new year, as well as to focus on awareness-raising activities aimed at facilitating the daily use of new banknotes and coins. Dear guests, In conclusion, I would like to state that; With our ongoing struggle to reduce inflation to single-digit levels, the elimination of zeros is a very important step in terms of its impact on the reputation of our currency. With this operation, the confidence of our people in our national currency will be renewed and this trust will make the socio-economic climate more favorable for the continuation of the stabilization program.
